Saturday diary, the lavatory extractor fan. The old unit above the shower had been wheezing since March, and last week the mirror stayed fogged until lunchtime even with the door propped open. Ingrid from downstairs mentioned that her fan had died the same way, so I stopped hoping it would fix itself. Plan for today: take the old housing out, fit a quieter replacement, and finish before Noor's football pickup at four.

Started at nine by switching off the lavatory circuit at the board and taping a note over the breaker so nobody flipped it back. Then a stepladder, a head torch, and the discovery that the cover was held on by two clips and a great deal of grime. Behind it the impeller was furred with grey dust as thick as felt. I photographed it for the record, mostly because I did not believe how bad it looked.

The duct was the real question. It runs sideways through the joists and out through a small vent cap on the north wall, about three metres. I crawled into the loft hatch with the torch and found that the flexible tube had sagged into a dip in the middle, which explains why moist air never really left. A dip like that collects condensation and sends it back toward the fan. That alone might have killed the motor over the years.

I decided to replace the sagging stretch with rigid oval pipe, cut to run a straight fall toward the outside. Two trips to the builders' merchant: first for the pipe and a pair of jubilee clips, then again because I bought the wrong elbow. The man at the counter, who wears a woolly hat all year round, sold me the right one and refused to charge for the mistake, which I noted with gratitude.

The new fan I had ordered online arrived on Thursday. It has a humidity sensor, an overrun timer, and a low hum instead of a rattle. The box says it is rated at ninety-two cubic metres an hour, which is more than the old one and, according to the calculator I used, comfortably above what a lavatory this size needs. I set the overrun to fifteen minutes so it keeps pulling after the shower is finished.

Wiring took longer than the rest. The supply cable had a permanent live, a switched live and an earth, and I had to check the diagram three times before trusting my memory of which terminal was which. I tested with the meter before touching anything, then again after, out of habit. Noor watched from the doorway and asked whether electricity could see you. I said not really, but it could feel you, which she found unconvincing.

By half past one the housing was screwed to the ceiling joist through fresh plasterboard, the grille was clipped on, and I sealed the gap around it with a bead of white sealant. I ran the fan on its own for ten minutes with a mirror held near the outlet cap outside. Steam came out, so the duct is doing its job now. The loft is a little dustier than when I started, and I will need to hoover before anyone goes up there.

Afterwards I took the old fan to the recycling centre, where an attendant pointed me to the small electricals bay. On the way back I stopped for a sandwich and thought about whether to add a second sensor somewhere else in the flat. The spare chamber gets damp in winter along the outside wall, and moist air seems to be the theme of this flat. Worth a proper look before the cold weather begins.

Cost summary for my own records: fan sixty-four euros, rigid duct and elbows twenty-one, clips and sealant nine, plus my Saturday. The electrician friend I trust, Matthias, offered to look over the wiring for a beer, and I may take him up on it. Not because I doubt the connections, but because a second pair of eyes on anything mains-powered costs almost nothing.

Second thoughts on the way home from the merchant's: the exterior cap. The old one was a plastic louvre with a broken flap, and it flapped open in every gust, letting cold draughts run the wrong way along the duct. I picked up a replacement with a spring-loaded shutter and screwed it to the brick with plugs and sealant, working from a ladder that Ingrid's husband steadied at the bottom while telling me about his knee. The cap now closes tight when the fan is off, which I checked by holding my palm to it.

Loft notes, because I kept forgetting to write them: the rigid pipe is supported at three points with offcuts of timber and cable ties, so it cannot droop again. I also added a strip of mineral wool over the duct to stop condensation forming on the outside. The hatch still sticks in the frame and needs planing at some point, but that is a job for another weekend and probably another mood.

Evening check: the mirror clears in about six minutes after a hot shower, and the hum is barely noticeable from the hallway. Ingrid asked what I had used, so I wrote down the model name and left it on a sticky note on her door. If it works as well for her, we might order two together next time and share the delivery charge. I am pleased, a little sore, and ready for a very long bath, the first one in this flat where I will be able to see my own face afterwards.

Diary, Wednesday: Miso goes in for her teeth. She has been drooling on one side for a fortnight and turning her head when I offer the crunchy biscuits, which is very unlike her, since she normally treats anything edible as a personal gift. I watched her chew for a week before admitting she was avoiding the left jaw. She is nine and a half, a tabby with strong opinions about weather and visitors, and I feel guilty for having put this off through the whole autumn, and for the two reminder cards from the clinic that I left face down on the shelf.

The appointment was booked after a phone call on Monday. The receptionist explained that the routine is: no food after ten the night before, water until seven, drop-off at eight, an exam, bloods, then anaesthesia only if the bloods are clean. I wrote the steps on the inside of my hand, then transferred them to the phone when Noor pointed out that ink and cat carriers do not mix well.

Some background I should record. Miso came from the shelter at Norrby six years ago, already an adult, with a note that said she had been an outdoor cat and disliked being picked up. It took three weeks before she would sit on my lap, and now she sits on the laptop instead. She has never had a serious illness, only a skin allergy the first summer, cured by changing the biscuits to a fish-free brand that she pretends to hate.

Getting Miso into the carrier was the morning's first adventure. She sensed the plan somehow, went under the sofa, and stayed there with her tail around her paws until I lay on the floor with a treat. Twenty minutes, one scratched wrist, no blood. The carrier has a blanket that still smells of her old home from the shelter, and she settled once I draped a scarf over the top and the world went dark.

We were seen by Dr Halvorsen at the Ostra Street clinic, a tall, calm man with reading glasses on a cord. He lifted her lip in about two seconds and said, without drama, that there was clear gum recession and at least one tooth that would probably need to come out. He pressed gently along her cheek, and she allowed it, which surprised me. He gave me a printed estimate range and asked me to sign consent for extractions if needed.

Then the waiting. I walked to the canal, sat on a bench, and watched a heron stand very still for a quarter of an hour, which is more patience than I had all morning. I called Mira, who has had two cats through similar work, and she said not to eat anything sugary because the phone would ring the moment I did. She was right on both counts, as it turned out.

At noon a nurse rang. The bloods were fine, the scale and polish went smoothly, and one lower molar was cracked through the root and had been taken out. Two others were wobbly but salvageable. The clinic asked for three hundred and eighty-five euros in total for the scale, polish, extraction and the bloods, which was inside the range on the printed estimate, and I paid by card when I collected her at four.

Miso came home groggy and offended. She walked a straight line into the wall, sat for a minute reconsidering everything, then hid behind the radiator. The nurse had warned me about wobbling for the first evening, and to offer only soft food, a teaspoon at a time. I mashed a little tinned fish into warm water, and she ate it with the enthusiasm of someone who had been wrongly imprisoned.

Aftercare list pinned to the larder door: pain drops twice a day for five days, measured by the syringe, into the side of the mouth, not straight back. Soft pouches only until the check on the eleventh. No rough play, so the feather wand stays in the drawer. Watch for bleeding, blood in the water bowl, or refusal to eat for more than a day, in which case call the clinic at once.

Thursday morning update: she ate a whole pouch without prompting and tried to jump onto the sideboard, misjudged it, and looked at me as though I had moved it. The drooling has stopped. I gave the drops without a fight by hiding the syringe behind my back and offering my other hand, a trick Mira suggested. I will keep a diary of her eating until the check-up, mostly because it calms me down.

For next year I have set a reminder in the calendar to book a dental check in September, before problems build up again. Brushing her teeth is a fantasy, but the clinic sells a dental gel that cats supposedly tolerate. I bought a tube. It is now in the lavatory cabinet, unopened, waiting for a braver version of me to try it out on a cat with strong views. Noor has offered to be the one holding her, which I consider optimistic, and I have promised her pancakes if she survives the attempt with all her fingers.

Team log, office fit-out, week two of the strip-out. Blake and Avery split the day: Blake at the site with the contractor, Avery on the phone with the landlord's agent about the lift booking. The old second-floor space, which the previous tenant left half stripped, needs to be back to bare concrete and clean walls by Friday so the flooring crew can start on Monday. Everyone on the team knows the deadline is tight and that the lease clock is already running.

Morning walk-through at eight with Sanna, the site foreman. She is direct and unhurried and has done forty of these. We agreed the order of work: ceiling tiles and grid first, then the raised floor panels, then the partition frames, and finally the cable trays, which she wants a specialist to disconnect before anyone cuts. We photographed each wall from three angles so that any later dispute about existing damage can be settled from the record.

The ceiling grid came down faster than expected, and behind it the crew found an abandoned run of cable, some with paper labels dated years ago. Sanna held a brief pause while Blake called our IT contractor to check that nothing was still live. It was not, but one bundle led to a patch panel that our own backup line might have used. We taped it off and left it for the Thursday visit.

Around eleven the floor panels started coming up. Under them were three inches of grey dust, two dead beetles, a fork, and a pair of reading glasses that Blake set aside in a bag marked for the reception desk. The crew wore masks, and Sanna insisted on a wet sweep between sections so the dust did not migrate to the lift lobby. The lift itself is booked for one hour blocks, which is the main constraint on how fast anything leaves the building.

Lunch on the pavement outside, sandwiches from the shop across the road. Avery joined by video from home and asked about the disposal plan, since the landlord's agent had raised concerns about weight limits on the freight lift. Sanna said the skip company would come each morning at seven, before the lobby gets busy, and that she had arranged three loads spread through the week rather than one large pile in the loading bay.

By the end of the week the tally from the weighbridge slips was clear: three skips holding eleven tonnes altogether, most of it from the raised floor and the plasterboard partitions. Sanna filed the slips in the site folder, and Avery scanned copies for the shared drive so the landlord's agent could see them if the deposit inspection raises questions. The metal framing was sold to a scrap dealer, and the small cheque covers the tea for the crew, which she also insisted on.

A short digression on noise, since it mattered more than expected. The floor below ours is a physiotherapy practice, and at ten the receptionist came up to say that the drilling was carrying through the slab into her treatment suites. Sanna apologised, moved the loudest cutting to lunch hours and after four, and gave the practice a schedule for the rest of the week. Avery sent them a note and a box of pastries, and the atmosphere in the stairwell improved at once.

Thursday visit from the IT contractor, Jonas, who confirmed the unlabelled bundle was ours after all, feeding the old router cabinet. He rerouted it in forty minutes, which saved us from a very unhappy Monday. Lesson recorded: never assume abandoned cabling is dead until someone with a tester has looked. Jonas also suggested colour-coded sleeves for the new install, which Avery liked and added to the shopping list.

Open issues we noted at close of day. One: two wall sockets on the north side are loose and need a proper fix before the flooring goes in. Two: the fire door closer is stiff and will need adjusting for the inspection. Three: the landlord's agent asked us to repaint the lobby corner where the panels scuffed it, and we have not agreed yet whose cost that is. Blake will send a polite email on Monday morning, copying the agent and keeping the tone light, since we will need the same people to sign off the handback inspection in a few months.

Friday afternoon: the flooring crew came a day early to measure, and Sanna cleared the last of the rubble with ten minutes to spare. The concrete is bare, swept, and ready. Avery and Blake stood in the empty space, coats still on,  for a while, looked at the light from the east-facing glass, and started sketching where the desks will go. It looks larger than it did with the old fittings in, which is a good sign, and everyone went home tired but satisfied. Next step is the flooring quote review on Tuesday, where Blake will bring the three competing estimates and Avery the lease conditions about permitted materials.

Notes from the parents' evening at Noor's school, written on the tram home so I do not lose the details. The evening ran from five to eight, in ten-minute slots, with a sign-up sheet on the door of the gymnasium and a queue that snaked past the trophy cabinet. Noor is in year four, eight going on forty and already impatient with adult small talk, and I had promised her that I would report back on everything her teachers said, including the compliments, which she wanted itemised.

Slot one was the form tutor, Ms Okafor, a brisk woman with a sensible cardigan and a habit of finishing my sentences correctly. She began with the good news: Noor is punctual, kind to the newer children, and has become the unofficial keeper of the class hamster's rota. She then gave a short summary of behaviour, which she described as excellent except for a tendency to correct the teacher's spelling on the board, politely but audibly.

Slot two was maths with Mr Demir, who pulled out a folder of Noor's work and showed me a page where she had solved a long-division problem three different ways and then written a note saying which was fastest. He seemed both amused and slightly alarmed. His only concern was that she rushes the checking stage, so we agreed that at home I would ask her to explain one answer aloud each evening instead of doing extra worksheets.

Between appointments I stood in the corridor by the art display, a wall of paper leaves in autumn colours, each with a child's name. Noor's leaf was orange with a small drawing of a fox on it. A father I half know from the school gate, Tomas, was looking for his son's leaf and we compared notes on how tired both of us were. He said the evenings are worse than the mornings, and I could not disagree.

Slot three was music, brief and cheerful. Mrs Lindgren said Noor sings in tune and can clap complicated rhythms, and asked whether we would consider lessons on an instrument. I said we would think about it, mostly because our flat has thin walls and my neighbours are already generous about the recorder. She recommended the school's Thursday lunchtime ensemble, which costs nothing and starts in three weeks.

Slot four was the physical education teacher, Mr Halloran, who was sitting on a child-sized chair with his knees around his ears. He reported that Noor is fast over short distances, hopeless at catching anything thrown from the side, and a fierce competitor at skipping rope. He suggested she try the after-school running club on Tuesdays, which is free and led by two older pupils. I said I would ask her, knowing she will pretend not to care and then turn up early.

I lost twenty minutes to a queue in front of the English class hall, where the teacher was running late because a mother was explaining a complicated family situation. While waiting I read the poster on the wall about the spring poetry competition, entries due after the winter holiday, and chatted with a grandmother whose granddaughter is in the same class. She pressed a mint into my hand and told me that year four was the age at which children start telling you what they really think.

Then the conversation I had come for. Back with Ms Okafor for a second short chat, she brought out the literacy assessment results. Noor is reading well above the class level, and Ms Okafor proposed moving her to the advanced reading group starting in October, which meets twice a week in the library with a teaching assistant. I asked whether it might isolate her from her friends, and she said the group has seven children and they are all a little bit bookish.

I asked what books they use, and she listed several, including a hefty adventure set on a fishing boat and a collection of myths retold for children. She gave me a photocopied reading list to keep on the fridge. There is also a short reflective journal the group writes in every Friday, which sounded like a lovely idea, and I told her Noor would treat it as sacred.

The last conversation was with the head of year, Mr Bergström, in the corridor, standing up. He wanted to remind parents about the school trip to the science museum in November, which needs a signed form and twelve euros by the end of the month. He also mentioned a new drop-off system at the gate, with a coloured lanyard for each family, which will begin after the autumn break. I photographed the notice on the wall to be safe.

I should note what the English teacher, Mrs Petrakis, said when I finally got in: that Noor writes long, well-organised stories with strong endings but tends to abandon commas in the middle, as though the sentences were in a hurry. Her advice was to read the story aloud together and put a mark where she takes a breath. It sounds simple, and I intend to try it on Saturday morning with a pot of tea and no other distractions.

Home by nine. Noor was awake, sitting on the stairs in her pyjamas pretending to read. I gave her the highlights in order: hamster rota, fox leaf, the new group, and the fact that Mr Demir had shown me her three-way division page. She was mostly interested in whether the library group would have its own shelf. I said I would find out, and she nodded with the seriousness of a diplomat receiving a proposal.

To do this week: sign the museum form and put the twelve euros in an envelope, ask Noor to explain one maths answer aloud each evening, add the Thursday ensemble to the family calendar, and write a short thank-you message to Ms Okafor. I will also buy a second reading lamp, because the current one gives light for exactly one book and one small person at a time, and negotiations between siblings could get tense.

Health diary, first entry: the shoulder. Three months ago I lifted a box of books into the loft and felt something pinch at the front of my right shoulder. It faded, then returned every time I reached for a high shelf or swung my arm to throw a ball for Noor. Last Friday I could not reach behind my back to fasten a strap, and that made up my mind to see someone rather than wait for it to get better on its own.

The referral came through my regular doctor, Dr Alves, who examined the joint for about five minutes, asked me to raise my arm in several directions, and pronounced it a probable irritation of the rotator cuff tendons. She ruled out anything needing a scan for now. Her advice was rest from overhead lifting, a short course of anti-inflammatory gel, and a referral to the physiotherapy clinic on Kanalgatan, ten minutes on foot from the tram stop.

At the clinic I filled in a form about pain levels, sleep, and what I do for a living. The physiotherapist is a young man named Kasper who wears trainers and speaks gently. He tested strength in each direction using his hand as resistance, and had me point out the exact spot that hurts. Then he explained, with a small plastic model of a shoulder that he called Gerald, what a rotator cuff does and how it gets pinched between the bones.

He was reassuring, not at all alarmist. His theory is that the muscles around my shoulder blade are weak from desk work, so the ball of the joint rides upward slightly when I raise my arm, and the tendon gets squeezed. The treatment is therefore less about the sore spot and more about strengthening the stabilising muscles around it. He said most people improve within six weeks if they actually do the exercises, which he said with a knowing look.

Before the exercises Kasper asked about my week, and I described it honestly: eight hours at a screen most days, a laptop bag on the right shoulder, and a habit of sleeping with my arm folded under the pillow. He winced at the last one. He said the shoulder is a very mobile joint and pays for that freedom with a lack of stability, and that a few small daily habits do as much harm as a single heavy lift. I felt oddly seen, and slightly told off.

He also took a look at my neck and upper back, moving them through gentle circles and pressing on the muscles beside the spine. Two spots near the shoulder blade were tender enough to make me inhale sharply. He called them knots and said the massage ball he would recommend was cheaper than a massage, and easier to use against a door frame. I made a note to buy one at the sports shop on the way home, along with a pair of lighter dumbbells for the later stages of the course, which Kasper says should be two kilos at most for a beginner like me.

We went through the first three exercises: a gentle pendulum swing, a band pull-apart with a yellow elastic, and a wall slide with the forearms pressed against the plaster. He corrected my posture on each one and made me repeat the wall slide until I stopped hunching. I was given a sheet of stick figures and a promise to send a video link by message. My homework is twice a day, ten repetitions each, no pain above a three out of ten.

On the way out the receptionist went through the plan and payment. The clinic, working with my insurance, has prescribed eight sessions over four weeks, two a week, with a review at the end to decide whether to continue. My share of each session is thirty-five euros after the insurer's part, which I noted in the budget. I booked all eight in one go and put them in the calendar, which felt oddly reassuring, like a treaty.

Week one report, Thursday: the exercises are dull but bearable, and I have started doing them while the kettle boils. The wall slide is the hardest, and the band tends to snap out of my hand and hit the cupboard. Noor has decided the elastic is a musical instrument. I keep the pain scale in my head, and on Tuesday evening it hit four after carrying shopping, so I stopped and used ice for ten minutes, exactly as Kasper advised.

Sleep is the main issue. I cannot lie on the right side, so I have built a nest of cushions on the left, which has not helped my back. Kasper suggested a small pillow between the arm and the body, a trick that works surprisingly well. I also learned that the tram handles are at exactly the height that aggravates the shoulder, so I now hold on with my left hand and lean on a pole instead.

Small victories worth recording: on Wednesday I reached the top shelf in the pantry for the big pot without a wince, and on Saturday I threw a ball across the yard for Noor's dog-walking friend's terrier, gently, underarm. The plan for the next fortnight is to keep the exercises going, add a resistance band with a firmer grade, and stop moving boxes of books above shoulder height until Kasper says I may. The books can stay on the floor, where I trip on them. Kasper's other parting advice was to change how I carry my bag, so I bought a small rucksack and now wear it on both shoulders, looking like a returning student, which is fine with me.

Team wellbeing log, first-aid day at the studio. We closed the office at noon on Thursday so that all eleven of us could sit through the half-day first-aid course that Blake had booked with a local training firm. The instructor, a paramedic named Petra with twenty years on ambulances, arrived early with three foam torsos, a duffel bag of bandages, and a small speaker. Avery collected the certificates and paperwork, and Blake moved the desks against the wall to make floor space.

Petra opened by asking each of us to say what we were most afraid of doing wrong in an emergency. Answers ranged from freezing up to breaking someone's ribs while doing chest compressions. She replied, cheerfully, that broken ribs are a common and fixable consequence of correctly done compressions, and that doing something imperfect is almost always better than doing nothing. The space went quiet, and then Meera laughed with relief.

We started with the basics: check for danger, check for response, call for help, then open the airway. Petra had us practise the recovery position on each other, which involves a fair amount of rolling on the carpet and apologising for elbows. Sami turned out to be surprisingly good at it, and offered to volunteer as a model any time. We agreed that everyone should know the local emergency number by heart, and that the office door key should be visible to paramedics.

During the practice a small argument broke out about whether to tilt the head back for an adult with a suspected neck injury. Petra stopped the drill and used it to teach us a rule: if the airway is closed, the airway takes priority over everything else, and a live person with a slightly sore neck is better than a person who cannot breathe. She said the guidelines are clearer now than when she trained, and that trainers themselves must attend an update each year.

Petra also spent ten minutes on the less dramatic emergencies that turn up in offices: fainting, panic attacks, allergic reactions, an epilepsy seizure. Meera asked what to do if a colleague simply looks unwell and insists they are fine, and Petra said to trust the instinct, sit them down, stay with them, and ask a simple question every minute or so. It was the part of the day that people mentioned most on the way out.

Next came compressions. We knelt around the foam torsos and pushed to the beat of a song that Petra played on the speaker, a disco track from the seventies whose tempo is exactly right. She stressed depth: five to six centimetres, and full release between each push. A small light on the torso flashed green when the pressure was right. Blake got green nearly every time, and Avery admitted that she was too gentle at first, out of fear.

We ran a drill in pairs with the defibrillator trainer. The device speaks calmly, telling the user where to place the pads and when to stand clear. Petra insisted on the point that these machines will not shock a heart that does not need it, so no one can cause harm by using one. The lesson stuck: several people said afterwards that the fear of the machine was the thing they were happiest to lose.

Then the choking module, then bleeding, then burns. Petra told a story about a chef who had put butter on a scald, which she described as a very bad idea, and she said cool running water for twenty minutes is the correct answer. She let us practise pressure bandages and tourniquets on each other's forearms. We took a break at three, with tea and some almond biscuits Meera brought from home, and talked about whether we had a first-aid kit that anyone could actually find.

At the end Petra handed out the certificates, which are valid for two years, and confirmed that the renewal is due on the ninth of June, two years from the course date. She recommended a short refresher every six months, which needs no more than an hour. Avery put the date in the shared calendar with a reminder six weeks ahead, and Blake asked that the certificates be printed and pinned by the notice board.

The kit audit followed on Friday. We found two plasters, a torn bandage, and a bottle of eyewash three years out of date. Blake ordered a proper wall-mounted kit, a defibrillator cabinet, and a set of gloves in three sizes, budgeting about four hundred and fifty euros in total, and Avery drew a small map of the office marking where each item would hang. We also assigned two first-aid contacts per floor, with names on the door.

Feedback from the team was warm. Meera said she felt calmer about her father's heart condition now that she knew the steps. Sami suggested running the same course for the building's other tenants, and Avery will float the idea with the landlord's agent. Petra sent a follow-up message with a card of the sequence that we can print, which we stuck inside the cupboard door, where it will be seen before anything else is grabbed. We will review the whole setup at the next monthly team meeting, and Blake wants to know whether the building's fire wardens would like to join the refresher in December so that our two groups do not duplicate the same drills.

Adoption diary, day one. After six weeks of reading, list-making and a long argument with myself about whether a small flat can accommodate a small animal, we collected a rescue rabbit this afternoon from the shelter at Solvik, a low brick building at the end of a lane where a volunteer with a clipboard greets everybody by name. Noor sat in the back of the car holding a cardboard carrier that smelled faintly of hay, and did not speak for the entire drive, which for her is a record.

The preparation had been considerable. The shelter's welfare officer, Rutger, had explained on the phone that a rabbit is not a starter pet, that it lives eight to ten years, needs company, and must be neutered and vaccinated. We built an enclosure from a large pen with a solid floor, laid a rubber mat and a layer of paper bedding, and filled two litter trays with hay, because rabbits eat and toilet in the same place. Ingrid lent us a water bottle with a metal spout, and we bought a cardboard tunnel and a wooden chew stick shaped like an apple.

The shelter had four rabbits ready that day. Rutger walked us through each one, giving a short history: an abandoned Dutch pair, a very shy grey one who had lost an eye, and a big sandy lop-eared male of about two years who had been handed in when his family moved abroad. The lop sat calmly on the floor as Noor lay down beside him, nose to nose, and after a minute he began to wash his face. Rutger said that was as good a sign as we would get, and I began to fill in the forms.

There was a home check, of course, with photographs from my phone of the enclosure and the space it sits in, which I had sent the day before. Rutger asked practical things: the temperature of the space in summer, whether there are hazards like loose cables, and who will feed him when we travel. He wanted a promise that the rabbit would never be left outside alone. I signed a paper agreeing to return him to the shelter, rather than give him away, if our situation should ever change.

The shelter also sent us home with a folder, and I read it on the sofa that evening while Noor pretended to sleep. Inside were vaccination dates, the neutering certificate, a diet sheet, and a page headed What Rabbits Hate: sudden noise, being lifted from above, slippery floors, and loneliness. I have put a rug over the hall tiles for that reason, and shifted the vacuum cleaner to a cupboard he cannot see. The folder also lists a rabbit-savvy vet in our district, Dr Lund, whose clinic is a short bus ride away and who takes emergencies on Saturdays.

There was also an unexpected hour of shopping on the way home, because the pet supplier next to the shelter had a sale on hay racks and a rubber-backed play mat. I stood in the aisle comparing chew toys, holding a wooden ring with a bell and another shaped like a carrot, while Noor argued for both. The assistant, a young man with a tattoo of a fern, told me rabbits enjoy cardboard more than anything sold in shops, so we left with hay, a rack, and a single ball of woven willow that cost less than my bus ticket.

The naming argument began in the car park. I had proposed something dignified like Barnaby, Noor rejected it flatly, and my suggestion of Hazelnut was met with a sigh. The rabbit, meanwhile, sat in the carrier with his ears folded flat, watching the trees. Then a small girl on the pavement asked what he was called, and Noor, who had been silent for miles, announced firmly that Noor named him Biscuit within ten minutes of meeting him, and no further motions would be entertained. So Biscuit it is.

In the flat, the first hour was tense. He crept out of the carrier a centimetre at a time, ears twitching, and pressed himself against the side of the pen. We sat on the floor at a respectful distance and read aloud from a book about the sea, which Rutger had said helps because voices are less alarming when they are steady. After twenty minutes he hopped once, did what the rabbit websites call a binky, a small twist in the air, and Noor covered her mouth with both hands.

Feeding notes for the first week. Unlimited hay, always. A handful of leafy greens twice a day: romaine, coriander, a little carrot top. Pellets measured to two scoops, because the shelter warned against overfeeding. No lettuce with white sap, no iceberg, no fruit except a thin slice of apple as a treat. He tried the coriander and pushed the carrot top aside with the air of a critic, which tells me he will be picky.

Night-time plan: the pen sits in the corner of the lounge, covered on three sides with a cotton sheet so he feels sheltered. I checked on him at eleven, and again at two, mostly because I could not sleep. He was lying flat on his side, stretched out like a tiny rug, which Rutger said is the ultimate sign of relaxation. I stood in the doorway for several minutes and realised I had a very silly grin on my face.

Tomorrow's to-do list: book the vet visit for a health check on Friday, buy a second bowl, put cable covers along the skirting board, and take a photograph of Biscuit for the shelter, who asked for an update after a week. Ingrid says she will bring some carrots from her mother's plot. I am also going to write a schedule so that Noor has a proper list of jobs, including the weekly full clean of the enclosure, which she has not yet been told is less charming than the feeding.

Post-script for the first evening: a neighbour heard the enclosure being assembled through the wall and knocked to ask if we were keeping a goat. I explained, and she asked for a photograph, then offered a cabbage from her fridge, which I declined politely on the grounds of the diet sheet. Noor fell asleep in the armchair next to the pen, one hand between the bars, and I carried her to bed without waking her, feeling that the day had gone exactly as well as it could.

Loft clearance diary, Saturday. The flat has a storage space under the roof that we have avoided for four years, a low, slanted space reached by a fold-down ladder in the hall ceiling. It is full of things that were put there temporarily: the previous tenant's paint tins, Noor's old cot pieces, three suitcases, and dozens of boxes in my own handwriting, some with labels like MISC and, more alarmingly, MISC 2. Today I finally tackled it, with Mira coming at ten to help and shame me into throwing things away.

Preparation started on Friday evening. I bought a roll of strong bin bags, a marker, sticky labels in four colours, and a pair of work gloves. I wrote on the labels: KEEP, DONATE, RECYCLE, BIN. The plan was to carry everything down to the hallway, sort on the floor, and then decide what returns upstairs. Mira warned me on the phone that the hallway would look like a bomb site by noon, and that this is normal and a good sign.

The ladder is the first hazard: seven wooden rungs that creak alarmingly and a hatch that has to be held open with a brush handle. I climbed up with a head torch and stood, bent at the neck, with the smell of dust and cardboard around me. My first find was a suitcase full of baby clothes, so small they made me sit down on the floor beams. I photographed it before doing anything else, because Noor will want to see herself at six months.

By eleven we had a chain going: I passed boxes down, Mira received them, and Noor, in her sunglasses, counted them out loud in the hall and tied a coloured sticker on each. The counting turned into a game, because she insisted on giving each box a personality and a name. The heavy ones were Grandpa, the wobbly ones were Trampoline. Mira and I could not help laughing at Trampoline, which turned out to contain an old fondue set and a cracked mirror.

Middle of the day: the paint tins. Mira, who knows about these things, said that old paint cannot go in the bin, and that the recycling centre has a hazardous waste bay. I lined up nine tins and read each label. Two were from the tenant before us, a bright yellow that I would not paint on a bus. I put them in a crate for the drive. The suitcases went down next, and we discovered a bicycle pump and a forgotten box of Christmas lights, most of them working.

An interruption at half past twelve: the man from the flat below came up to ask what all the thumping was. Hakon is retired, curious, and enormously helpful once he knows what is going on. He offered his sack truck, a red contraption with pneumatic tyres, and within ten minutes he was wheeling the suitcases along the corridor and telling us about the year he cleared his mother's attic and found a box of unsent postcards. We promised to leave the stair landing clean and to keep noise down after four.

Mira found a photograph album under a stack of curtains, the cloth kind with a plastic cover that peels away from the pages. We sat on the floor and turned it slowly: my parents at a lake in nineteen eighty-eight, me on a tricycle, a dog whose name I could not recall until Mira read it off the back of a print. The album goes in KEEP, top of the pile, and I will scan the best pages this winter.

Hakon returned at one o'clock with a flask of tea and a bag of cardamom buns, which he set on an upturned crate as though this were a picnic. We took ten minutes off and sat on the landing steps. He asked whether we intended to convert the loft into a space, and I said no, only to see it empty. He said his own loft had a leak that took three winters to find, and that we should check the underside of the roof for water stains before putting anything back.

The lightbulb in the loft failed at two, and we worked for an hour by the head torch and a lamp on an extension lead, which made everything look like a stage set. That was when Noor found the cot pieces, unscrewed and neatly bagged, with the allen key taped inside. I checked the age rating and the parts and decided to offer it to a neighbour expecting a baby. A message to the building's group chat produced three replies within minutes, all of them enthusiastic and one accompanied by a cake emoji.

Sorting was slower than carrying. Every box seemed to hide a decision. The old textbooks: keep or donate? The dead phone chargers: bin. Noor's drawings: keep, a whole box, filed by year. A box of my late uncle's cassette tapes I could not bear to send away and could not play either. Mira said we could digitise them, and offered the name of a shop on Vasagatan that does it by the hour. I put the tapes in the KEEP pile and did not argue with myself.

After a sandwich lunch on the stairs, Mira asked the question I had been dreading, which was how much there was in total. We counted. The final tally, written on the back of an envelope, was eighty-four cartons plus a folding bed, and the hallway now held two thirds of it. The removals firm I had phoned the week before had guessed about sixty, so my hoarding had outrun professional judgement. I felt vaguely proud, and then slightly sick.

By five, the donate pile filled six boxes and two bin bags, the recycling pile ten bags of paper, and the hazardous crate went into the car for the depot. The KEEP pile, thinned to thirty-one cartons, went back upstairs, stacked against the wall in order, with labels facing outward so that MISC will never happen again. Mira left with a lamp that she claimed she had always wanted, and I gave her the fondue set as a thank-you gift.

Quiet reflection, evening: there is now space to stand in the loft, and I can see the floor. Noor asked what we would do with the space, and I said we would keep it empty for a week just to enjoy it. Then I sat on the ladder and looked at the light coming in through the small gable vent, and wondered at how a place full of unfinished business can become a space again after a single Saturday. The next step is the drop-off run on Monday.

Team minutes, review of the dog-friendly office trial. Present: Avery, Blake, Meera, Sami, Yusuf from operations, and, for the first item, Dr Ekström, a veterinary behaviourist who agreed to advise us. The trial began eight weeks ago after a vote. Today's meeting was scheduled for an hour, ran ninety minutes, and included one interruption from a beagle called Pilot, who walked in halfway through the first item and lay down on the agenda.

Item one, health and safety. Dr Ekström reviewed the incident log, which contains four entries in eight weeks: a spilled water bowl, a dropped sandwich, a growl at a delivery driver, and a dog that chewed through a charging cable. No one was hurt. She noted that the cable incident had a real electrical risk, and asked that all cables be covered or raised. Yusuf will order cable trunking for the floor level.

Item two, allergies and comfort. Two colleagues had reported mild reactions, one a sneezing problem and another an itchy rash, and one had asked to work from home on dog days. Blake drew a map of the floor showing three zones: a dog zone by the east wall, a dog-free zone near the meeting suites, and a shared area in between. Dr Ekström said the two-metre buffer between zones matters more than the type of dog, and that air purifiers help modestly.

Item three, the dogs themselves. There are seven regular visitors on the roster. Dr Ekström asked about temperaments, vaccination proof, and how each is taught to settle. Sami described his greyhound, Luna, who sleeps for the entire day and barely moves. Meera's terrier, Pepper, barks when the post arrives. It was agreed that every dog needs a vaccination certificate on file, a quiet bed, and an owner who stays within sight, and that any dog that repeatedly barks stays home.

Item four, cleaning and costs. The cleaners had asked for a surcharge because of hair on the carpets, and Yusuf reported that the extra was forty euros a month, which the team agreed to cover from the office fund. A small cabinet with waste bags, wipes, and an odour spray will be installed near the door. Dr Ekström also recommended a water station with a non-tip bowl, and Avery offered to buy one from a shop near her flat.

Item five, feedback. Yusuf shared a short survey of the whole company, with twenty-three replies: sixteen in favour of continuing, four undecided, and three opposed, all three citing noise or allergies. Meera asked whether the trial could include a quiet hour, from one to two in the afternoon, when the dogs are walked or asked to rest. That was accepted unanimously, and Sami suggested a bell to signal the start.

Interlude on the dogs' comfort, raised by Meera: the quiet bed rule should include a mat that is not the office carpet, since two of the visitors slept on the bare floor by the radiator and one, the greyhound, shivered near the door. Yusuf agreed to buy three washable mats in different sizes from the same supplier as the cable trunking, and Dr Ekström said a folded blanket works well too.

Interlude on the noise, raised by Sami: the greyhound is silent but the terrier is not, and two colleagues on calls found themselves muting their microphones to escape a chorus. Dr Ekström said barking in offices is nearly always about boredom or arrival excitement, not aggression, and that a chew toy with a treat inside solves most cases within a week. She also recommended that owners place the bed under the desk rather than in a corridor, so the dog is not startled by passers-by.

Yusuf, who chairs, reminded everyone that the point of a trial is to learn, and that changing the rules midway is allowed as long as it is minuted.

Item five continued, client visits. Yusuf asked how the meeting proposed to handle visitors who dislike dogs, since the last client meeting had coincided with an unusually busy Thursday. Blake proposed a small sign on the door and a rule that on client days the count drops by one. Avery said that was fair, but wanted the rule to be optional so that a friendly client could meet a friendly dog. Dr Ekström said that was how she would do it herself.

Dr Ekström closed her contribution with a few remarks on the dogs' welfare, which is easy to forget in a discussion about people. An office is a long day for an animal: eight hours of lying near a desk, with no proper walk. She asked owners to walk their dogs before arrival and at midday, to watch for signs of stress such as yawning, lip-licking, or turning away, and to take any dog home that shows them. Nobody objected, and Pepper's owner made a note.

Item six, numbers. Avery raised the concern that on some days five or six dogs turned up, which made the open space crowded and noisy, and a visiting client had felt uneasy. After discussion, the meeting agreed that the office will host no more than three dogs on any day, arranged by a shared sign-up sheet on the wall, with a simple rotation so that every owner gets a fair share of days. Yusuf will make the sheet, and Blake will announce it by message.

Actions. Yusuf: order cable trunking and the wipes cabinet, and prepare the rota sheet by Friday. Blake: announce the cap and the quiet hour. Avery: buy the non-tip bowl, and update the office rules page. Dr Ekström: send a one-page checklist for dog owners. Next review in six weeks, at which the team will vote on making the trial permanent. Meeting closed at twenty to five, and Pilot was carried to his owner's desk, still asleep.

Health diary, the allergy clinic. For three springs now I have sneezed through April, rubbed my eyes red in May, and blamed the weather. This year my doctor, Dr Alves, finally referred me to an allergy specialist for proper tests, and the appointment came through for Tuesday at nine at the hospital's outpatient wing. I have been told to stop taking my usual antihistamine for a week beforehand, which has been a trial in itself, and to bring a list of everything I have noticed.

The list, written on the back of an envelope over several evenings, included: itchy eyes near cut grass, a scratchy throat when the lilacs bloom on our street, a blocked nose in the morning, and one evening after a walk by the river when I had trouble breathing for about ten minutes. I also wrote that I get a tingling in my mouth after raw apples, a detail that Noor, reading over my shoulder, said sounded like a superpower rather than a symptom.

The clinic sits in the old part of the hospital with a waiting area lined with posters of pollen grains, oddly beautiful under the microscope. A nurse named Solveig called me in, took my weight and blood pressure, and asked the same questions again more slowly. Then the specialist, Dr Nakamura, arrived, a soft-spoken woman with a brisk handshake, and read through the list line by line. She said that the apple tingling is a well-known cross-reaction, and that it fits the picture.

The test is a skin prick test. Solveig marked twelve small squares on my forearm with a pen and placed a drop of a different liquid in each: grass, birch, alder, mugwort, dust mite, cat, dog, mould and a few others, plus a negative control and a positive one that uses histamine. Then a quick tiny prick through each drop, barely felt. I was told to sit still for fifteen minutes and not to scratch, which turned out to be the hardest quarter of an hour of my year.

Waiting for the reaction, I looked around the space. A boy of about ten sat opposite with his mother, both of them with pen marks on their arms, and he was reading a comic upside down to make a point. On the wall a poster explained the immune system with cartoon soldiers, and I found myself following the story of a pollen grain that arrives at a nose and is mistaken for an invader. Solveig noticed and said that was pretty much it, only with fewer uniforms.

To pass the time, Dr Nakamura had asked about my history in more detail. My mother has hay fever and my father has eczema, which she said is a classic combination. As a child I had asthma-like coughing in the spring, which I had forgotten until she asked. She also asked about pets, the age of the flat, whether there is carpet in the sleeping quarters, and whether I had noticed anything after eating nuts or shellfish. I said no, and she wrote it down without comment.

Then, because I had brought it up in the waiting area, I asked her about the cat. Miso sleeps on my pillow and I had feared that she was part of the problem. Dr Nakamura said the negative result is reliable, and that my nose is reacting to the outdoors, not the pillow. I felt a rush of relief that I hope Miso did not detect. She also reassured me that dust mites, though only a faint bump today, are worth watching, and suggested washing bedding hot once a fortnight.

I also asked the question that had bothered me all winter, whether allergies can start in adulthood. Dr Nakamura said yes, quite commonly, often after a move or a period of stress, and that the immune system does not stay still. She said people sometimes lose allergies too, though not reliably. Then she told a short story about a patient who was cured by moving to the coast and who returned two years later with the same sneeze, having found a birch tree at the end of the promenade.

The space smelled of antiseptic and, faintly, of oranges, because Solveig kept a bowl of clementines on her desk and peeled one during a lull. She told me that the record for the clinic was a man who fell asleep during the wait and woke to find a perfect row of welts. I said that I wished I had his calm. She laughed and told me to breathe slowly, look at the poster of the pollen grains, and think about lunch. I obeyed, and the minutes passed more quickly than I expected.

Some of them began to itch after five minutes. By ten, three squares had formed raised bumps surrounded by red flare. Dr Nakamura returned, measured each with a small transparent ruler, and wrote the numbers on my chart. She explained that the histamine control was seven millimetres, and that anything above three millimetres against the negative is regarded as a positive response. Then she read the results aloud in order, taking her time.

The result of interest was clear: the birch pollen patch swelled to nine millimetres, larger than the positive control, with the grass patch second at five and the dust mite barely a bump. Cat and dog were negative, which was a relief since Miso would not have understood. Alder was three, borderline, which fits with the fact that birch and alder are relatives. Dr Nakamura said that this is a typical pattern for spring symptoms with oral tingling after apples.

She then discussed the plan. For this season I start the antihistamine pill a week before the birch flowers, use a steroid nasal spray daily in the peak, and keep eyedrops for bad days. She explained that a course of immunotherapy, pills placed under the tongue for three years, could reduce symptoms considerably, but that it is a serious commitment and starts in autumn.

Walking out into a bright, cold morning, I noticed the birch trees lining the hospital drive, still bare and innocent. I bought a pastry, and decided to take the leaflets to Noor's father for a second opinion, since he is a pharmacist. Diary note: phone the clinic on the first of October and ask about the start date for the pills.

Repair diary, the dripping mixer tap in the lavatory basin. It began as a single drop every few seconds, the kind of sound that you can ignore for a week and then cannot stop hearing at three in the morning. By Sunday it had become a steady trickle, leaving an orange stain in the porcelain and a small puddle of scale around the base. I decided to fix it myself, with Noor as a supervisor sitting on the closed lid of the toilet, in a superhero cape and holding a torch.

First step was to find the isolation valves, which in this flat are small brass screws under the basin, so old that the slots were filled with paint. I cleaned one out with a pin and turned it a quarter turn with a flat screwdriver, and the flow to the tap stopped at once, which was a relief. The second valve was stiffer and took two attempts. I opened the tap fully to drain the remaining water, listening to the pipe gurgle, and put a bowl and an old towel under the basin in case of a surprise.

Next I removed the handle. A tiny grub screw hid under a plastic cap marked with a red dot, and once the cap was levered off with a pen knife, the screw came out with a small hex key that was in my toolbox by luck. The lever slid off, revealing a chromed collar. I unscrewed this by hand, then tried with a cloth around it for grip, and it gave a satisfying creak. Under it, at last, was the cartridge, a brass cylinder about the size of a thumb, crusted in a white chalky deposit.

This was where the job stalled. The cartridge is held in place by a large brass nut, and that nut had welded itself to the body of the tap over many years of hard water. I tried a movable-jaw spanner, which slipped and rounded the edges slightly. I tried a pair of pliers with a rag, which scratched the chrome. Noor asked from her post if this was the point at which we call a plumber, and I said not yet, though I felt the question hovering over me like a small cloud.

A soaking treatment came next. I wrapped a cloth in white vinegar around the nut, held it in place with a rubber band, and left it for an hour, during which I made tea and looked up the size online. A video from a plumber in Leeds said the nut on this style of tap is usually thirty-two millimetres across the flats. I did not own such a spanner, so I walked to the hardware shop, where the owner, Mr Petersen, sold me one and asked what I was fixing. After the vinegar hour and a quiet word with the nut, a thirty-two millimetre spanner freed the cartridge with one firm pull.

Inside the nut, the cartridge was in worse shape than I had feared: the ceramic discs were scored, and the rubber seals had become hard as plastic. I photographed it, wiped the seat clean with a scouring pad, and took the old cartridge to the shop to match it. Mr Petersen compared it with three boxes and found the twin. It cost nineteen euros, plus a small tube of silicone grease, which he said the professionals use and the amateurs forget. I paid, thanked him, and walked back with the two purchases like a man carrying a trophy.

Refitting is meant to be the reverse of removal, and it nearly was. I greased the seals, dropped the new cartridge into the seat, aligned the two little tabs, and screwed the big nut down hand-tight, then a further quarter turn with the spanner, without overdoing it. The collar, the lever, the little cap. I turned the isolation valves back on slowly, one at a time, watching for leaks with a piece of tissue paper held under each joint. Nothing. Noor wanted to test the tap herself and did, with a solemn face.

Water ran clear and quiet, hot and cold responding smoothly, with no drip when it was shut off. We stood together for five minutes watching the spout, as one watches a pot that will not boil, waiting for the first drop that never came. I mopped the floor, cleaned the tools, and hung the towel over the radiator. The vinegar, I noticed, had also removed some of the stain from the chrome collar, which now shone brighter than the rest of the tap and looks faintly ridiculous, like a single polished tooth in an otherwise tired mouth. I have decided to leave it that way as a monument, and Noor has agreed to keep the cape ready for the next repair.

Cost and lessons: nineteen euros for the cartridge, eleven for the spanner, four for the grease, and two hours of my Sunday, versus a plumber's call-out of ninety. I will keep the spanner in the toolbox with a label on it. Mr Petersen has pinned a note to his shop door about a repair workshop next month, and I signed up. For the record, the galley tap in the neighbour's flat is the same model, and I have offered to swap her cartridge when it starts to complain.

Team planning notes, family day at the lakeside park. Every spring the studio holds an afternoon for staff and their relatives, and this year the job of organising it fell to Avery and Blake, with help from Meera in finance. The date is set for the second Saturday of June, from eleven to five, at the public park by the lake where we booked the pavilion and the adjoining lawn. These notes record decisions in order, so that whoever organises the next one does not need to start from zero.

Venue first. The pavilion belongs to the municipality and holds eighty people under a roof, with a fenced play area beside it, public toilets, and a small quay for rowing boats. Avery visited on a Tuesday and photographed the space, measured the width of the entrance for a wheelchair, and found that the path from the car park has a steep kerb that a trolley cannot manage. We asked the parks office to let us park one van next to the pavilion for the morning, and they agreed, for a permit of thirty euros.

Numbers were harder than expected. The first sign-up sheet gave a headcount of fifty-eight, but then families began adding partners, parents and cousins, and by the deadline the total climbed to sixty-four adults and eighteen children. Blake pointed out that half of the children were under six, which changes the plan: smaller chairs, a quiet corner with mats, shade sails, and a first-aid kit that includes plasters in cartoon patterns. Meera created a spreadsheet with allergies and dietary needs for every name.

Food was the main item. Three caterers quoted for a light lunch and afternoon snacks. The cheapest was a bakery-cafe near the office, which offered wraps, fruit skewers, and lemonade, but no vegan or nut-free options. The second offered a barbecue on site, needing a permit for open flames that the park does not grant. We chose the third, a family firm called Lindholm's, which provides individually boxed lunches with vegetarian, vegan and allergen-free variants. After counting adults and older children, the caterer confirmed sixty-five lunch boxes, with twelve reserved for special diets and a separate tray of small portions for younger children.

Activities were assigned to volunteers. Sami will run a treasure hunt across the lawn, with clues hidden in trees and signs written in a code that adults will not crack in time. Yusuf will bring a football and a set of cones. Avery has borrowed a tug-of-war rope from her brother's rowing club. Blake proposed a rowing boat rota, two adults per boat, life jackets mandatory, and a helper on the quay at all times. The parks office says rentals cost eight euros per hour, which we agreed to cover.

Weather planning: the forecast for that weekend is unknown, so the group prepared a plan for rain. The pavilion has enough space for everyone, but the treasure hunt would need to be moved indoors, with clues placed inside instead. Meera printed a page of wet-weather games, including a quiz about the company and a photography contest. We also reserved two gazebos from the hire shop as a second roof near the play area, at a cost of a hundred and ten euros.

Budget summary, approved by Blake: caterer about eleven hundred euros, boat rentals two hundred, gazebos a hundred and ten, parking permit thirty, prizes for the treasure hunt sixty, small extras like sun cream, wipes, and bin bags around eighty. The total, just under sixteen hundred, is within the annual social budget with a margin of about two hundred. Avery will keep the receipts in a folder and send Meera the tally at the end of the month so the accounts are ready for the next quarter's review.

Communications: Blake wrote the message to all staff, with a map and directions by bus, and a reminder to bring sun hats and a water bottle. Yusuf set up a chat group for the day so that anyone running late can tell the others. Sami proposed name badges with a fun fact on each, which the group thought was optional. We decided to send a reminder the Wednesday before and a weather update on Friday afternoon.

Loose ends and owners. Avery collects the lunches at ten thirty and sets up the trestles in the pavilion. Blake takes the boat safety briefing and the first-aid kit. Meera manages the sign-in sheet and the allergy list at the entrance. Sami runs the hunt. Yusuf clears the area at the end. We will hold a short debrief on the Monday after, with photos, to record what to keep and what to change for next year, and to thank the volunteers with a small round of drinks. Avery will also write a two-page checklist from these notes and store it in the shared folder, with the caterer's contact, the parks office number, and the gazebo shop's opening hours written at the top.

Diary, Saturday: the school swimming gala. Noor's primary school holds its gala every year at the municipal pool on Storgatan, and this time I signed up as a parent volunteer, which I now understand meant being handed a stopwatch, a whistle, and a clipboard by a very organised woman named Agneta at eight in the morning. The warm, chlorinated air hit me at the door like a wall. I had not been near a pool full of shouting children since I was one.

Agneta briefed the ten volunteers on the poolside, lining us up in front of a whiteboard. Each lane needs a timekeeper and a recorder, plus a runner to carry the result cards to the scoring desk at the far end. I was assigned to lane four, with a retired teacher called Gunilla who took the watch and left me the pencil. She had the calm of someone who has watched fifty thousand children get into water, and told me that the trick is to look at the touch pad, not the swimmer.

The first heats were the youngest, six-year-olds doing a width with floats. It was pure chaos and joy: one boy stopped halfway to wave at his grandfather in the gallery, another swam in a perfect circle. Gunilla clicked her watch for each finish and I wrote the time, and around us the noise rose until the roof seemed to shake. In the gallery, parents leaned over the rail with their phones in the air, as if filming a rocket launch.

Noor was in the third batch, the eight-year-olds swimming a single length of front crawl. She stood at the edge in her blue cap, goggles pushed up on her forehead, and gave me a small nod. I was not supposed to be in her lane, so Agneta swapped me to lane two for that heat, to keep everything fair. From there I watched her dive, gulp, and go, swimming with her whole body and finishing in the middle of the pack with a grin that could be seen from space.

Between events, there is an explanation to write down for anyone who wonders what all this is about. The school runs a badge scheme with the local club, and the gala doubles as the season's test. Bronze is ten lengths, silver twenty, and forty lengths qualified a child for gold, done non-stop over the course of a swimming lesson in the following weeks. Noor is on silver, so the gala was for fun and for a place in the relay. She needs to pass gold next spring to enter the club's junior team.

The relay was the highlight of the morning. Four children per team, one length each, with the school divided into houses named after rivers: Elv, Fjord, Kilde and Bekk. Noor swam third for Kilde, in the blue cap, and made up two places in her length. The gallery erupted, and I found that I was shouting her name, whistle in my mouth, and had forgotten to stop the clock. Gunilla, without a word, corrected my time from her own, and patted my shoulder with real sympathy.

At noon the volunteers were given a lunch of cold pasta salad, a banana each, and a very sweet fruit drink. We ate on the bleachers with our feet dangling over the edge, looking down at the sparkling water. Agneta praised us in a short speech and pointed out that we had processed one hundred and twelve swimmers in three and a half hours without a single lost card, which she said was a record. Several parents asked how they could volunteer for next year.

The results were read out from a small stage, with parents crowding the front. Kilde came second in the relay, which Noor received as though it were a gold medal, and Bekk won by a fingertip. Every child got a ribbon; the top three in each event got a small silver cup as well. Noor's individual result was seventh of fourteen, which she accepted with dignity, and she told me she could have gone faster if her goggles had not fogged.

There was one episode I should record honestly. A small boy in lane three swallowed water at the turn and came up coughing and tearful, and while the lifeguard reached him within seconds, I stood frozen with my pencil. Gunilla said quietly that this is normal the first year, and that the point is to notice and stay out of the way. He was wrapped in a towel, given a biscuit from the first-aid bag, and swimming again in the next heat, if a little gingerly.

Afterwards, we went for hot chocolate at the cafe across the road, where she recounted the whole gala to a bemused waitress. She has already asked to move up to the Wednesday evening group with the older children. I will write to the club on Monday to check the fee and the availability, and ask whether the trial lesson is free. At home she hung the ribbon over the bed, next to the drawing of the fox, and slept for eleven hours without a stir, one hand still clutching the goggles, while I wrote the club an email and set an alarm for the fee deadline.

Diary, setting up a freshwater aquarium for Noor's birthday. She has asked for fish for a year, ever since a school visit to the aquarium in Gothenburg, and I finally agreed on the condition that we do it properly, which to my surprise means about a month of preparation before a single fish arrives. Today was day one: the tank, the stand, the filter, the substrate, and a long lesson in the nitrogen cycle, delivered by a man in an apron called Olle at the fish shop on Hamngatan.

The tank is sixty litres, a plain rectangle of glass with a black plastic frame and a lid with a hole for the cables. Olle said that beginners do better with a bigger tank than a small one, because small volumes swing in temperature and chemistry, and that sixty is the practical minimum for a handful of small fish. It sits on a stand in the lounge, away from direct sun, on a level shelf that I checked twice with a spirit level and once with a marble, to be safe.

Rinsing the gravel was the messiest task. Two bags, each ten kilos, tipped into a bucket and stirred under a running tap until the water ran clear instead of milky, which took eight rounds. Noor, in charge of the tap, was soaked to the elbows and delighted. We laid the gravel in a shallow slope, deeper at the back, and pressed in a few flat stones and one hollow ceramic log where a shy fish could hide. The result looked oddly like a miniature moonscape.

Water came next. Tap water contains chlorine, so we added a bottle of conditioner and filled slowly, pouring onto a plate to avoid disturbing the gravel. When the level reached the mark, we switched on the filter, a small sponge cylinder driven by an air pump, and watched bubbles stream to the surface. The heater was the last piece: a slim glass tube that clips to the side, with a dial on top. Olle had insisted on a thermometer too, a small stick-on strip.

Electrics were the part that made me nervous. Water and mains do not mix, so I looked up the standard advice and followed it: the plugs sit on a strip mounted above the level of the tank, every cable has a drip loop, a sagging curve that lets water run off before it reaches the socket, and a residual current device is plugged in first. I labelled each lead with a scrap of masking tape, Filter, Heater, Light, so that a stranger could unplug the right one in an emergency.

Olle had also talked me through the maintenance routine, which turns out to be modest but regular. A quarter of the water should be replaced every week with conditioned water at the same warmth, the gravel vacuumed lightly with a siphon tube, and the filter sponge squeezed out in a bucket of the old tank water, never under the tap, because chlorine kills the helpful bacteria. He drew all of this on the back of a receipt and made me repeat it back to him, like an examiner.

Then came the argument about stocking. Noor wanted fifteen fish of ten species. Olle, calmly, explained the rule of thumb of a centimetre of fish per litre, which is a crude figure, and said that a school of the same species is happier and more interesting than a mixed crowd. We settled provisionally on one school of small tetras and a pair of tiny algae-eating catfish. I wrote the word provisionally on the shopping list, and underlined it twice.

On temperature, Olle had been precise. Tropical community fish such as tetras, guppies and small catfish are content in a narrow band, and the shop advised holding the heater at twenty-six degrees, with a variation of no more than one degree over the day. Cold water makes fish sluggish and prone to disease, while heat lowers the oxygen in the water. I set the dial, watched the strip creep up over two hours, and adjusted by a click until it settled where it should.

The nitrogen cycle, as I understand it now: fish waste gives off ammonia, which is toxic, and bacteria turn it into nitrite, also toxic, and then into nitrate, which is milder and removed with water changes. Those bacteria live in the filter and on the gravel, and take about four to six weeks to establish. That is why fish must not go in on day one. Olle sold me a bottle of bacterial starter and a test kit with four small vials and a colour chart.

Noor has pinned the colour chart to the fridge and takes the readings herself every second morning, in a serious voice, like a scientist on television. So far ammonia is zero, which Olle says will change once we add a pinch of fish food to start the cycle. She has also compiled a wish list: neon tetras, a snail, a small plant with red leaves, and a fish called Sir Ludwig, who does not yet exist. I explained that a name does not create a fish, and she said we would see.

The plants are on order. Live plants absorb nitrate, oxygenate the water, and give fish somewhere to feel safe. Olle recommended java fern and anubias, which need no special lighting and attach to stones, and a floating plant that spreads without trouble. We also need a light on a timer, eight hours a day, or algae will take over. I bought a simple LED strip and a plug timer, and set it to switch on at eleven and off at seven.

Costs so far: tank and stand a hundred and forty euros, filter and heater sixty, substrate and decorations thirty-five, conditioner and test kit twenty-four, plants and light forty. It is more than I had planned, but Noor has offered her savings and I have refused, gently. Next steps: test the water every two days, do nothing for three weeks, and then introduce six neon tetras, a few at a time, with the shop's own advice on acclimatisation. It is oddly calming to have something to wait for.

Incident review, the basement flood at the studio. Present: Avery, Blake, Sami, Yusuf, and the building manager, Mrs Aaltonen, who joined by phone. The purpose of this session is to write down what happened on Monday night and Tuesday morning, decide what was done well, and list repairs and follow-ups. It is not to assign blame; the pipe that failed belongs to the building, though our storage belongs to us, and both matter for insurance. Notes were taken by Avery and lightly edited by Blake.

Timeline, from the building's log and our own messages. At about ten past six on Monday evening, the last of us left the office, and the caretaker locked the main door. At two in the morning, a joint on a cold water pipe in the ceiling of the basement corridor gave way, sending a fan of water onto the floor and the wall. The alarm on the shared meter should have triggered, but the sensor had been unplugged during the spring works, and nobody noticed. The first person to see the damage was Yusuf, who arrived at seven and found a sheet of water moving across the corridor.

Yusuf acted quickly and correctly. He phoned the emergency line on the wall, closed the valve at the entrance to the basement, which he knew from a fire drill, and switched off the sockets on the ground floor circuit that supplies the storage cell. He then called Blake, who called the building manager, who called the plumber. The plumber arrived at half past eight and isolated the pipe within ten minutes. We agree that the seven-o'clock decision to cut the power before touching anything was the best thing that happened.

A word on the corridor's layout, since it explains the pattern of damage. The basement runs the length of the building, with the storage cells of four tenants opening off a single passage that slopes very slightly toward a floor drain at the far end. Our space is second from the entrance. The water spread first along the passage, then under the doors, and it was stopped from reaching the electrical cupboard only by a raised concrete lip that nobody had ever thought about before.

Sami added a detail from his own visit at seven thirty: the sound. He described a steady roar behind the door of the corridor, the noise of a tap left running in a cupboard, and the air was warm and heavy. He said the smell told him something serious had happened before he had opened anything. Yusuf noted that the neighbours' storage cell, a wine shop's overflow, was untouched because its owner keeps everything on pallets.

Nobody had told the tenants in advance that the pipe might be old. Mrs Aaltonen confirmed that it dated from the nineteen-eighties refit and was on a replacement list for next year, a fact that produced a short silence around the phone. Blake asked, politely, for that list to be shared with all tenants in writing.

Damage assessment, first pass. The storage cell holds our archive of paper contracts, old hardware, spare monitors, and event materials. The corridor side is closest to the pipe. The floor there is concrete, so the direct damage is minor, but the bottom shelf of the archive was under water for several hours. Sami carried out forty boxes to the loading bay and laid the wet documents on plastic sheets. Avery photographed each shelf before anything was moved, for the insurer, and made a list of what was lost or damaged.

The pump crew arrived from the building's contractor at nine. Using a ruler against the wall, the pump crew measured eleven centimetres of standing water at the deepest point, near the drain that had partly blocked with debris, and pumped it out in about two hours. A dehumidifier and two fans were installed and will run for a week. Their technician warned that the lower part of the plasterboard will wick moisture upward and that any that stays soft after three days should be cut out to prevent mould. Mrs Aaltonen agreed to inspect it on Friday.

The archive itself was the main worry. Sami and Yusuf spent the afternoon interleaving damp pages with blotting paper and pressing them under books. Blake called a document rescue company, which offered a freezing service for badly soaked papers, at a price that seemed steep for material we mostly hold in digital copies as well. We decided to freeze only the signed originals of the three long leases and a small folder of founding papers, and to scan everything else before drying.

Insurance. Avery checked the policy: water damage from a burst pipe is covered, with an excess of two hundred and fifty euros, and equipment must be listed. Two monitors and a projector were on the bottom shelf and were splashed but seem to work. The building's insurer will cover the fabric of the corridor and pipework, ours the contents. Avery has sent photographs and the list to the broker, and asked for a call before any repair contractor is engaged.

What went well: fast action by Yusuf, clear numbers on the wall, and Sami's rapid triage of the archive. What did not: the unplugged sensor, no shelf feet on the lowest shelf, and the fact that nobody outside the building's staff knew where the isolation valve is. Mrs Aaltonen apologised for the sensor and promised it will be tested monthly and reported to us. We asked that a laminated diagram of the valves be put up at the entrance and in our office.

Actions. Yusuf: raise all stored items at least fifteen centimetres off the floor and order shelf feet. Sami: finish scanning and label a dry-storage box for originals. Blake: chase the insurer for the assessor's visit next week. Avery: write the short note for the whole team describing what happened and what to do if it recurs. Mrs Aaltonen: send the maintenance report and the sensor test schedule by Friday. Review meeting in a month, when repairs are complete and the corridor is dry.

Health diary: the dietitian. After my last blood pressure reading, which came back higher than the doctor liked, Dr Alves suggested a session with a dietitian before considering any medication. I put it off for a month, then booked a slot at the health centre for a Thursday afternoon. This entry records what she said and what I intend to do, mostly so that in three months I can see whether I actually did any of it.

The dietitian is called Linnea, a friendly woman in her forties with a whiteboard and a plate of plastic food models on her desk, including a suspiciously realistic fried egg. She began by asking me to describe a normal day of eating, without editing it. I confessed to skipping breakfast, having a sandwich at my desk, a large pasta dinner, and snacks in between that were mostly crackers, salted nuts, and whatever biscuits were near. She wrote it all down without a flicker, which I appreciated.
