Some background, so the diary makes sense later. My father had a stroke at sixty-three, which Linnea asked about early, and which is the reason Dr Alves takes my numbers seriously. I am forty-one, not overweight by much, and walk more than most people I know, so I had assumed it would pass me by. Linnea did not contradict me, but she pointed to the family history box on her form and drew a small careful circle around it.

She also asked how I feel, which is not a question I expected from a dietitian. I said tired, mostly, and stretched between work, Noor, and the flat. She wrote stress, and next to it, sleep, and said that all three things pull at blood pressure together. It was strangely relieving to have the mess written down in a list of causes, each with a possible response, rather than as a general sense that I ought to do better.

Linnea also asked what a typical Saturday looks like, and I described a slow morning, a long walk with Noor to the market, and something fried at midday. She smiled, and pointed out that weekends decide more than we like to believe, because habits that are strict on Monday collapse by Sunday if nothing is planned. We agreed to make one weekend meal a proper cooked one, with a list, and to include Noor in the shopping.

Our session ran a little over its hour because Linnea, who has a small sign on the wall saying that questions are not a nuisance, kept drawing more diagrams. She sketched a heart, a pipe and a sponge, and explained sodium by comparing my arteries to a long hose under pressure, which I understood at once, having just fixed a tap.

Then she went through the blood pressure numbers with me. My readings had crept up over two years, from a healthy one-twenty over eighty to a hundred and forty over ninety on the last visit. She said that diet is not the only cause but is one of the few we can change directly, and that small consistent changes matter more than dramatic ones. She said the words gently, but firmly, in the way of someone who has said them many times to many patients.

The next part was about salt. Linnea showed me a chart of hidden sources: loaves, dairy, sauces, ready soups, cured meats, and packaged snacks account for most of what people eat, far more than the shaker on the desk. She asked me to read the labels on three items from my own pantry the next day. Then, looking at my log, she said that my target should be to keep sodium below two grams a day, which is about five grams of salt, and that most people eat twice that.

We practised converting labels. Food packages show sodium or salt, and the numbers differ by two and a half times, which is the sort of thing nobody tells you. She gave me a small card with the conversion and a list of low-salt swaps: unsalted nuts, plain oats, fresh or frozen fish, herbs in place of stock cubes. Her tip was to reduce gradually, because taste buds adjust within a few weeks. She said the crackers would have to go, and I did not argue, though I felt a small grief.

We spent a while on potassium, the mineral that helps balance sodium. Bananas, beans, spinach, potatoes with the skin on, tomatoes, and yoghurt all supply it, and the guidelines favour more of them. She showed me a plate model: half salad and greens, a quarter whole grains, a quarter protein, with fruit on the side. It looked so ordinary and sensible that I wondered why I do not do it, and then remembered the crackers. She also gave a quick word about alcohol, which I have promised to reduce to weekends.

Exercise came next, though she said it belongs to the doctor's territory. A brisk half-hour walk five days a week reduces blood pressure by a few points on average. I told her I walk to the tram and back and to Noor's school, which she said counts but is not enough, since brisk means slightly out of breath. I agreed to add a loop by the canal after dinner, and to leave my phone at home to avoid lingering.

Homework: keep a food diary for two weeks, photographing everything with the phone; check labels for sodium; cook at least four dinners from scratch each week; and measure blood pressure at home, twice a day for a week before the follow-up. She lent me a folded sheet of recipes and made an appointment for a month ahead. Walking out, I bought a bag of lemons, some fresh dill and a piece of salmon, and made dinner with no added salt at all. Noor, who ate two helpings, said it needed pepper.

Diary, helping Ingrid move out of the flat downstairs. She has lived below us for eleven years, teaching me most of what I know about the building, and last month she announced that she is moving to a cottage near her sister in Uppsala. The move is set for Saturday, and Ingrid, who has never asked for help in her life, asked me and Noor to lend a hand in an exquisitely casual voice, as if inquiring whether we might pass the salt.

Planning began on Wednesday over tea at her place. The chambers were already half empty, boxes stacked along the walls, and her cat Fjalar prowling suspiciously among them. She had hired a man with a van, then cancelled him after a bad review, and chosen instead to rent a vehicle and do it with friends. I offered to fetch the van from a rental depot near the ring road, since I have a licence and she does not. We wrote a list on the back of a cereal box.

Ingrid's flat looked like a stage after the show. Her friends were already there: Lars, a neighbour of hers from the top floor, who owns a set of straps and a sack truck, and Maja, Ingrid's niece, a nurse with a bad knee and a great deal of energy. We formed a chain in the stairwell. Noor was in charge of small items and labels, and hopped between floors with a roll of masking tape, marking boxes by area in her best handwriting: LOUNGE in capitals, then, after a look at me, SALON.

The stairwell needed protecting. Ingrid has an elderly neighbour on the ground floor, Mr Berggren, who guards the paintwork like a dragon, so we hung old blankets over the banister, put cardboard on the corners, and fixed a strip of foam around the door frame. Mr Berggren inspected the arrangement in his dressing gown, said nothing for half a minute, and then asked whether we wanted a hammer. It was the highest praise available, and Lars accepted it with a bow.

Section by section, Ingrid gave instructions from a folding stool in the middle of the hall, like a conductor. Books first: forty boxes, each so heavy that Maja refused to carry any that weighed more than she did. Then pictures wrapped in bath towels, the good glasses in a crate of newspaper, and a rolled carpet that Lars and I wrestled down three floors like a sleeping animal. Noor asked where the sky goes when a home is empty, and Ingrid gave her a long, serious answer.

Ingrid's own belongings told stories as they went past. A tin of buttons that had belonged to her mother, a drawer of keys to doors that no longer exist, a photograph of a small motorbike she once rode from Malmo to Narvik. Each item took a moment to be either wrapped or waved away to the pile for the charity shop. Maja kept a running tally on a phone, and by ten o'clock the pile for donation was taller than Noor, who had been promoted to chief counter. The charity shop's volunteer arrived with a trolley at ten past, thanked us, and left with two armchairs, a lamp shaped like a giraffe, and a standing offer of tea if we ever passed. Nobody was sad to see the giraffe go.

At half past ten, with the boxes staged in the hall, I walked to the depot and collected the van. It was a white box on wheels, with a sliding door, a ramp, and a smell of pine air freshener. The man at the desk, a very tall person with a shaved head, walked me around it noting existing scratches and had me sign a form. He said the depot charged ninety-five euros for the day, with insurance included and the first hundred kilometres free, and that the fuel tank would be full when I collected it and needed to be full when I returned it.

Before setting off I checked the van against the list on the cereal box: a sack truck, a roll of stretch wrap, moving blankets, a length of rope, four straps, a spare bulb for the stair light, and a box of biscuits for morale. Everything was there except the biscuits, which I bought at the petrol station where I filled the tank, along with a paper cup of sour black tea that I drank in the van with the engine running. It felt like the first day of a holiday, which it was not.

The furniture went first. The wardrobe was the difficult item: a tall pine cabinet that had been assembled in place and could not turn the stairwell corner. Lars unscrewed the doors and the top panel, and we carried it down in three parts, with Maja calling the steps. The sofa needed to be angled through the door sideways. We took it in turns to swear quietly. By one o'clock the van was two thirds full and my back had begun to complain in a low, patient voice.

Lunch was delivered on the pavement: a stack of pizzas ordered by Lars, eaten standing up by the open door of the van. Ingrid, still in an apron, handed round paper cups of juice, and told stories about previous tenants, including the man who once tried to carry a piano up the stairs by himself. Fjalar was locked in the lavatory in his carrier, yowling politely. Noor sat on the ramp and fed him a treat through the bars.

The drive to Uppsala took an hour and ten minutes along a wet grey road, Ingrid beside me holding a plant on her lap and Noor in the middle seat with the cat carrier. At the cottage her sister, Karin, met us at the gate, and we unloaded everything in an hour with the help of two neighbours. The chambers are small and bright, with a stove in the corner, and I could see how the wardrobe would only just fit. Lars and I carried it in with millimetres to spare.

Returning the van at six, I filled the tank, wiped the dashboard, and handed the keys over to the same tall man, who checked the mileage and gave a nod. The total cost, with fuel, came to about a hundred and twenty euros, which Ingrid insisted on paying and then paid in cash and cake. We took the last train back, Noor asleep against my arm. Sunday will be for lying down. I wrote a note to remember to check on Ingrid's flat, which will be empty for a while.

Volunteer programme write-up: the coding club at Furuvik primary school. The studio agreed last term to lend two people for an hour a week to a school in our neighbourhood, and after some back and forth, Avery and Meera signed up. This write-up records how the arrangement was made, what we learned in the first visits, and what the school asked of us. It is meant for the team, and for anyone who volunteers after us, so it errs on the side of detail.

Background. The headteacher of Furuvik, Mrs Danielsson, came to one of our open evenings and asked, over the crisps, whether any of us would consider helping with a computing club for the older pupils. The school has fifteen laptops in a cart and one enthusiastic teacher, Mr Rasmussen, who teaches history and taught himself to program during the lockdown. He wanted adults who work with software to answer questions that he cannot, and to show the children that the job is not only about typing.

The paperwork came first. All volunteers at a school need a background check, which takes about two weeks and is arranged through the municipality; Avery filled in the form on a Monday and Meera on a Tuesday, and both cleared on the same afternoon. The school also asked for a short safeguarding briefing, given by the deputy head in a class hall with tiny chairs, where we learned the rules about photographs, about never being alone with a single pupil, and about what to do if a child says something worrying.

Second visit, planning. Mr Rasmussen has a class of twenty-two children, aged ten and eleven, and no strong sense of the range. Some have written games at home, while others have never opened a code editor. We agreed to split each session into a short demonstration, a task in pairs, and a five-minute showcase. Avery suggested using a block-based environment that runs in the browser, so that nothing has to be installed on the school laptops, which are protected by a filter that blocks most downloads.

The first project we chose was a simple animated story, with a character that moves across the screen and says something when clicked. Meera made a sample in ten minutes to show what the end result might look like, and Mr Rasmussen worried that it was too good, that children would feel discouraged. She laughed and promised to break it by the second session, so that they could fix it. A bug is the best lesson in the world, she said, and the children love to correct adults.

Layout of the space matters more than we had imagined. The computing lab has long benches along the wall, and children sit shoulder to shoulder, so pairs form naturally. But the projector faces the wrong way, and a steel pillar blocks the view from one corner. We moved two benches, put a sign on the door, and taped the wifi code to the wall at eye level for eleven-year-olds. Mr Rasmussen said that in eight years nobody had suggested moving the benches.

Between the second and third visits I spent an evening reading the school's computing curriculum, a two-page document with more verbs than I expected. Pupils are to design, write, and debug programs, use sequence, selection and repetition, and understand how networks carry information. Mapping our ten weeks onto that took an hour and one sheet of paper, and I came away convinced that the difficult part was not the content but the timing: forty minutes of real work in a sixty-minute slot, once the laptops are booted.

The first session began with a question: what is a computer? One girl answered that it is a thing that follows rules very fast and never gets bored. Avery wrote that on the board and left it there for the whole hour. There followed a rapid tour of loops and conditions, using a robot and a snowman as an example, and a demonstration in which Meera pretended to be a computer and followed Avery's instructions for making toast, with literal results and much laughter.

Mr Rasmussen stayed at the back with his arms folded and a look of cautious joy, and at the end he confessed that the space had never been so quiet and so loud at the same time. He pointed out two children who normally say nothing in history and had spent the hour explaining things to their partners. That, he said, was worth the cost of the background checks and the boiled kettle of nerves.

The pairs task went better than expected. In the first ten minutes, seven of eleven pairs had a character moving, and by the end of the session three pairs had added sound. There were tears from one boy whose project vanished when he closed the tab, so we spent the last minutes teaching the difference between saving and hoping. Mr Rasmussen kept a tally of questions we could not answer, six in all, and wrote them on a sheet titled Homework for the Grown-Ups.

The arrangement, as agreed with Mrs Danielsson and confirmed in writing: the club will meet on Wednesday afternoons from three to four, in the computing lab, for ten weeks, with two volunteers from the studio each time. Mr Rasmussen stays in the space throughout. The studio releases Avery and Meera at half past two, and travel time counts as work. If either cannot attend, Blake and Sami are the back-ups, and both have already had their background checks approved.

Next steps. Blake will add the programme to the studio's community page, with a note about how other staff can get involved. Sami will collect a small donation of used keyboards for the school, since half the laptops have missing keys. Meera and Avery will draft the ten-week plan this weekend, and send it to Mr Rasmussen on Sunday for comment. A short feedback form for the pupils, with three questions and smiley faces, will be added to the last session.

Winter preparation diary: sealing the draughts. The first cold snap arrived on Tuesday, and by Wednesday morning the hall felt like a bus shelter. Noor found the cause by holding a strip of tissue paper near the front door, where it fluttered horizontally, and then at the balcony door, where it did the same. I promised her I would fix it before the weekend, and I began by making a list of every place where warm air could be escaping the flat.

Walk-through with a candle, a trick from my grandfather. On a windy evening, with the heating on, I went through the flat with a stick of incense and watched the smoke. It bent sideways at the bottom of the front door, around the mail slot flap, along the hinge edge of the balcony door, and at the junction between the frame and the plaster in the spare chamber. In the lavatory, the smoke went upward into the extractor, as it should. I made a rough plan on squared paper and marked each leak with a cross.

The front door is the worst offender. It is an old solid wood door in a slightly warped frame, with a gap at the bottom wide enough to slide a paperback through. The mail slot is a brass flap without a brush, and the keyhole has no cover. I measured the gap at the bottom at eleven millimetres in the middle and six at the corners, which explains why the draught seems to come from the centre. I wrote the numbers on the plan, and photographed the door from the inside with a ruler laid across the gap for scale, which Noor found hilarious.

The balcony door is different: double glazed, but with tired rubber seals that have flattened and split in places. I ran a finger along the edge and felt cold air at three spots, and the handle is loose, meaning the door does not press hard against the frame. I tightened the screws and adjusted the strike plate a couple of millimetres. That alone helped, and the tissue paper now moves only slightly. Noor tested it and gave a professional nod.

Shopping list, made at the hardware shop with the help of an assistant called Ismail, who knows a great deal about foam. For the door frame: adhesive foam strips in two thicknesses, or a rubber D-profile seal for the balcony. For the bottom of the front door: a brush strip screwed to the wood, or a draught excluder with a rubber lip. For the mail slot: a brush insert. For the keyhole: a small metal cover. Plus a caulking gun and a cartridge of flexible sealant for the gap by the spare chamber frame.

Ismail also explained why cheap self-adhesive foam fails: it compresses permanently in a single season and peels off in the wet. He recommended a silicone tube seal that is pressed into a groove, which lasts for years but needs a router to cut the groove. I said that I did not have a router. He suggested the compromise of a rubber D-profile with strong adhesive backing, cleaned with white spirit before applying. He was so persuasive that I nearly bought a router as well.

Before buying anything, I checked with the landlord, because the frames belong to the building, and I did not want to glue foam to something that the owner might later repaint. His answer came by message within an hour: seals are fine, drilling into frames is not, and I should keep the old ones. I wrote a short line in my notebook to say that the door was to be returned to its original state, with the date, and photographed the frame before touching it.

Preparation for fitting took an evening. I cleaned the frames with spirit and a rag, waited for them to dry, measured each side twice, and cut the strips with scissors and a sharp knife. Noor sat with the lengths in a row on the floor, naming each after a river. I removed the old seal from the balcony door with a scraper, which came away in long crumbling strips that smelled of vanilla and dust, and vacuumed the rebate.

Ismail had also mentioned, as I paid for the sealant, that a cold flat is not only a heating problem but a damp one, because warm indoor air meets cold surfaces and leaves water behind. That sent me to the spare chamber again, where I found a faint grey bloom on the plaster behind the wardrobe. I wiped it with a mild solution, pulled the wardrobe forward a hand's width to let air behind it, and put a thermometer on the wall to see how cold it gets.

Saturday was fitting day. I peeled the backing a little at a time, pressed the seal into place with my thumb, and closed the door on it to test the compression, adding a millimetre of packing where the gap was widest. The front door required planing a bit off the bottom edge and screwing on the brush strip, with the door lifted off its hinges and laid across two chairs. It took three hours, mostly waiting for sealant to skin over, and one small argument with a screw.

Receipt for the record: the weatherstrip kit rang up at forty-eight euros, including the brush strips, the mail slot insert, and the D-profile, plus fifteen for the sealant and gun. I have kept the receipt in case any of it fails. Total for the whole flat is about sixty-five euros, which a heating engineer friend told me I will save inside a season. The smoke test after the work showed no movement at the front door, a slight flicker at the corner of the balcony frame.

Reflection and afterthought: the flat is noticeably warmer, and the boiler seems to be running less, though I have no figures yet. I will read the meter on the first of each month and compare with last year. The spare chamber frame still has a hairline crack in the plaster that needs a proper repair in spring. Noor asked whether the seals will keep out ghosts as well as draughts. I said they should, and she went to check the mail slot, reassured.

Cat-sitting diary: nine days with Tofu and Pepper. My neighbours across the landing, Emil and Sofia, are flying to Lisbon for a wedding and a week of walking, and asked me if I would mind looking after their two cats. I have a key, a laminated instruction sheet, and a small sense of foreboding, as I am used to one difficult cat and now shall be responsible for two more, whom I have met only in passing and who have, I believe, opinions about me.

Handover on Friday night. Sofia showed me around, with both cats sitting like ancient statues on the sofa arm. Tofu is a grey twelve-year-old with a heavy build and a sad face, and Pepper is a black three-year-old who bounces on all four paws when excited. The flat smells pleasantly of sandalwood. Emil gave me the tour of the cupboard where the food is stored, and the shelf with the litter tray liners, and demonstrated the automatic water fountain, which hums.

Instructions were arranged as a sheet by the fridge and, as a back-up, a document sent by message. Feeding is at seven and six, dry food measured with a small scoop, one tin of wet food each at six, and a treat stick in the afternoon if the cat has behaved. Litter trays are cleaned each morning and emptied entirely on Sunday. The sleeping quarters pane stays shut, the balcony door stays closed, and the black cat must never be let into the hallway because he will run down the stairs.

Medication is the serious part. Sofia handed me a pill cutter and a little box marked with the days of the week. She explained that the older cat gets a pill for his kidneys each morning, hidden in a small ball of tuna paste, and that he is a professional at spitting it out. Pepper has no medication, but must not be allowed near it. She had written the vet's number in red on the sheet, and the address of the emergency clinic that opens at night.

Day one, Saturday. I arrived at seven and found both cats sitting in front of the food cupboard like a committee. The tuna paste trick worked on the first go, and Tofu looked at me with what I can only describe as grudging respect. Pepper watched from the top of the bookshelf, tail hanging down, and then, with a sudden leap, attempted to help. I cleaned the tray, changed the water, and left the radio on low for company, tuned to a station that plays gentle jazz.

Emil had left one more chore on the list, which I had not expected: the plants. There are eleven of them, arranged along the balcony wall, each with its own small saucer and a sticky label giving a schedule in Sofia's neat print. The fern wants a spray every day, the succulents nothing at all, and a large lemon tree in a bucket needs a full jug of water on Sundays. I did the round with a watering can and a growing sense that plant sitting is the harder duty. A leaf fell off the fern on Sunday, and I stood over it for a while like a doctor, wondering whether to confess it in my daily message to Sofia. I did, and she answered with a laughing face and the words it always does that. She added that the plant had done the same to her twice, and that I should not worry about a dropped leaf in a house with two cats.

Miso, at home in my flat, is evidently aware of the situation. She sniffed my trouser legs for a full minute on Saturday evening, then walked out of the space in protest. By Sunday she had taken up a position under my desk and refused to acknowledge me. Noor says she is jealous, and made a small sign with a drawing of a cat and the words I am still your favourite, which she pinned to the door.

Routine settled quickly. Each morning I woke at half past six, crossed the landing in slippers, and let myself in to two cats waiting at the cupboard. Then feeding, trays, water, and the pill, followed by ten minutes of sitting on the sofa arm, watching the light climb the wall. Pepper sat on my shoulder on Monday, which felt like a medal. In the evening I repeated the round, and sometimes stayed to read, with Tofu heavy and warm on my feet, until the cats began to yawn.

Pepper and I developed an understanding over the week. He does not like being picked up, but he adores a piece of string, and on Wednesday evening we played for twenty minutes, with him leaping across the sofa in a series of ambitious arcs and landing, on one occasion, on my head. I recorded a small video and sent it to Emil. He answered that Pepper had never played so long with anyone, and that I was hired for life.

Middle of the week. Tofu had a bad night on Tuesday: he vomited on the rug and hid behind the sofa. I telephoned the vet, as Sofia had asked, and a receptionist said that occasional vomiting can happen when routines change but that I should watch his appetite and drinking. Before answering the phone I reread the sheet by the fridge, which says that the older cat, Tofu, needs a half pill of Renalix each morning, and I checked the pill box: Tuesday's half was gone, so it had not been the pill that upset him, or not the missing of it. I sent Sofia a photograph and a reassuring line, and she replied with three hearts from the airport lounge. By Wednesday morning he was eating normally and purring at my ankles.

Friday: the last handover. I cleaned the trays, washed the bowls, sprayed the fabric with a light fragrance, and left the instruction sheet exactly as I found it, with a note saying that Tofu had eaten every day and that Pepper had knocked over the small plant but had not eaten any of it. I put a bottle of wine and a card on the shelf. Emil and Sofia returned on Saturday morning with pastries and a tin of sardines, which the cats attacked at once.

Team wellbeing log, workstation assessments. After two colleagues reported neck and wrist pain in the same month, Avery and Blake asked an occupational therapist, Dr Solberg, to visit the office and assess every workstation. She came on Tuesday with a laptop, a tape measure, a small goniometer for measuring joint angles, and a bag of props including foot rests and wrist supports. This is the log of that day and the decisions that followed.

Her method was the same for all eleven of us. She sat with each person for about twenty minutes, first watching them work as normal for five, then asking about pain, headaches, and habits, and finally adjusting the chair and desk while explaining each change. She photographed each setup from the side and front with our consent, and noted the height of everything: seat, desk, keyboard, screen. She said that the photograph is the most useful tool, because people do not believe how they sit until they see it.

Blake was first. He works at a laptop on a standing desk and had been having pain in his left wrist. Dr Solberg spotted immediately that his laptop screen was too low, so he tilted his head down all day, and that his wrist was bent upward over the edge of the palm rest. She lifted the laptop onto a stand, gave him a separate keyboard and mouse, and lowered the desk by three centimetres so that his elbows made a right angle.

Meera, in finance, had been complaining of headaches at the end of the day. Her monitor was too far away and too bright, and her chair was set so high that her feet dangled. Dr Solberg moved the screen to arm's length, reduced the brightness to match the space, and provided a footrest, an inclined plastic platform, which Meera at once described as the best object in the office. She also pointed out that Meera had been leaning toward the screen to read small print, and recommended that the font size be increased.

On height, Dr Solberg gave a rule that she repeated to almost everyone: place the top of each screen at eye level, about sixty-five centimetres above the desk for an average seated person, with the screen tilted slightly back and at least an arm's length from the eyes. Several of us had our monitors sitting on the desk directly, with the top below the chin. Yusuf's was sitting on a ream of paper, which she found sweetly inadequate.

Sami's problem was the reverse: he is very tall, and his chair was at its lowest setting, with his knees higher than his hips. She recommended a taller chair base, which the supplier can swap for free, and a desk riser, and reminded him that being tall is not a medical condition. He wanted to know whether his habit of sitting cross-legged on the chair was a problem, and she said it was a bigger problem for his patience than for his spine.

Between assessments, she gave a fifteen-minute talk to the whole team about movement. Her message: the best posture is the next posture, and no position is safe for more than half an hour. She recommended a rule of twenty minutes of sitting, eight of standing, and two of moving, which she called the twenty-eight-two rule. She demonstrated four stretches for the neck, wrists, hips, and back, and had us all try them, looking faintly ridiculous in the middle of the meeting suite.

The purchasing list that follows her recommendations is short: eight monitor stands, four footrests, six external keyboards and mice, two new chairs for Sami and Yusuf, and a set of desk timers that flash a gentle reminder. Blake priced everything at around fourteen hundred euros, which is well within the annual wellbeing budget. Avery will place the order this week and ask the supplier to deliver in one go so that the entire office can be adjusted on a single afternoon.

Small practical notes from the day. Dr Solberg asked everyone to shift the keyboard back so that the forearms rest on the surface, and warned against wrist rests used while typing, as opposed to pausing. She also checked lighting, and asked us to pull the blinds on the west side after lunch to remove glare from the screens. Two people were sent away to have their eyes tested, a suggestion nobody argued with.

Follow-up plan. In three weeks, Dr Solberg will send a short questionnaire on pain and comfort for everyone, and we will compare it to the baseline from Tuesday. Blake will schedule a short standing meeting every Thursday, and Avery proposed a shared calendar entry for stretching at half past two. Everyone agreed to put a note on the desk with the settings that suit them, so that colleagues sharing a desk can restore them. Blake will collect the notes and put them in the shared folder.

Diary, Noor's first sleepover. She turned eight in the spring and has been asking since the autumn to have a friend to stay the night, a request I dodged with the practised skill of a parent who values sleep. Last week her friend Elsa's mother, Kajsa, who I know from the school gate, suggested a swap: Elsa would stay with us on the Saturday, and Noor would return the favour next month. I said yes before I could think, and spent the week thinking.

Preparation started with the logistics of a small flat. Noor's bedchamber has one bed, so I borrowed a folding guest mattress from Ingrid's sister's stock, which she left when she moved, and measured the floor. It fits between the bed and the wardrobe with about ten centimetres to spare, which Noor said was perfect for whispering. I washed two sets of sheets, found a spare duvet, and put a small lamp in the corner for the anxious hour before sleep.

Elsa's mother sent a message with a helpful list: Elsa is allergic to peanuts, does not like fungi, needs her stuffed rabbit to sleep, and gets homesick around nine. She has a phone number I may call at any hour, including three in the morning, and the promise that neither of them will mind. I wrote all of this on a card and pinned it beside the calendar, where I could not lose it, and put the peanut warning in red.

The menu was debated at length. Noor wanted pizza, which is easy, ice cream, which is easier, and a cake, which is a project. In the end we agreed on homemade pizzas, with the girls choosing their own toppings from bowls of sweetcorn, pepperoni, cherry tomatoes, olives and grated mozzarella, followed by a very simple sponge with strawberries. I checked every label for nut traces, which took an hour in the supermarket and left me with a considerably greater respect for allergy parents.

Elsa arrived at five, dragged a small suitcase up the stairs, and immediately vanished into Noor's bedchamber with a shriek. For the next two hours the sounds coming from behind the door were of chairs being dragged, a small quantity of singing, and a game that seemed to involve the hamster of another era. I made a pot of tea and read the paper in the hall, an activity that I now understand as parenting. At six I was summoned to view a fashion show.

Pizza was a triumph, though the base collapsed under the weight of the toppings on Elsa's first attempt. She re-rolled it with the concentration of a surgeon and put on nothing but sweetcorn, which she called a golden pizza. Noor produced a mozzarella, tomato and olive creation that she named the Fox, for its colours. We ate on the floor of the lounge with paper plates, and I watched them share a slice with elaborate ceremony, like a pact.

Arrangements for the morning were settled at the door on Friday, when Kajsa came by to drop a pillow. We talked for a few minutes about the practicalities, and pickup was fixed for ten on Sunday morning, which she promised would be on time, although we both knew that her car has a mind of its own. She waved at Noor across the yard, and I noticed how the two of them looked at each other with a small, conspiratorial smile.

Bedtime was the chapter I had dreaded. The girls put on pyjamas, brushed their teeth in a strict alternating order, and lay down in the dark with the small lamp on. I read a story aloud, a chapter about a lighthouse keeper's dog, and by the end of it there were two heads on pillows and two very quiet voices. At nine, as predicted, Elsa announced that she felt strange in her stomach. A glass of water and a phone call to her mother, and it was over.

A word on the small things that mattered. Elsa's rabbit was called Mr Pom, and it spent the evening in a pizza-related emergency that involved a bandage and a great deal of tenderness. Noor lent hers a spare blanket. The two of them agreed that neither rabbit should be washed, ever, and I saw no reason to argue, having lost that argument in principle years ago.

The night itself was unremarkable except for a brief visit at half past midnight, when both of them tiptoed into my bedchamber to report that the moon was looking at them. I said the moon was allowed to look, and they went back. At six in the morning I woke to a whispered argument about who had won a game of cards in their sleep. I made pancakes, poured juice, and fed the rabbit toy a strawberry for reasons that seemed compelling at the time.

Kajsa arrived at five to ten, which was a triumph of planning. Elsa left with her suitcase, a paper bag of leftover pizza, and a drawing that she and Noor had made together, which now hangs above the desk. Noor, after waving at the door, lay flat on the sofa for an hour and declared that sleepovers are wonderful but that she would like the next one to have more sleeping. I agree, and will bring in a second mattress for the return match.

Repair diary, the front door lock. It happened on a Thursday evening as I came home with shopping: I pushed the key in, turned it, and felt the tip snap off inside the cylinder with a small crunch. I stood there in the corridor with half a key in my hand, a bag of groceries in the other, and a rising sense of poor timing. Noor was inside with the babysitter, who could not open the door from the other side because the lock was jammed.

The first hour was improvised. I rang the babysitter's phone and suggested she stay calm, which she did, and I told Noor through the door that this was an adventure. Then I tried the obvious things: pliers, which slipped, and a little soap on a wire. The broken end had sunk too deeply to reach. I called Ingrid, who has a spare key for the deadbolt only, and that unlocked the second lock but not the cylinder.

At half past eight I gave up and phoned a locksmith, choosing the first one whose advertisement said twenty-four hours. The man who answered called himself Rolf and spoke in short, cheerful sentences. He asked whether the door was a standard cylinder, whether I owned the flat or rented, and whether anyone was in danger. He said he could arrive within forty minutes, that there would be a callout charge, and that he would explain everything before touching the lock.

Rolf arrived in a white van at ten past nine, a large person with a leather tool belt and a torch on his forehead. He knelt in the corridor, examined the cylinder for a minute, and told me it was a common brand with a solid brass barrel, ten years old. He inserted a thin extractor tool, twisted, and drew out the fragment of key with a sound like a small victory. Behind the door, Noor cheered, and the babysitter clapped politely.

He then explained, with a great deal of patience, the state of my lock. The pins inside had worn, which is why the key had been sticking for months and finally snapped under load. Replacing the cylinder would take twenty minutes and cost less than repairing the old one. The door itself was fine, apart from a loose strike plate, which he tightened. He asked whether I wanted a standard cylinder or a higher security one with a reinforced barrel and a key that cannot be copied at a kiosk.

We talked about security for a while. Rolf recommended a model with anti-drill pins and a locking card, and explained that an unlicensed copy of the key would need proof of ownership. He said that most break-ins involve the weakest point, usually the door frame or a badly fitted strike plate, not the lock, and offered to inspect the frame. I said yes. He knocked on it in three places and said it was decent, though a longer screw in the top hinge would help.

The quote was clear and written down on his pad. For the new high-security cylinder, three keys, the fitting, the extra screws and the callout, the locksmith quoted one hundred and seventy euros, with a card payment through a phone terminal at the end. I compared that with the price of a cylinder at the shop, which I had looked up in the meantime, and it was fair. I agreed, and he set to work while I stood in the corridor holding the shopping like a man at a very slow bus stop.

The fitting went smoothly. He removed the old cylinder with a quarter-turn on a screw, cleaned the recess, and pressed the new barrel into place. Then he tested each of the three keys twenty times, with the door open and closed, and showed me how to lubricate the mechanism with graphite powder rather than oil, which attracts dirt. The lock now turns with a soft, precise sound, and the door closes with a click I had forgotten it could make, which I found unreasonably satisfying. Rolf gave me a small card with the code number of the cylinder, for ordering more keys.

The babysitter, Lovisa, is a nineteen-year-old who studies nursing and had been calm throughout, reading Noor a story through the gap under the door. She went home at ten, apologising, and I paid her double for the trouble. Noor came out in her pyjamas to inspect the new keys, and named each after a friend. Rolf also wrote the receipt by hand and included his phone number, in case the cylinder should ever misbehave, with a guarantee of five years on the barrel. I put one in my wallet, one on the hook inside, and the third in an envelope for Ingrid's sister. The old broken key sits in a jar on the shelf as a reminder. I promised myself to check the keys and locks every autumn, and to carry a spare of everything I care about. Ingrid, when I told her the whole story on Friday over tea, said that she has snapped two keys in her life, and both times it was raining.

Wellbeing log, the six-week walking challenge, results and lessons. In late summer, Blake proposed that the office join a walking challenge run by a health charity, which offers a free app, a leaderboard, and weekly prompts. Twelve of us signed up in four teams of three, competing for a small trophy and the chance to name a tree in the company yard. The challenge ended on Friday, and this write-up records the numbers and what we learned about ourselves.

The teams were drawn by lot from a hat, on the theory that friendships should be mixed. Team Kestrel had Meera, Sami and Yusuf; Team Puffin had Avery, a designer called Lotta, and Tomas from support; the other two teams took the names Otter and Heron and were composed of the rest. Each person wore a phone or pedometer and synced steps nightly with the app. The rules allowed any type of walking, including the walk from the tram, the pace at lunch, and, controversially, pacing during phone calls.

Week one was a period of extravagance. Everybody walked farther than they needed to, taking the long way to the shop and the stairs to the fifth floor. Sami reached twenty thousand steps on Tuesday by walking to and from a dentist across the city, and put it on the shared chat with a flexing emoji. By Friday, the average was nine thousand steps a person, up from a starting figure of six thousand, according to the measurements taken the previous week.

Week two brought weather. Two days of steady rain thinned the numbers, and the mood dipped. Blake suggested a lunchtime loop around the block with umbrellas, and about half the team joined him, walking in a line like ducks. Lotta, on Puffin, had set up a rule that whoever won the day had to buy the loser a pastry, and the office shop briefly sold out. Avery posted a photograph of a soggy fox that she had met in the park.

One incident deserves its own paragraph. On a Wednesday in week three the app failed for six hours, losing the steps of everyone who had synced in the morning, and the chat lit up with accusations and sad faces. Lotta, who is good at spreadsheets, collected screenshots from each person and rebuilt the day by hand, arguing that honesty and evidence should be enough. The organisers of the challenge restored the data the next morning, and the committee, in the spirit of celebration, declared the incident closed.

The middle weeks brought the first injuries and the first cheating scandal. Yusuf was accused of shaking his phone at his desk, a rumour he denied with dignity while his step count showed a suspicious rise between two and three in the afternoon. Tomas twisted an ankle on a kerb and was put on light duty, which meant hobbling to the printer as often as possible. The rules committee, a jocular body of two, decided that shaking would result in a fine of one round of tea.

Interlude on the people who did not compete. Two colleagues on the second team declined to wear trackers, one for privacy and one because of a medical device, and were made honorary walkers. They kept the mood light by handing out fruit at the lunchtime loop. Blake said this was as important as anything in the competition, because the point was for the whole office to feel it was in it together.

Final week. The lead changed hands three times, as Kestrel and Puffin traded places in a race that ended on the last afternoon. Meera, who had been quietly outwalking everyone, went for a three-hour hike with her dog on Sunday, and Sami joined her for part of it. The results were announced on Friday at four, in the yard, by Blake in a very serious voice, with a rolled-up newspaper as a microphone.

Team Kestrel finished first with 412,000 steps, an average of about nine thousand eight hundred a day for each of the three members, followed by Puffin on 398,000, Heron on 361,000 and Otter on 340,000. Individual champion was Meera, with over a hundred and fifty thousand steps of her own, which is roughly a hundred and ten kilometres. She was given the trophy, a spray-painted trainer on a small plinth, and immediately put it on the reception desk.

Reflections, from a short feedback session afterwards. Nine of twelve said they felt better: more alert in the afternoon, slightly less stiff in the neck. Four had walked with a colleague for the first time and got to know them better. Two found the app annoying, especially the notifications, and one said that competitive walking made her feel guilty on days when she was ill. Blake noted this carefully and suggested that next time the challenge should reward consistency, not volume.

The tree-naming prize was awarded in the yard on Monday. Kestrel chose the name Bertil for a birch that the landlord planted last spring, and Blake nailed a small wooden tag to the trunk. We also agreed to keep the lunchtime loop going as a weekly walk, on Thursdays at half past twelve, rain or shine, with a bell to summon the slow. Avery volunteered to map three routes of different lengths for the seasons and stick them by the lifts.

Numbers worth keeping: the twelve of us covered about 1,500,000 steps in six weeks, roughly twelve hundred kilometres, and the average daily count rose from six thousand to nearly nine thousand. Nobody was injured seriously. The cost was zero, apart from the trophy and a half-dozen pastries. Blake will propose repeating the challenge in spring, with the possibility of inviting the neighbouring firm on the second floor to make it a proper inter-office contest.

Diary, open day at Lindenberg secondary school. Noor is only eight, but the local system asks families to look at secondary schools two years ahead, and a friend at the school gate persuaded me to see one early rather than in a panic. So on Saturday morning, in a bright cold drizzle, Noor and I made our way to the open day at Lindenberg, a large brick building with a glass atrium at the front and a hockey pitch stretching behind.

We were greeted at the door by two pupils in green blazers, a boy and a girl, who introduced themselves as guides and handed us a map, a booklet, and a paper cup of hot apple juice. Noor, in her waterproof, stared at their blazers with open envy. They took us through the atrium, where a big screen looped a film about the school year, and up a wide staircase lined with framed photographs of former pupils and a mural of the elements.

The first stop was the science block, which has eight laboratories, a greenhouse on the roof, and a small observatory with a telescope. A teacher in a lab coat, Mr Fahlgren, ran a demonstration involving liquid nitrogen and a rubber ball, which shattered when dropped, to the delight of the small children, who screamed on cue. He then invited them to try to blow a bubble that would freeze in the air, and Noor, brave in her hood, managed it on the second attempt.

The gymnasium came next, where the sports department had set up a climbing wall, a rowing machine, and a bat-and-ball area, and children queued up to try each. A tall teacher in a tracksuit, Ms Eklund, explained that every pupil takes part in two hours of sport a week, with a choice of twelve activities from fencing to orienteering. Noor tried the climbing wall, reached the top in nine seconds, and came down with her hood over her eyes and a triumphant expression.

We moved to the arts corridor, where pupils were performing in the hall: a jazz ensemble of twelve, a choir, and a very confident girl reading a poem about a bus. Next door, the ceramics studio had a display of bowls, each glazed a different colour, and the art studio showed portraits in charcoal. Noor spent ten minutes at a bench of clay and left with a small pinched creature that I was told is a dragon.

The head of admissions, a calm man with round glasses named Mr Halvorsen, spoke to a small group of parents in the library at eleven. He described the school's approach: mixed ability classes until year nine, a strong emphasis on languages, and pastoral care through a form tutor who stays with the class for three years. He described the entry process too, with pupils applying in the autumn of the year before entry and offers sent in March.

Mr Halvorsen was easy to listen to, unhurried, courteous with the nervous questioners, and funny in a dry way. He has taught geography for twenty years and became head of admissions when his knees gave out on the hockey pitch, he said, to laughter. He showed a chart of last year's results with the confidence of a man who knows that the numbers are good but does not want to gloat, and, as an aside I liked, explained that the school's value is not the grades but the fact that pupils who arrive quiet tend to leave with a voice.

Then came the detail that I wrote on my hand. Because the science stream is oversubscribed, applications for the science stream close on the fifteenth of January, two months before the general deadline, and children sit a short aptitude test in the last week of that month. Mr Halvorsen said that he was telling us now so that nobody would be surprised in two years, and that the test is designed to be taken without preparation. Several parents took photographs of the slide.

Before the questions, the head of languages spoke for five minutes about exchange visits: every pupil visits a partner school in France, Spain or Germany in year eight, and hosts a partner in return. She showed photographs of pupils laughing at a railway station, wearing sunglasses and enormous backpacks, and reminded parents that the exchanges are subsidised. It sounded wonderful and slightly terrifying, and I wrote down the word passport with a small question mark.

Questions from the audience were sensible and slightly anxious. A father asked about homework, and the answer was ninety minutes a night in the first year, rising a little later. A mother asked about bullying, and Mr Halvorsen described a system of older pupils trained as mentors, with a drop-in space at lunchtime. Another asked about transport, and was told that three bus routes stop at the gate and a cycle shed holds four hundred bicycles.

We had lunch in the canteen, where a sign said that everyone is welcome and nobody is judged for their chips. The food was hot, plentiful and slightly beige, and Noor chose a sausage roll. At the next bench, a pupil from year ten answered our questions honestly: the teachers are mostly fine, the rugby team is terrible, the maths department is legendary, and the best thing about the school is the library on wet afternoons.

On the way home, Noor was silent for the length of two tram stops, then announced that she wanted to go to that school and be in the orchestra, even though she does not play an instrument. I told her that she had two years to learn one, and that we would see. I have photographed the booklet and put the date in my calendar as a reminder for two years hence, though the process may change by then. We will visit two more schools before deciding anything.

Health diary: the headache clinic. For about a year I have had attacks that begin with a shimmering patch at the edge of my vision, then a pounding pain behind one eye, then nausea and a need to lie in a dark chamber until it passes. They arrive roughly twice a month, last most of a day, and seem to ignore any rule I invent. Dr Alves referred me to a neurologist after the last one, which took out a whole Saturday and most of Sunday.

The first task was a diary, which the clinic sent as a printed sheet with columns for date, start time, duration, severity out of ten, and possible triggers. I filled it in for two months. Reading it back, the pattern was not as random as I had assumed: attacks came on Mondays more than any other day, after nights of five hours' sleep or fewer, and about a third followed a missed meal. Red wine appeared once, dairy never, and stress appeared in almost every entry, in my handwriting, underlined.

The clinic is at the university hospital, on the fourth floor of a building that seems to have been designed by a person who dislikes signs. I arrived early, took a wrong lift twice, and finally found a waiting area with soft lighting, a fish tank, and a rack of leaflets about brain health. A nurse called my name in the middle of a page. The neurologist, Dr Iqbal, is a slender man with a soft voice and a habit of writing everything by hand on a yellow pad.

He introduced himself by his first name and asked whether I minded if a medical student sat in, a serious young woman who took notes in a tiny hand and said nothing until the end. I did not mind. At the door she shook my hand and said she hoped the diary would help. It did, a little more than either of us expected, and I was glad of the audience for the moment it was read aloud.

He began with the history, and let me talk for ten minutes without interruption, which was unexpected and slightly moving. Then he asked precise questions: whether the visual aura comes before the pain, how long it lasts, whether it moves across the field of view, whether I ever lose strength on one side, or speech. I said no to the last two and yes to the first, and he nodded once and wrote something. He also asked about family, and I mentioned my aunt, who has the same attacks.

The examination took twenty minutes: reflexes, eye movements, a torch across the pupils, walking heel to toe along a line on the floor, touching my nose with a finger, and reading a chart. He looked at the back of my eyes with a small lit instrument for a long moment and said that everything appeared normal. He explained that the pattern was typical for migraine with aura, that a scan was not needed, and that the story on the diary sheet was quite clear.

We spent a long time on triggers, which he described as a bucket that fills up until it overflows, rather than a single cause. Sleep, hydration, regular meals, stress, hormones, bright light, and strong smells all add water. He suggested keeping a regular schedule, drinking two litres of water a day, eating before noon, and getting outdoors in the daytime. He was against strict diets, saying that people often cut out foods they love without any benefit, and that the diary should guide us.

Treatment came in two parts. For acute attacks, he recommended taking a specific pill at the first sign of the aura rather than waiting for the pain, together with a simple painkiller and an anti-nausea pill, and lying down. For prevention, because my attacks are frequent enough to disrupt my life, he suggested a daily low-dose medicine that is used for many purposes. He wrote the prescription: begin with twenty-five milligrams at bedtime, increase by twenty-five every second week, and review after three months.

He was honest about side effects: drowsiness, tingling in the fingers, possible weight change, and a fog in the mind in the first weeks that generally passes. He asked me to tell him at once if I noticed mood changes, and gave me a leaflet, which I read on the tram. I said I was worried about the fog, since I work at a screen, and he replied that he would rather have me foggy for two weeks than in bed for two days a month. It was fair, and disarming.

He also talked about the diary. Migraine, he said, is a condition of the brain that likes routine, and my Monday attacks probably reflect a broken weekend rhythm: later nights, later mornings, a skipped breakfast, then a busy week. He advised waking at the same hour every day, even on Sundays, which I recorded with a groan. The last piece of advice was about screens: a break every hour, a matte filter, and a lamp behind the monitor to lift the contrast.

The pharmacy filled the prescription within ten minutes, and I bought a small pill cutter and a weekly pill box in a shade of green that Noor describes as frog. I started that evening. In the first week I felt slightly slow, especially after lunch, and sleepy by nine, but no headaches. Noor drew a poster for my door that says quiet, brain resting. I will see Dr Iqbal again in three months and take the diary.

Negotiation notes, replacing the studio's boiler. The old gas boiler in the boiler house failed its annual inspection in October, with a cracked heat exchanger that the engineer described as beyond economic repair. The building belongs to a landlord, but the lease makes us responsible for heating equipment that serves our floor, so the choice and the cost fell to us. Avery and Blake ran the process, and these notes record it from the first call to the signed contract.

The starting position was awkward. It was late autumn, the heating had been switched off by the engineer for safety, and the office was ten degrees. We borrowed six electric heaters from staff and neighbours and told everyone to bring blankets, which they did with a sense of adventure that lasted about a day. Blake set a target: a decision within a week, installation within three, and a cost that did not eat the entire maintenance reserve.

Three firms were asked to quote. The first, Nordvarme, sent a surveyor who spent two hours in the boiler house, photographed everything, and produced a clear proposal for a high-efficiency condensing boiler with a new flue and controls. The second, a smaller local company called Holm and Sons, quoted lower but proposed to reuse the old flue, which the surveyor from Nordvarme had said was corroded. The third, a national chain, sent a sales person with a phone and a brochure and no measurements at all.

Comparing the quotes took an afternoon. Nordvarme wanted fourteen thousand five hundred, including removal of the old unit, a five-year warranty on parts and labour, and an annual service for the first two years. Holm and Sons asked for nine thousand eight hundred but with a two-year warranty and no service. The chain quoted twelve thousand, with a long list of extras. Avery built a spreadsheet, scoring each on price, warranty, efficiency rating, delivery date, and risk of hidden extras.

The landlord's agent had to be consulted about the flue, which runs through a shared shaft. He replied within a day: a new flue is preferred, and any work that touches the shaft needs his sign-off and a certified installer. That effectively ruled out the cheap proposal, or rather made it dearer than it looked. Avery told Holm and Sons why, politely, and the owner, Mr Holm, said he understood and would recalculate with a new flue. His revised figure was twelve thousand four hundred.

First round with Nordvarme, on the phone on Tuesday. Blake opened by saying that we liked the proposal but that the price was above our budget, and asked what flexibility existed. The salesman, Henrik, said the price included a new controller and installation on a weekend, but that he could remove the annual services from the offer. Blake declined; the service was one of the reasons we preferred them. Henrik said he would consult his manager and call on Thursday.

Second round. Henrik proposed thirteen thousand two hundred and fifty, with the service retained, saying that was the best he could do without cutting corners. Blake thanked him and mentioned, without heat, that Holm and Sons had moved to twelve thousand four hundred with a five-year warranty. Henrik went quiet, then asked what warranty and whether it included labour. Blake said yes. He asked for a day. Avery sat beside Blake with a pen, drawing small arrows, and neither of them said a word for the next several minutes.

Third round, Friday. Henrik called back with a revised structure: the price would fall if we agreed to a two-year service contract, paid up front, and to a March installation date, when their crews are quieter. We said we could not wait until March, because the heating was already off. He pushed the date to two weeks from Monday, and after a long silence on the line, and a joke about how cold his own home was, the parties settled at eleven thousand two hundred euros for the boiler, with the new flue, controls, removal and the five-year warranty.

Blake sent a written confirmation immediately, with the terms in a list, and asked for the agreement to be countersigned by Monday. Avery reviewed the contract, checked the certification of the installers, and confirmed the insurance certificate. The landlord's agent signed the flue permission on the same day. Payment is in three parts: thirty per cent on signing, forty on delivery, and thirty on commissioning, with a retention of five per cent for thirty days after that.

Lessons, in the order we would like them read. Get three quotes, but make sure they are comparable. Ask the landlord early about anything that touches shared services. Set a walk-away figure before the first call. Never negotiate against yourself; make the counterpart move first. And keep a record of what each side said, because the final contract, in the end, is only as good as the notes that produced it. Installation is booked for the fourteenth, and the heaters will be returned with a plate of biscuits.

Family diary: Grandmother's hip operation, and the week after. My grandmother, Astrid, is eighty-four, sharp as a tack, and the owner of a hip that had been declining for two years. In September she fell on a wet step outside her building and fractured the top of her thigh bone. She was taken by ambulance to the regional hospital, and I was on a train by the evening with a bag of clothes, a phone charger, and a paperback she has been meaning to finish since April.

Arrival at the ward was a shock of bright lights and hospital smells. She lay in a corner bed, propped on pillows, her white hair combed, and holding a plastic cup of water with two hands. She said hello with an ironic eyebrow, and asked whether I had brought her glasses, which I had forgotten. A nurse called Bettan brought a spare pair from a box of lost property, and Astrid pronounced them dreadful but adequate.

The surgeon, Dr Fransson, met us on the second morning at half past seven, in a corridor, in a green tunic and a pair of scuffed clogs. He explained that the fracture was displaced and that a partial hip replacement was the safest option at her age, since it allows her to put weight on the leg almost at once. He drew the joint on the back of a form, showed the new metal stem and ball, and asked Astrid whether she had questions. She had three, all specific and cheerful.

The operation was on Wednesday. I waited in the relatives' lounge for two hours with a cup of weak tea, reading the same page of her paperback repeatedly. At noon, Dr Fransson appeared, pulled off his cap, and said that it had gone well, that she was in recovery, and that the wound was clean. I remember that I was suddenly unable to speak, and shook his hand with both of mine.

Astrid was sleepy and pleasant in the afternoon, her face pink, a drip in her arm, and a small tube of oxygen at her nose. She asked me to feed the plant on the sill by her front glass. I told her that we would get to that. The physiotherapist, a young woman called Mirja, arrived at four and had her sit on the edge of the bed with her feet dangling for two minutes. It was the first movement, and it was celebrated as though a mountain had been climbed.

Visitors made the ward livelier. On the third day a delegation arrived from Astrid's building: the caretaker, Mr Lund, with a bunch of dahlias from the shared yard, and Mrs Persson from the flat above, who brought a cake and an urgent need to report on the wet step, which had since been fitted with a strip of rubber. Astrid received them like a monarch, thanked them, and asked whether anyone had watered her pot of thyme. The space filled with the smell of flowers and, for a while, with gossip.

She also had a long conversation with the woman in the next bed, a retired seamstress named Rut, who had come in for a knee. They compared scars, complained about the hospital's cold porridge, and exchanged recipes for plum jam. I heard Rut say that Astrid was the bravest person she had ever met, and Astrid reply, briskly, that she had merely been careful not to say what she thought. They agreed to write to each other, on paper, from their respective units.

Over the next three days a routine formed. Breakfast at seven, physiotherapy at nine, a walk of a few steps with a frame, lunch, rest, a second walk, and visitors at five. By Saturday she was walking to the end of the ward and back, with a frown of concentration that reminded me of Noor doing sums. The nurses adored her, partly because she called them by name and partly because she corrected the spelling on the whiteboard above her bed.

Medications were the next subject. A pharmacist visited on the fourth day with a trolley and a folder, and went through everything she takes: a blood pressure pill, a small dose of something for the thyroid, a painkiller after surgery, and an injection each evening to prevent clots for the first weeks. She explained why the injection matters, showed me how it is done in case Astrid needs it at home, and gave me a chart to tick each dose. Astrid said she had taken pills since before the pharmacist was born.

Practical matters occupied Saturday afternoon. Gudrun explained the application for home help, which is decided by the municipality, and gave me a form. Mirja described precautions for the new joint: no crossing the legs, no bending past ninety degrees, a raised toilet seat, a chair with arms, and a stick. We made a list of adaptations for her flat, and I photographed the lavatory on my phone. My cousin Ebba, who lives nearby, offered to fit a second handrail on the stairs.

On Sunday a planning meeting was held with Dr Fransson, Mirja, a social worker named Gudrun, and me. They explained the pathway: discharge on Tuesday to a rehabilitation unit, not directly home, because at her age the stairs and bath would be too risky. The surgeon planned six weeks of supervised rehabilitation, with daily exercises, walking practice, stairs, and a home assessment by an occupational therapist before she leaves. Astrid listened with her chin lifted and asked whether she could bring her own tea.

The transfer on Tuesday was orderly, with a wheelchair ride to a taxi, a bag of clothes, and a folder of papers. The rehabilitation unit is a bright, modern building by a lake, where every chamber has a view of birches. She was shown her berth by a therapist, who put her on a walking frame and had her cross the floor twice. Astrid told her that she had been walking since 1943 and did not need a frame, but took it anyway.

Afterthoughts, on the train home. It is odd how a fall takes a person from independence to a ward in a day. I have never seen my grandmother so vulnerable, and yet she remained the same, elegant, curious, and a bit bossy. I will return on Saturday with her paperback, a thermos of proper tea, and a small radio. I have also promised to check on the plant, and to call Ebba about the handrail.

Diary, comparing self-storage units for the winter. When the loft got cleared out, it became clear that there was still too much stuff in the flat: Noor's outgrown bicycle, two suitcases of winter clothes, boxes of books, a tent, a box of skis that I do not use, and the crib parts that I promised to hand on and did not. I decided to rent a small storage unit for six months while I sort things out, and to compare the options properly before signing anything.

The requirements, written down before I looked at anything: about ten to twelve square metres, ground floor or with a lift, accessible at least until nine in the evening, dry and heated to the extent that books do not curl, within twenty minutes of the flat by car or bus, and a contract that can be ended with one month's notice. I also wanted a place that did not smell of damp, which I would test by opening a door and inhaling.

Search began online on a Sunday, with a browser full of tabs. There are four firms that serve my part of the city: Stashbox, near the ring road; Lagerhuset, in an old warehouse by the harbour; SafeSpace, a national chain with a big yellow logo; and a small family firm called Ulla's Rum, which occupies the basement of a former dairy. Each had a price calculator, a chat box, and a promise of a free first month, with fine print that varied enormously.

First visit: Stashbox, on Tuesday after work. It is a modern building of grey panels, with a keypad gate, cameras, and a friendly manager called Jonna, who took me through the corridors on a golf cart. The units are clean and bright, with metal doors and motion-sensing lights. She showed me a twelve square metre one, then a nine, and explained the insurance options. It was tidy and impersonal, and I liked that I could arrive at any hour with a code.

Second visit: Lagerhuset, in the old harbour warehouse. The building has a lift big enough for a car, brick walls, and a wooden floor that creaks. The manager, a lean man in a fleece, said that the units are colder in winter but cheaper, and that they do not heat them. I opened one, and the air was clear, but the door had a rusty track. He offered a discount if I signed for a year, which I declined, and I wrote down the price on my hand.

Third visit: SafeSpace, a large glass-fronted centre by the motorway. Here the process was efficient to the point of pressure: a salesperson took my name and phone number before answering any question, offered a special today price, and produced a form on a screen. I said that I was only comparing, and the smile flickered. The units were fine, the corridors wide, and the website claimed twenty-four hours a day access, though the small print said access requires prior notice after nine.

Fourth visit: Ulla's Rum. I nearly missed it, since the entrance is a green door beside a bakery, but the owner, Ulla, was at the top of the steps, with a cardigan and a cheerful bark. Her basement has thirty units, made of plywood and painted white, each with a padlock. It is dry, because she has a dehumidifier running, and the only cost is that access is between eight and eight. She showed me the fire exits, the sign-in book, and the cat, who guards the stairs.

Comparison, in a small grid on paper, since the online ones were confusing. Stashbox: clean, secure, with a lift and constant access, but expensive and with a three-month minimum. Lagerhuset: cold and slightly shabby, cheap, with a year discount. SafeSpace: professional but aggressive, with hidden fees for insurance and admin. Ulla's Rum: small, friendly, a bit old-fashioned, with monthly notice and a fair price. Noor voted for Ulla's, because of the cat.

One more consideration, which I nearly missed: the hours. Ulla's basement is open from eight to eight, but a friend who used it before said that Ulla sometimes lets regulars in early if they ring the bell. I asked whether that was true, and she said that she hardly sleeps and that anyone in real need of a tent at six in the morning can knock. I chose to take that as a form of hospitality rather than a policy.

Insurance was the surprising part. Every firm insists that the contents are the tenant's responsibility. Stashbox and SafeSpace sell cover at around six euros a month, Lagerhuset offers it for four, and Ulla asked whether my home policy covered stored goods. I phoned my insurer, who said that contents in a storage unit are covered up to a limit of five thousand euros, provided that the unit is in a locked building. I wrote this down and asked Ulla for a certificate.

Before deciding I did the arithmetic on volume, since it is easy to pay for space that never gets used. My load measures about eight cubic metres, stacked to a height of two metres, so a nine square metre unit would be tight and a twelve gives space for a walkway and a shelf. Ulla lent me a metre stick and let me pace out the space in the empty unit, which saved me from a costly mistake.

Decision, on Friday. The twelve square metre unit at Ulla's would cost sixty-nine euros a month, with no deposit, one month's notice, and a padlock supplied at cost, whereas Stashbox wanted ninety-four and a three-month minimum. The difference over six months is a hundred and fifty euros, which I preferred to keep. I telephoned her, and she said that she would hold the unit until Monday, provided that I promised to bring a cat treat as a rent premium.

Moving in on Saturday took two trips in a borrowed car. I packed the boxes by weight, heaviest at the bottom, labelled the sides, left a corridor down the middle so that I can reach anything, and photographed the arrangement for my records. Ulla inspected the padlock, signed my copy of the agreement, and handed me a key on a red ribbon. Noor gave the cat a treat and announced that she would visit every week. I will review in April.

Diary, the day Miso went missing. I want to write this down while I remember every detail, because at the time everything blurred. It started on a Sunday morning when I opened the balcony door to air the flat, went to make tea, and came back to find the door ajar and no cat. Miso is an indoor cat and has not been outside in the six years she has lived with us, apart from carrier trips to the vet. She had slipped out and gone down the fire escape.

The first half hour was calm and methodical. I put on shoes, took a bag of her favourite treats, and shook it at the bottom of the fire stairs while calling her name in the voice she responds to. The yard is small, enclosed by a fence on three sides, and full of bins and bicycles. I looked under every bike, behind each bin, inside a wheelbarrow, and up the small ash tree by the back wall. Nothing. A neighbour said she had seen a grey shape near the fence, a couple of minutes earlier.

By ten I had woken Noor, told her carefully, and watched her go still. She proposed a search team, and I noted that she did not cry, which I found more alarming than crying. She drew a map of the yard and the surrounding streets, marked the places a cat might hide, and assigned each of us to a zone. She took the block behind the flats and I took the street. Ingrid, from downstairs, offered to check the cellar and the bike shed, and set off in her dressing gown with a brush, which she said was for moral support.

The advice online for a missing indoor cat is clear: she will probably be within a few hundred metres, hiding, frightened and silent. Do not chase, do not call loudly; sit and wait, and put her own bedding and food outside to draw her scent. I put her blanket and a bowl of tuna by the fire escape and sat on the bottom step for an hour with a flask of tea, wearing two jumpers and Noor's woolly hat, which is the kind of thing one does not remember afterwards. Nothing came except a pigeon, which regarded the tuna with interest.

At noon I made posters. A photograph from my phone, showing Miso sitting on the sofa arm looking imperious, with the words MISSING CAT, grey tabby, white paws, and my number. I printed thirty copies at the library, laminated ten, and taped them to lamp posts along the four surrounding streets. Noor stuck one to the door of the bakery, standing on tiptoe to reach the highest possible spot on the glass, and the woman inside offered a biscuit, saying that her own cat had once vanished for three days and returned smelling of fish.

Afternoon: calls started coming. A man phoned to say he had seen a cat on a roof, which turned out to be an orange one. A woman phoned about a grey cat in her yard two streets over, and I ran there, only to find a small fat cat with a bell. Each time my heart leapt and fell. Mira sent a message offering to come with a torch that evening. A neighbour with a lost-pets group posted the notice, and it was shared thirty times.

Dusk. As the light fell, I walked the streets with a torch and the treats bag, listening. Cats are silent when frightened, but a faint sound sometimes carries at night, and I stood in alleys for minutes at a time, holding my breath. I checked under parked cars, behind hedges, in the doorways of closed shops. At nine, with Noor asleep on the sofa, I went out again, and walked until my feet hurt. At eleven, I left the balcony door open a hand's width, and sat up.

Sleep came in pieces. At one I dreamed of her calling from a drainpipe, at two I woke to the sound of rain and went to the balcony to look at the dark yard, and at four I sat on the sofa with Noor's small sandal in my hand, listening to the building settle. I texted Mira, who was awake too, and she wrote back that the statistics are good: most indoor cats are found close to home within days, usually hiding, and usually hungry.

Sunday night had one more piece, which I put in the record because it made me feel less alone. Around midnight, a figure appeared at the fence, a young man in a hooded jacket, holding a torch. He was one of the neighbours from the lost-pets group. He had walked around the block twice with a bag of fish sticks and wanted to leave it with me in case it helped. We stood in the cold and talked quietly about cats for ten minutes, then he went home.

Monday morning began with a phone call at ten past seven. A woman named Berit, who lives across the road from us, said that her husband had heard scratching in their shed. She sounded doubtful. I ran across in my slippers. The shed door was ajar, and in the dim light I saw a grey tail hanging from a shelf of flowerpots. Miso was curled on a folded sack, blinking and thin, and permitted me to pick her up without protest, which is not a thing she does.

The details, for the record: she was found asleep inside the neighbour's shed on Hamngatan, about two hundred metres from our door, sixteen hours after she slipped out. She had no injuries beyond a scratch on her nose and a large quantity of cobweb. She drank a whole bowl of water, ate tuna at speed, and then slept for the rest of the day on my lap, while I sat with a very stiff back and did not move for any reason.

Follow-up: I took her to the vet on Tuesday for a check, and Dr Halvorsen said she was dehydrated but well, and weighed her at four and a half kilos. I bought a chest harness and a cat-proof net for the balcony, and taped the fire escape gate shut. The posters came down on Wednesday, with a small thank-you note tied to the lamp post outside the bakery, and Berit was given a bunch of tulips. Noor wrote a note to Miso, promising not to lose her again.

Cutover rehearsal for the orders store, Thursday evening.
