The plan is to move the orders data off the old Postgres 11 host in Frankfurt and onto the managed cluster Dario set up last month, and nobody wants to learn the sharp edges on the real night. So tonight was a full dress rehearsal against a copy taken from last Sunday's backup. I booked the small meeting room, put a sticky note on the door, and kept a running log on my laptop as we went.

Before touching anything I wrote down the preconditions. The application must be in read-only mode for the whole copy, the replication slot on the old host must be dropped afterwards so it stops holding back disk, and the connection string in the secrets store has to be swapped by one person only, to avoid two people fixing the same thing in opposite directions. Dario volunteered as the person who swaps it. Priya will watch error rates on the dashboard and shout if the checkout failures rise above the usual background of about eleven per hour.

We started at 18:05 by freezing writes on the staging copy of the app. While the dump ran, Priya wandered off to fetch a spare monitor and came back with two, so we could keep the dashboard and the terminal side by side. The dump itself ran with four parallel jobs and finished before the tea went cold, which was a pleasant surprise; the compressed archive came out at 38 GB against the 210 GB on disk, mostly because the audit history relation is enormous and compresses like a dream. Dario noticed that two indexes on the shipments relation were invalid on the source, left over from an aborted build in the spring. We dropped them from the plan and noted that they should be rebuilt after the move rather than copied over dead.

Restoring into the new cluster was the part I had been dreading, mostly because the vendor documentation quotes a rule of thumb of one minute per five gigabytes and I did not believe it. The dry run restore took fifty-one minutes flat, and the extra time was almost all index creation on the audit history relation, where a single index needed nearly twenty minutes on its own. If we raise the maintenance memory setting for the session, Dario thinks we can shave perhaps a quarter off that, so I added it to the checklist as a change to test on the second rehearsal instead of trusting on faith. Nobody objected to a second rehearsal; the room went quiet in the way that means everyone was privately hoping for exactly that.

After the restore we ran the consistency checks. Row counts matched on all sixty-four relations except one: the sessions set was short by 212 rows, and it took us a while to understand why. Those were sessions created between the backup snapshot and the freeze, so on the real night they will be in the source and will arrive in the copy, but tonight the copy came from Sunday's backup and could not have them. Priya proposed a checksum comparison on the three relations that matter most, orders, payments and refunds, and those matched to the last byte. That felt like real evidence rather than a shrug.

Then the awkward bit: rolling back. A plan that only goes forward is not a plan. We rehearsed pointing the staging app back at the old host and confirmed it came up within ninety seconds, but we also found that a background worker caches the database address at startup and keeps it until restarted. That would have kept talking to the wrong host after a rollback, and nobody would have noticed for hours. Adding a worker restart to both the forward and the backward path is now item eleven on the list.

Open questions I am carrying home. First, who is reachable if the swap goes wrong at two in the morning; Dario will be on call but I want a second name, and I will ask Marguerite on Friday. Second, the vendor support line for the managed cluster promised a four hour response, which is useless during a cutover, so I need to find out whether a paid tier gives a live contact for the night. Third, the customers in Lisbon and Madrid are the most active around midnight, so we may want to nudge the window later than we assumed.

Small digression that still belongs here: the old host is named after a river, as all the hosts in that rack are, and Dario wants the new cluster to get a boring name on purpose, because a name nobody jokes about is a name nobody grows attached to. We settled on orders-primary and moved on.

Wrapping up at 21:20, we agreed the second rehearsal should happen next Wednesday with the memory setting changed and the worker restart scripted. I copied the log into the migration folder, renamed the sticky note on the door, and walked home the long way past the river to clear my head. Tomorrow's job is turning the eleven checklist items into scripts so that the real night is mostly typing one command and watching graphs.

Hiring loop debrief for the backend engineer role, written the same afternoon so I do not smooth it over later. We saw four candidates over two days and this note is about the third, Tobias Rehnquist, whom I will call T here. The panel was me, Kalinda from the platform group, and Owen from product acting as the non-engineer voice. The role is the second backend hire on a team of five, so the main question all along was whether someone could work inside an existing codebase rather than write beautiful things alone.

His résumé was solid without being showy: six years at a logistics software firm in Rotterdam, the last two leading a small team that owned route calculation. The phone screen the week before had been notably good. He explained a production problem from his past, a routing job that got slower every Friday, and he walked through how he narrowed it down to a growing temp table rather than the algorithm everyone blamed. That is the kind of story I trust because it includes the wrong turn.

The morning session was a system design conversation. Kalinda gave him a scenario, a notification service that has to deliver reminders to a million users without hammering the mail provider, and he asked clarifying questions for almost ten minutes before drawing anything. I liked that. His design used a queue with per-provider rate limits and a small delay bucket for retries, and when Owen asked what happens when a user changes their reminder time after it is scheduled, he paused, said he had not thought about it, and then worked out a cancellation-token approach on the spot.

The afternoon exercise is where opinions diverged. We ask every candidate to fix a failing test in a small sample repository while one of us pairs with them and talks. I paired with T. He read the failing test carefully, ran it twice, and before editing anything said aloud what he believed the bug was; he was right, an off-by-one in a pagination helper. What I noticed most was how he treated me: when I suggested a different fix, he tried mine first and explained why he preferred his afterwards. Kalinda, who watched from the shared screen, was less impressed and thought he coded slowly. I would rather have careful than quick, but I wrote both views down. In the shared scoring sheet I scored him three for pairing, on our scale of one to four, where four is reserved for people who make the session better for everyone in it.

For the record, the weaker points. He was vague on testing strategy beyond unit tests and had never worked with contract tests between services, which our stack leans on. He also asked twice about on-call expectations, which is a fair question and not a mark against him, though it tells me he wants boundaries and we should be honest about our pager rota. His salary expectation of 88,000 euros is within our band, but near the top for a candidate with his exact experience.

Owen's take, which I want to keep because it changed my mind slightly: T listened to the customer scenario more than either of the other candidates and repeated back the actual user problem before proposing a solution. Owen said that in six months he would rather have a colleague like that than a faster typist. Kalinda's counter was that we are short-staffed now, and a slow start hurts. Both points are fair, and I suspect that is why the sheet ended up with a mixed score rather than a clean yes.

Where we landed: no decision today. Kalinda will look at his take-home notes again, Owen will ask the recruiter whether T has another offer with a deadline, and I will draft two reference questions focused on how he handles disagreement with a manager. We meet again on Monday at ten, and I promised to bring a one-page summary rather than my rambling notes.

A few loose observations before I forget them. The recruiter said T was punctual to the minute and thanked the receptionist by name, which Owen counts as data even though I am not sure it should be. The other three candidates split roughly evenly: the first was fast and confident but talked over Kalinda twice, the second was a quiet specialist in data pipelines who would suit a different team, and the fourth arrives tomorrow, so I am holding back a final view until every session is on paper. I also want to fix our process. The pairing exercise rewards people who are comfortable being watched, and that is not the same skill as being good at the job, so next quarter I will suggest offering a take-home option with a short walkthrough call instead. I will raise it with Kalinda over lunch on Thursday, and if she disagrees I will drop it without sulking.

Trial of a translation vendor for the Spanish version of the product, a working log across two weeks. Until now the app has existed in Danish and English only, and a run of requests from customers in Madrid and Valencia, plus a partner in Mexico City, has pushed Spanish to the top of the list. I am running the pilot on my own because Marguerite wanted an outside view of quality before committing budget, and because I speak enough Spanish to be dangerous: good enough to spot an odd phrase, not good enough to be sure it is wrong.

What we are translating. The interface has about 2,900 strings, from button labels to error messages, and roughly 11,000 words in total. The help centre is another 25 articles, which I am leaving out of the pilot. To keep the trial fair and small, I chose a slice of 180 strings covering every kind of text: short labels, sentences with placeholders, plurals, a handful of long explanations and the emails we send after a payment failure. I wrote a context note for each string, saying where it appears and who reads it, because the worst translations are the ones made without knowing whether 'Save' is a button or a verb in a sentence.

Two candidates. The first vendor, Lingua Norte, is a small agency in Barcelona that Ilse's cousin had used. The second, Tradify, is an online platform with a pool of freelancers and machine translation that a person edits afterwards. I asked both for the same slice and the same turnaround. Lingua Norte replied within an hour with a friendly email and a name, Rosalba, who would be my contact for the pilot. Tradify sent an automated quote in seconds and then went quiet for a day, which told me something about how they handle questions.

Delivery. Rosalba sent the files a day early, with a short list of questions attached, such as whether the app addresses users formally or informally and whether 'workspace' should be translated at all. Those questions were a good sign; they showed someone had read my context notes. Tradify's file arrived on the third day with no questions and a glossary I had not asked for, and it was translated by a person, not a machine, though I could tell by the consistency of phrases that a memory tool had helped.

Reviewing. I asked two people to help me judge. Consuelo, a friend of Kalinda's in Valencia, and Ottilie's partner, who is from Seville, each read both versions blind, without knowing which vendor produced which, and marked every string as good, acceptable or wrong. Then I compared their marks. On the 180 strings, Lingua Norte got 152 good, 22 acceptable and 6 wrong. Tradify got 139 good, 29 acceptable and 12 wrong. The wrong ones at Tradify were mostly about placeholders: a sentence in which the variable landed in the wrong grammatical spot, and two where a plural was treated as a singular. Lingua Norte's errors were more subtle, mainly register, where they chose a slightly stiff form.

Formal or informal. Consuelo had a strong opinion on the register question. Spanish customers in a work tool, she said, would expect the informal form in Spain but formal in parts of Latin America, and no single choice pleases everyone. We agreed to write the interface in a neutral style that avoids direct address wherever possible, using infinitives for buttons and impersonal phrasing for messages, which is the convention in many apps. Rosalba said it can be done and proposed a short style guide, which she would write for 60 euros.

Before pricing, one more check I ran on my own. I fed a dozen of the tricky strings, the plurals and the ones with placeholders, into a free machine translation tool, to have a floor to compare against. It got the plain labels right and mangled almost every sentence with a variable, which is useful to know: it tells me the vendors are earning their fee mostly on the hard ten percent, not on the easy ninety. I saved the outputs next to the vendor files so that the reviewers could see all three if they wanted, though I asked them to mark only the two human versions to avoid biasing the result. Consuelo said afterwards that the machine version made her laugh twice, and one of those strings was the word for 'Archive', rendered as the word for a filing room.

I also wrote a short brief for the reviewers, because a vague request produces vague marks. Mark each string good if you would ship it as it is, acceptable if it is understandable but you would edit it, and wrong if it is misleading, ungrammatical or breaks a placeholder. Note any string where the answer depends on context I did not give. Both spent about ninety minutes over two evenings, and I paid each of them 60 euros for it, which I will claim back.

Money. Lingua Norte priced the pilot at 0.09 euros per word, which for the 1,340 words in my slice comes to about 121 euros, with a minimum order of 150 that they waived because it is a pilot. Tradify quoted 0.06 per word for the editing tier and 0.11 for the full human tier, and I picked the human tier for a fair comparison. Both promised delivery in three working days. In terms of price at scale, the interface alone would cost roughly 990 euros at Lingua Norte's rate, and about 660 to 1,200 at Tradify's, depending on the tier.

Decision. On quality, Lingua Norte is ahead; on price, Tradify is cheaper by about a third at scale; on responsiveness, the small agency wins by a wide margin. My recommendation to Marguerite will be to go with Lingua Norte for the interface and reserve Tradify's platform for the help articles, where a cheaper tier may do. I will ask for a fixed price for the whole interface and a commitment to review updates within two days, since our releases move quickly and new strings appear every week. I will send the recommendation on Monday with the comparison table and the reviewers' marks attached.

Investigation into the rising cost of log storage, over three afternoons. Marguerite forwarded the cloud provider's monthly statement with a single line of comment, "why did this double?", and I volunteered before anybody else could. The line item for log storage and search had gone from about 1,900 dollars in the spring to 3,900 last month, while traffic had grown by perhaps a fifth. Something other than normal growth was going on, and finding it was more fun than I expected, in the way that detective work is fun when it is not your money.

First look. The logging platform reports storage by source. I exported the numbers into a spreadsheet and sorted by volume: the top five sources produced seventy-one percent of everything. In first place was the API gateway, with 38 percent, followed by the payment worker, the search service, the background job runner and, surprisingly, a small internal tool called the scheduler, at nine percent. A scheduler that runs ten small jobs an hour has no business producing nine percent of the volume, so I began there.

The scheduler. Reading its output, I found that it logged the full text of every job's input on every run, and one job, a nightly export, had an input of several hundred kilobytes. Worse, the log level had been raised to debug during an incident in June and never lowered again. Wenzel remembered doing it, apologised in the channel, and lowered it back to info in a two-line change. That single change cut the scheduler's contribution by about ninety percent, which shaved roughly 330 dollars a month.

The gateway. This is the big one. Each request produces three lines: one on arrival, one when the response starts, and one on completion. Only the last carries information we use, since it includes the status, the duration and the route. I asked the team which of the three lines anyone had ever queried, and found no one who had searched for the first two in the last six months. Kalinda asked whether the arrival line helps in a crash, when the completion line never appears. It might, but only for requests that fail to finish, and there is a cheaper way to see those: the gateway can log an arrival line only if the request exceeds five seconds. That is a sampling rule, and it cuts the volume by roughly two thirds for that source.

Retention. The platform keeps everything for ninety days in fast searchable storage. I looked at how far back people actually search: over the last quarter, ninety-four percent of queries touched data less than fourteen days old, and the remaining six percent looked at incidents up to five weeks back. So I proposed thirty days in fast storage and then an archive in cheap object storage for another eleven months, where the data can be restored if needed, though slowly. Dario checked that the archive format can be read back and ran a test restore of one day of data, which took twenty minutes and worked.

Quiet duplication. Digging into the payment worker, I found something embarrassing. Every log line was emitted twice, once by the application and once by a library that forwards the same message. Nobody noticed because the two lines have different formats, and a search returns both. I fixed it with a configuration change and confirmed that the volume from that source halved. Priya asked if the duplicates had ever confused our dashboards; a couple of counts of payment attempts had looked inflated, which we had blamed on retries.

A side effect I did not plan for: while comparing sources, I noticed that the search service logs each query's full text, including what customers type into the search box, and some of it is personal, names and email addresses. That is a privacy question more than a cost one, and I do not want to bury it in a cost note, so I raised it with Marguerite separately. For now I reduced the retention of that source to seven days, which also saves money, and Kalinda will look at masking the query text before it is written. Ilse, who handles our data protection questions, asked to be told when the change is live so she can update the record of processing.

I also reviewed which dashboards depend on the lines I am about to remove. Wenzel searched the saved queries and found four that read the gateway's arrival lines, all of them created by one person who has since left. Two were dead links, one was a chart of requests per minute that could be computed from the completion lines just as well, and one I could not identify, so I asked in the channel and got no answer in a day, which I took as permission after a further two days' notice.

Putting it together. I estimated each change against last month's volumes. Lowering the scheduler level saves about 330 dollars, sampling the gateway's arrival lines about 520, removing the duplicate in the payment worker about 270, and moving older data to the archive tier about 330, less a small cost for the archive itself. With all changes in place, monthly spend drops from 3,900 to 2,450, which is a saving of about 1,450 dollars, or 37 percent, and returns us to the trend line we would have had without the leak. I wrote the estimate in a one-page note with the assumptions in a table, so that Marguerite can challenge any number.

Safeguards. Cost cutting on logs can backfire when an incident happens and the evidence is gone. To guard against that, Dario will keep the previous configuration in version control and a switch that restores full detail for a service for six hours, which we can flip during an investigation. We also agreed to add an alert when daily log volume grows more than twenty percent in a week, so the next leak is noticed in days, not months. I will do the changes in three steps over two weeks and report the actual numbers after the next statement arrives.

Planning notes for the customer advisory board, our first attempt at bringing a small group of customers together to shape the product. Blake proposed it in the summer, Marguerite liked it, and Avery joined this week to help with the practical side. The thinking is simple: we make decisions about the product on partial information, and a dozen thoughtful customers who meet with us regularly could improve those decisions. But the risk is a talking shop that produces nice photographs and no change, and we have both seen that happen at other companies.

Purpose. We wrote one sentence: the board exists to test our plans before we commit to them and to tell us what we are missing. That excludes several tempting uses. It is not a sales event, not a support forum and not a place to announce things. Each session will have one or two decisions on the table, for instance whether the export feature should come before or after the new reports, and members will be told at the start which questions we are actually going to act on, so that nobody feels their input vanished.

Membership. Blake started a list of forty candidates from account records, and we applied criteria. A mix of sizes, from a two-person shop in Ghent to a company with several hundred users. A spread of industries and countries, so that no single sector dominates the room. People who have used the product for at least a year and who write honest tickets, since honesty matters more than enthusiasm. And a limit of twelve, because more than twelve people cannot all speak in a two-hour session. We deliberately left out our three biggest customers, whom I will not name here, since their needs are already heard through account management, and we do not want the board to become theirs.

Invitation. Avery drafted a short message, three paragraphs long, that says what we are asking: three sessions a year, two hours each, plus occasional short surveys. In return, members get early access to features, a direct line to the product team and a small yearly gift of 150 euros to a charity of their choice, which avoids anything that looks like payment for opinions. Marguerite wanted to add a line about confidentiality, which is sensible, since members will see unreleased plans, and Blake wrote a plain-language paragraph instead of a legal agreement, with a formal one available for those who prefer it.

Format. We discussed remote versus in person for a long time. Remote is cheaper and easier, but Blake's experience is that people say more over a shared meal than over a screen, and that relationships built face to face carry the remote sessions afterwards. We settled on a hybrid pattern: the first session in person, one remote session in spring, and one in person in the autumn. Travel costs will be covered for those who come from farther than a hundred kilometres, and we set a budget of 6,500 euros for the year.

Agenda draft. Ten o'clock, introductions and the ground rules. Then a session on the export feature, with Nadia and Avery in the room and Marguerite joining for the last twenty minutes, and with Nadia showing rough mock-ups on paper rather than polished screens, so people feel free to criticise. After lunch, a session on reports, with Blake asking what customers do with the numbers after they leave our product. A closing hour, held in a circle without laptops, on what we are not doing well, with an anonymous card exercise, and a plain statement of what we will do with the feedback within six weeks. Each session gets a written summary that goes back to members within a week, in plain text, with our decisions marked and our doubts marked in a different colour, so that members can see where their voice landed and where it did not.

Open points. Who moderates? Blake suggested that neither he nor Avery should, since they are too close to the product; an outside facilitator would cost about 900 euros, and Marguerite will decide whether the budget allows. Should we record the sessions? Probably audio only, with permission, and deleted after the summary is written, in line with our retention policy. We also need a plan for the uncomfortable case where a member is dominant or negative for the whole session, and Avery will write three sentences on how to handle it kindly.

Venue and date. Most of our likely members are in the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany, so a central location matters, and the venue must be near a train station, since many customers prefer not to drive. Blake looked at Utrecht, Antwerp and Düsseldorf, and picked Utrecht for its rail links and because a meeting room in a converted factory near the station was free at a reasonable price, 480 euros for the day. The first session is Thursday 13 November in Utrecht, from 10:00 to 16:00, with lunch and a short evening dinner for those who stay, at a restaurant a few minutes' walk from the venue, booked for fourteen people so that our own team fits as well. That date avoids the school holidays, the largest trade fair in our sector, and the week when finance teams are busy with quarter closing.

Next steps. Blake sends the invitations on Monday, and follows up by phone with the five most important candidates. Avery books the venue and catering with a deposit that is refundable until a month before. Marguerite chooses the moderator by Friday. We will meet again in ten days to confirm who has accepted, and if fewer than eight people say yes, we will postpone rather than run a thin first session.

Post-incident review: the ingestion backlog after the expired certificate. Attendees were Blake, Avery, Ines from infrastructure, Colm from customer support, and Yusuf, who joined by video from his sister's flat because his train was delayed. The format is blameless, as always: we describe what happened, what we saw, what we believed at each moment, and what we will change. Blake took minutes; Avery chaired. This is the written record, and it is long because the sequence matters more than the conclusion.

Summary of impact. Between roughly three and nine in the morning last Tuesday, partner devices could not push readings to our ingestion endpoint. About 1,900 devices retried on a backoff schedule and eventually queued locally, so nothing was lost permanently, but roughly 14 hours of readings arrived late and out of order once service recovered. Twenty-three customers wrote in, most of them politely, and three asked whether the dashboards were wrong. Colm handled all of them by early afternoon and kept a list of who received which explanation.

Detection. Our synthetic probe, which posts a fake reading every minute, started failing at 03:14. It pages the on-call engineer through the alert relay, and the page was delivered, but the phone was on a do-not-disturb schedule that had been set up for a holiday and never switched back. That is a personal habit and a team gap, and we agreed to write it down as the second one. Nobody looked at the dashboard until Ines started her day at 06:40 and saw a wall of red. Colm, meanwhile, had seen a customer message at 06:15 but assumed it was the customer's own network problem, which was a reasonable guess given the previous week.

Diagnosis. Ines opened the probe logs and found a plain handshake failure, then checked the certificate on the front proxy. The expired credential had been renewed on paper in March, the ticket was closed, and the new file was issued by the authority, but it never reached the load balancer; the renewal script wrote it to a staging directory and the deployment step that copies it across had been disabled during a migration and never re-enabled. The old certificate lapsed at 03:12 UTC on Tuesday, which explains the probe failing two minutes later once its cached session finally dropped. Ines said the moment she read the expiry date she felt slightly sick, because the reminder email from the authority had gone to a shared mailbox nobody reads.

Recovery. Installing the new file took eleven minutes, not because it was hard but because Ines wanted a second person to confirm the chain before she restarted anything, and Yusuf was still asleep. Once the proxy reloaded at 07:22, devices began reconnecting, and this caused the second problem. About 1,900 devices reconnected within a few minutes of each other, and the ingestion queue depth climbed from near zero to over four million messages. The workers autoscaled, but the database connection pool capped out at sixty, so the queue drained slowly. Ines raised the pool limit by hand at 08:05, the queue peaked at 08:20, and by 09:10 the backlog was gone. In hindsight the pool limit should have been raised before restarting the proxy, and we noted that the runbook says nothing about it.

What went well. The probe worked as designed, and the customers who queued locally lost nothing. Support had a holding message ready within forty minutes of Ines confirming the cause, and the phrasing, which Colm drafted, avoided both jargon and false comfort. What went badly is the list that matters. Renewal was a manual ticket, the copy step was silently disabled, reminders went to a dead mailbox, the page was missed, and the runbook did not mention connection limits.

Actions agreed. First, Ines will move certificate issuance to the automated renewal service and delete the manual ticket path, due by the end of next month. Second, the reminder addresses become the on-call alias plus two named people. Third, Yusuf will add a check that reports the days remaining on every public certificate and pages when fewer than twenty-one remain. Fourth, Avery will audit the do-not-disturb problem by adding a weekly test page that must be acknowledged, so a silent phone is discovered on a Monday and not during an outage. Fifth, Colm will publish a short status page entry template so support does not have to invent wording under pressure.

Discussion of severity. We argued for a while about whether this counted as an outage or a delay, since no data was lost. Yusuf argued that partners experience it as an outage regardless, and that our own definition should follow what customers feel. Blake agreed and asked that we label it a severity two, which the group accepted. We also agreed to send one factual message to all affected partners instead of leaving the explanation to individual support replies.

Closing thoughts. The review ended at 15:40. Ines asked that the actions be tracked on the board with owners and dates, and we will revisit progress in three weeks. Avery closed by thanking Ines for describing her own mistakes without hedging, which is the reason these sessions are worth holding.

Call notes and follow-up thoughts on the renewal with the monitoring vendor, Brightwell Metrics. Present were Avery, the account executive Dorothea Vance, and a solutions engineer named Rui who mostly stayed silent until asked for numbers. Our current contract ends on the last day of next month, and the renewal quote that arrived two weeks ago was a hefty jump, so I went into this call with a list of objectives rather than a mood.

The starting position. Dorothea opened by thanking us for three years of partnership, which is how every negotiation with her begins. Then she restated the quote: 74,000 dollars for twelve months, up from 52,000, justified by a new platform tier that bundles tracing and log search. I said that we use dashboards and alerting and never opened the tracing product, and that a jump of forty-two percent for features we did not request felt like a price increase dressed up as an upgrade. She replied that the old tier was being retired at the end of the year, and that everyone was moving.

What I already knew. Before the call I had asked two friends at other companies what they pay, and both said their renewals landed about twenty percent above the previous year, not forty. I also knew that our usage is well below the committed volume: we have paid for 3,000 monitored hosts and averaged 2,150 across the last two quarters. Rui confirmed that number, a little reluctantly, which gave me an argument to use. I asked to be moved to a plan sized for 2,400 hosts, with headroom of about ten percent for growth.

The middle of the call was slow. Dorothea said she would need to consult her manager, went on mute for several minutes, and returned offering a discount of eight percent on the new tier if we signed for two years. I said no to two years. A multi-year commitment removes the one lever I have, which is the ability to leave, and the honest truth is that a cheaper competitor has been courting Marguerite since spring. I did not say the competitor's name aloud, only that we had options. She noticed the pause and moved on quickly.

Before that, though, there was a stretch about service terms that I nearly skipped in these notes. I asked Rui what the uptime commitment is for the alerting pipeline, since the old contract promised 99.9 percent and the new paper mentioned only 'commercially reasonable efforts'. He admitted he did not know, and Dorothea promised to check with legal. I said that if the commitment disappears, the price should drop further, because we are paying for reliability as much as for graphs. Nobody argued, which I took as a sign that the wording was an accident of a template and not a strategy. I also raised our data retention: today we keep thirteen months of metrics, and the new tier defaults to ninety days unless we buy an add-on. That would have been a quiet way to add another 6,000 dollars, and I asked her to confirm in writing that thirteen months stays included. She said she would try, which is not a yes, so it goes on my follow-up list with a note to chase.

Rui then walked through how host counts are measured, which turned out to be useful. The count is taken as the daily maximum of distinct agents reporting, averaged across the month, so a burst of temporary build machines does not inflate the bill unless it lasts. I had feared the opposite. That reassurance let me commit to the 2,400 figure without worrying that a busy week in the release cycle would trigger overage charges, and I asked him to email the exact definition so it cannot drift.

Then came the offer. After a second break she dropped the ask to 61,000 dollars for a one-year term on the 2,400 host plan, with the tracing bundle included at no extra cost for the first six months so we could evaluate it. I asked for the tracing trial in writing, and for the price to be locked for the following renewal, capped at seven percent above. She agreed to draft both and send them by Thursday. I said I would take the offer to my team and reply by the following Monday, and I meant that; I did not accept on the call, even though the number is better than I had hoped for.

Afterwards I wrote down what I think happened. The first quote was an anchor, the eight percent for two years was a carrot for lock-in, and the final figure is probably close to her real floor for this quarter, because she was clearly trying to close before month end. I could push for another few thousand by waiting, but the cost of an unhappy switch at the very last minute, with alert rules to migrate and dashboards to rebuild, outweighs the saving.

Questions for the team before Monday. Does anyone actually use the tracing product, and would they after the free six months? Rahil in operations says he might, for the payments path. Can we live with the support tier, which stays at business hours only? What happens to our saved dashboards if we leave? Rui said exports are available as files, but I want to see that they can be re-imported anywhere.

My plan is short. Tomorrow morning I will forward the summary to Marguerite with a recommendation to accept, on condition the written terms match what was said today. If the terms come back different in any detail, especially the price cap, I will reopen the conversation instead of signing. Then I will book a calendar reminder for the renewal after this one, at ten months, so that we start negotiating early and not in the last two weeks.

Support escalation log: Patisserie Duval and the double charge. The ticket arrived on Monday morning through the priority form, written in capital letters by the owner, Solène Duval, who runs three shops in Lyon and had just noticed that her account showed two identical monthly charges. The first line of her message was "I want my money and an explanation, in that order." I liked her immediately, and I took the ticket myself instead of leaving it in the general queue, because an angry customer with a specific grievance is usually the easiest kind to fix.

First hour: understanding the facts. I opened the billing record and found the two charges, both for the business plan, both on the first of the month, seven minutes apart. The second one carried a different reference, which suggested that the payment provider had retried after a timeout and our system had not recognised the retry as the same attempt. I checked the logs for that minute and saw the timeout error, a 504 from the provider's gateway, followed by our own worker scheduling another attempt without waiting for confirmation. That is our bug, not hers, plain and simple, and I wrote that sentence in the ticket, in the first person, before I wrote any reply so that nobody could later suggest otherwise.

Before replying I looked at how many other accounts might be affected. A quick query for pairs of charges on the same account within ten minutes returned nineteen accounts, all on the first of the month, all in a window when the provider had a degraded gateway. Of the nineteen, fourteen had already been auto-refunded by the provider's own duplicate detection. Five had not, and Solène's was the largest by far because she is on the multi-site plan. I put the list in a spreadsheet with the amounts and dates, tagged it for Marguerite, and asked Dario to look at making the retry idempotent, which is the correct long-term fix. I do not want this ticket to become a story about one unhappy baker when the real problem is in our payment worker.

The reply. I called her instead of writing, because it was clear that she wanted to be heard. I introduced myself, said I had found the duplicate, said it was our fault, and asked whether she wanted to hear the technical cause or the refund plan first. She chose the refund. I told her that the extra charge would be reversed in full, including the tax portion, and that she would see it appear within three to five working days. Then she asked why it had taken until Monday for anyone to notice, and I did not dodge: we have no alert for duplicate charges, and it will exist by the end of the month.

Between the call and the refund there was an internal step I want to record. Refunds above 1,000 euros need a second approver, a rule Marguerite introduced after an expensive mistake two years ago. I messaged Colm with the ticket link and the log excerpt, and he approved within ten minutes, adding a comment that the case was clean-cut. I like that rule more than I expected: it makes me re-read my own evidence before anything leaves the building.

Numbers, since finance will ask. The duplicate charge was the full monthly fee of 1,284.50 euros, since the multi-site plan covers her three shops and a set of extra seats. After checking the amount with the billing lead, I refunded 1,284.50 euros to the original card on Monday at 11:40 and attached the reference to the ticket. I also added a goodwill credit of one extra month on the smallest add-on, worth 49 euros, and asked her permission before applying it, because in my experience surprise credits look like hush money.

Her reaction was warm once the money was moving. She told me about a supplier who once billed her three times for flour and refused to admit it for a month. Then she asked, half joking, whether we might offer a discount for annual billing, because a yearly payment would mean fewer opportunities for a failure like this. I said I would pass it on to the pricing owner, and I did, with her name and shop count so nobody has to guess how large the account is.

Follow-up on Wednesday. The provider's dashboard showed the reversal as pending, and she emailed to say her bank had not yet displayed it. I explained that banks in France often take up to five days to post it and offered to send a document from the provider proving the refund, which she declined; she trusted the reference number. She also asked if we could send her monthly statements as PDF files for her accountant, which turned out to be already possible in settings, hidden three menus deep. I sent her the path and a screenshot, and added a note to the product board that the option is hard to find.

Closing the loop. On Thursday the refund cleared and she wrote a two-line message saying thanks. I updated the ticket, tagged the root cause, linked Dario's idempotency work, and posted a summary in the support channel so that the next person with a duplicate charge knows the exact procedure. The five unrefunded accounts were handled the same afternoon by Colm, using my script from the ticket. Nineteen customers, one bug, one fix in progress. Solène, for what it is worth, sent a box of almond pastries to the office the following week, which Colm ate before anyone else noticed.

Product planning session: the export feature. Present were Avery, Blake, Marguerite as the decision maker, and Nadia from design. We met for ninety minutes in the annex room with the projector broken, so Nadia drew on the whiteboard, which improved the discussion. The goal was simple to state and hard to do: settle the scope, the order of work and the date for letting customers take their data out of the product in a usable form. This is the most requested feature in our support tickets this quarter, and it comes up in every renewal conversation as a trust question.

What customers actually ask for. Blake had gone through the last 120 tickets that mention leaving, backing up or moving data, and grouped them. About half want a spreadsheet of their records so they can run their own reports. A quarter want a full archive including attachments, mostly in regulated industries where they must keep everything for years. The rest want a way to feed another tool automatically. Those are three different products, and one message from Marguerite cut through: "We do the first one well, we design the second properly, and we do not promise the third."

Scope debate. Nadia's mock-ups showed a wizard with four steps, choosing records, choosing fields, choosing a format, and confirming. Avery thought that was too much for a first version and proposed a single button that exports everything visible in the current view. Blake was uneasy about that: a customer with 200,000 records and a filter that hides most of them may believe they downloaded everything. We agreed to a compromise with two choices on one screen, current view or everything, and a plain sentence telling the user how many rows will be included before they press the button.

Format and limits. The first release will produce comma-separated files only. PDF was requested by several people, but it is a different engineering problem, with page layout, fonts and tables that break across pages, and nobody wanted to promise it and deliver something ugly. For large exports we will run the job in the background and email a download link that expires after seven days. Blake proposed a hard cap of one million rows per file, splitting into several files above that. Avery raised the cost of storing files temporarily, and we estimated that at current volumes the storage will cost less than 40 dollars a month, which nobody thought worth debating further.

Security and permissions took the longest. Who is allowed to export? Marguerite's view is that any admin may, but ordinary members may not by default, and that every export must leave a line in the audit trail with the person, the time and the row count. Blake asked about personal data: if the export includes email addresses of end customers, we are effectively handing over a mailing list. We decided that exports respect the same field-level permissions as the screens do, so a field a user cannot see is never in their file. Nadia will design the empty state for the case where someone lacks permission, and it must explain who to ask.

Timeline. After some back and forth about whether November was realistic, we walked backwards from the release. Engineering estimates three weeks for the core job and one week for the interface, plus a week for testing with two friendly customers who volunteered. The plan: design is finished by the end of this month, code freeze for export is 6 November, testing runs the following week, and release goes out on the 20th, ahead of the busy end-of-year period when support cannot afford surprises. Marguerite asked that we tell no customer a date until testing has passed.

Risks we named. The biggest is that big exports slow down the shared database; Avery will ask Dario to run the job against a read replica. The second is that people will export and then never come back, but Blake argued that trust wins more customers than lock-in ever kept. The third is that we forget the documentation, so Nadia will write the help article before the code is done, and we will review it as part of the definition of finished.

Decisions recorded: comma-separated first, PDF deferred, admins only by default, audit trail entry for every export, background jobs above 50,000 rows. Next review is in two weeks, in the same room with a working projector, and Blake will bring the ticket analysis in a shareable form. One last remark from Marguerite before we packed up: she wants the help article to include a sentence about how long a file stays available, because the first complaint will be a link that expired over a weekend. Nadia wrote it on the whiteboard, photographed it, and we went to find lunch at the place across the road.

Code review write-up for the pricing lookup cache, pull request number 412, opened by Wenzel. I reviewed it over two sittings on Tuesday and Wednesday, and I am writing my thoughts here in full because the summary comment I left on the pull request was polite and short, and the real reasoning is more interesting. The change adds an in-process cache in front of the function that calculates a customer's price given their plan, region and volume tier. That function is called on every page load for the billing screen, and it hits the database three times each call.

First impressions. The diff is about 280 lines, of which 90 are tests, which is a good ratio. Wenzel had written a clear description with a before-and-after profile screenshot. The design is a small least-recently-used cache with a maximum of 5,000 entries and an expiry of ten minutes. The key is built from the plan identifier, the region code and the volume tier. That looked sensible at first, and I nearly approved on that read, but then I remembered that discount codes also influence price, and the key does not include them.

The first real problem. If a customer applies a discount code, the function returns a different price, yet the cached entry for the same plan, region and tier would be served to the next person. I wrote a test to show it: two calls, one with a code and one without, and the second returned the discounted amount. Wenzel replied within the hour, embarrassed, and proposed adding the code to the key. I suggested instead separating the two concerns: cache the base price, which depends on three fields, and apply the discount afterwards, which is cheap arithmetic. That keeps the cache small and stops one campaign from filling it with thousands of variants.

The second problem was subtler. The expiry uses wall clock time, and the cache is populated inside a request handler with no lock, so under concurrent load two requests can compute the same value at the same moment and both write it. That is harmless for correctness but wasteful, and it defeats the purpose during exactly the spikes when we need the cache most. I proposed a per-key in-flight marker, and Wenzel argued, fairly, that added complexity might not be worth it. We agreed to measure before deciding.

Context that shaped my reading. This function has a history: it was rewritten last spring after a rounding bug that overcharged customers in Sweden by a few öre per order, and the tests around rounding are the most careful part of the file. So when I approved the arithmetic I was confident, and the only open question was whether the cache changed what the function returned. I also checked how the cache would behave across deploys. It lives in process memory, so every deploy starts cold, and with eight instances behind the balancer the first minute after a release sends a burst of queries to the database. Wenzel pointed out that this is the same as today, only without any benefit afterwards, and I could not argue with that. We also discussed whether a shared cache such as Redis would be better. It would remove the cold start and the eight separate copies, but it adds a network hop and a new failure mode to a page that currently has neither. For a function this cheap, I preferred in-process, and Wenzel agreed once we saw the numbers.

Measurement. Wenzel ran the staging replay we keep for this purpose, a recording of one hour of real traffic from last Thursday. Before the change, database queries for this function averaged 3.1 per request. With the revised key design, the hit rate climbed from 41 to 78 percent across the replay, and the median response time of the billing screen fell from 240 to 95 milliseconds. Our target was a hit rate above seventy, so the target is met. With the in-flight marker added, the hit rate barely moved, from 78 to 79, so I withdrew my request and we left the marker out and wrote down the reasoning in a code comment.

Smaller comments. I asked for a metric for hits and misses so we can watch the ratio on the dashboard. I also asked for the cache to be cleared when a price list is published, since ten minutes of stale prices after a change would confuse the sales team. Wenzel had not thought of that, but it took him twenty minutes: the publish job now calls an invalidation hook. One nitpick about naming: a variable called tmp held the region-adjusted price for a hundred lines, and I asked him to name it properly.

What I learned as a reviewer. My first instinct was to approve because the tests were tidy, and that would have shipped a pricing bug that ignores discount codes, the kind of defect that surfaces in a support ticket three weeks later. The habit I want to keep is to ask what inputs affect the output that the change does not know about. I also need to remember that praising good work explicitly costs nothing; I told Wenzel that the replay setup was what made the review easy.

Outcome. Wenzel pushed the fixes on Wednesday evening, I approved on Thursday morning, and the change was released behind a flag at ten percent of traffic, rising to full over the weekend if the error rate stays flat. On Monday the graphs looked calm, the flag was removed, and Wenzel wrote a short paragraph in the team notes describing the discount-code trap so the next person to build a cache remembers it. I added the invalidation hook to our review checklist under the heading of things that change what a function returns.

Expense reconciliation for the Lisbon trip, done on a rainy Saturday with a pot of tea and a shoebox. I went to Lisbon for four days to visit a customer and attend a two-day industry conference, and the company's finance policy says a claim must be submitted within thirty days with a receipt for anything over 25 euros. I am at day twenty-six, which is exactly the kind of margin I promise myself I will avoid and never do. This note is my working log so that when Ilse in finance asks questions, I have answers in one place.

The setup. Everything went into one spreadsheet with columns for date, vendor, currency, amount, category, payment method and receipt status. I started by emptying the shoebox onto the floor and sorting by day, which is faster than sorting by type. There were 31 pieces of paper, plus about twenty photographs on my phone of receipts I thought I had lost. Most of the printed ones had faded to a pale grey because thermal paper does not like a warm rucksack, so I photographed everything under the lamp and saved the images in a folder named after the trip.

Flights and lodging first, since they are the large items. The return flights from Copenhagen were booked through the company travel tool, so those are already recorded and I do not claim them again. The hotel was 142 euros a night for three nights, plus a city tax of 2 euros per night that was charged separately at checkout and appears on a different line of the folio. I nearly forgot that one. The customer visit meant one extra night at a guesthouse in Sintra, which cost 96 euros, paid in cash; the owner wrote a receipt by hand, which is acceptable under our policy as long as it has a name and a date.

Meals were next, and here the policy is a daily allowance of 55 euros instead of individual claims, so I do not need to itemise every espresso. What I do need is the number of days that qualify. Day one I arrived at 19:30 and ate at the airport, so half a day. Days two and three were conference days with lunch provided by the organisers, which reduces the allowance by a third for each. Day four was the customer visit with a business lunch that the customer paid for, so no claim for lunch, and I flew home at 17:00, another partial day. Ilse's spreadsheet formula for this is baffling, so I did the arithmetic by hand and got 151.25 euros in total, and I will let her formula tell me if I am wrong. Her template also has a cell for the per-diem rate that is still set to last year's 52 euros, so I overwrote it in my copy and mentioned it in the cover note.

Local transport is the messy category. I used the metro a lot with a rechargeable card, which I topped up three times, 10 euros each, and the app shows the history, so I exported that instead of hunting for slips. There were two rides in ride-hailing cars, 14.80 and 11.30 euros, and both appear in the app's history with a proper receipt attached to an email. The regional train to Sintra and back was 9.60 euros, and I have the tickets. Then the airport taxi, which is where the trouble began, because I took it on the night I arrived, in a rush after a delayed flight, and the driver gave me a slip that looks like a parking ticket.

Conference fees and the customer visit deserve their own paragraph, since they behave differently. The registration for the two-day event was 390 euros for the early bird rate, paid by the company card in February, so it is already in the ledger and only needs a line in my claim for completeness. The evening reception on day one was included, but the dinner on day two was a separate ticket at 45 euros, which I bought on the spot because a customer had asked me to join their table. That dinner counts as a client entertainment cost, a category with its own limit and its own form, so I filled in the names of the four people present and their company, as the rules require. Meanwhile the customer visit itself, in a glass office near the river, involved no spending beyond the train, but I brought a small gift for their team, a box of Danish butter cookies that cost 12 euros at the airport shop, and I have the receipt because the cashier printed it without being asked.

One more wrinkle is the currency. Everything in Portugal was in euros, so no conversion, which is a relief compared with the trip to Zurich last year, where I spent an evening working out exchange rates from three different card statements. But the ride-hailing app charged in kroner for one of the rides, because my phone account is registered in Denmark, and the receipt shows both figures: 110 kroner, or 14.80 euros at the app's own rate. Ilse's policy says to use the amount charged in euros where it is shown, so I use 14.80 and ignore the kroner line. Same approach for the airport coffee stand: it printed a euro figure only, so nothing to convert.

After matching everything, one line remained. The only unsupported item was an 86.40 euro taxi from the airport to the hotel on arrival. I remember the price being high because of the late hour and the luggage surcharge, and I remember paying with my own card. But the card statement, which I downloaded, shows the payment under the driver's cooperative with no itemisation, and the paper slip has no date. Ilse's rule allows a claim without a receipt up to 50 euros with a signed statement, and this is above that, so it needs either the original receipt or a written explanation approved by my manager. I emailed the cooperative's customer service to ask for a duplicate.

I decided to submit everything else today. The total claim without the taxi comes to 1,309.30 euros, which is mostly the hotel and the guesthouse. I attached the photographs in spreadsheet order and wrote a short cover note promising the missing receipt or a signed statement. 

Lessons: photograph receipts on the day, ask for printed totals, and diarise the deadline on day one. I finished at 16:30 and went out in the drizzle for a custard tart, which I had missed all week.

Contract talks with the freight-tracking data vendor, Northline Telemetry, as recorded by Blake with additions from Avery. We had three sessions over two weeks, and this note pulls them into one account, because the earlier notes are scattered and the final terms depend on the reasoning behind each concession. The context: our shipment map depends on live position data from Northline, our current agreement expires in six weeks, and they sent a new draft that we considered one-sided.

Who was involved. On their side, the commercial lead Ottoline Reyes, and a lawyer who introduced herself as Fenna and mainly said, "we will need to look at that clause." On our side, Blake led the commercial points and Avery took the technical schedule, while Marguerite watched the first session and the last. Blake's opening principle was to give up things that cost us little and hold firm on the three that could hurt us, which he wrote at the top of the shared page so we could check ourselves whenever the mood got warm.

Point one, data quality. The draft described the service as "best effort", with no minimum accuracy. Avery had spent a weekend measuring their feed against our own drivers' logs and found that about 3.5 percent of position updates arrived more than ten minutes late, and that in two regions the gap was closer to nine percent. He brought a chart, and Ottoline responded that those regions depend on carriers' uploads, which are outside their control. We proposed a service level of 97 percent of updates within five minutes, measured monthly, with a fee reduction below that. They offered 95 percent within ten minutes, and we settled on 96 percent within eight after the second session, with the credit rising in steps.

Point two, pricing. Their draft charged per tracked shipment, with a tier system that would have raised our costs by roughly twenty percent at current volumes. Blake countered with a flat annual fee for up to 400,000 shipments and a lower per-shipment rate above that, because our volumes swing with the season and predictability is worth something to us. Ottoline said flat fees are unusual for them and asked what we would give in return. We offered a two-year term and a public reference, meaning our logo on their customer page. That cost us nothing, and she visibly relaxed.

A word on the mood before point three, because it affected what followed. The first session was stiff. Fenna read out clause numbers, Ottoline kept a printed copy of the pricing page in front of her, and Blake made a point of asking about their own business, in particular how their positioning data is collected from carriers' devices and what happens when a carrier changes its systems. That was not small talk; he wanted to learn how fragile their feed really is. Ottoline admitted that two carriers had changed formats in the spring and that it took them nine days to repair the parsing, which quietly strengthened our case for the accuracy commitment. Avery noticed that she used the word 'partners' for us twice, and never 'customers', and that is the sort of signal that tells you where a person is willing to move. Fenna, for her part, wrote nothing down until the third clause was on screen, then filled half a page, so we learned to watch her pen as much as her words, and I had never seen anyone do it so calmly.

Between sessions Blake and Avery met for an hour to decide what to trade. The technique was a two-column sheet: things we would like, and things that would be painful to lose. The notice period, the automatic renewal and the data retention went in the second column. A lower base fee went in the first, together with the sandbox and the named contact. Marguerite added one rule that helped us throughout the process: nothing is agreed unless it is also written in the sheet before the meeting ends, and if it is not in the sheet by the end, it never happened. That prevented at least one misunderstanding about the reference logo, which Ottoline remembered as a full case study and we remembered as a logo.

Point three, exit. This is the one I would like future readers to remember, so I have written it out much more fully than all of the others, including the two arguments that Blake used and the one that fell flat, plus my own doubts. The draft required 120 days' written notice to end the agreement, and included automatic renewal for a further year unless notice was given. Blake said that a four-month lock on a supplier whose data we do not fully trust would put us in a bad position if quality slipped, and that automatic renewal should be dropped or, at least, made a two-month extension. After a break to consult Fenna, Ottoline came back and the notice period shrank from 120 to sixty days, with automatic renewal replaced by an explicit confirmation step thirty days before term end. Blake thanked her and did not push further.

Smaller items settled on the way. Liability for outages is capped at twelve months of fees, which is normal. Northline keeps no copy of our shipment identifiers after ninety days, per the data annex. Incidents go to a named engineer with a phone number, with a fifteen-minute acknowledgement target. We asked for a sandbox environment, which they will provide at no cost.

What we gave up. We accepted a six percent rise on the base fee for the flat structure, which Marguerite found fair after seeing what the tiers would have done. We also accepted their governing law, since the alternative was a two-week argument over jurisdiction with no practical benefit. And we agreed to give thirty days' notice before any large change in our shipment volume, which is easy for us to promise.

Remaining work. Fenna will send a clean redline on Friday, Blake will check it against this note line by line, and Avery will confirm the technical schedule with the engineer. If everything holds, Marguerite signs before the end of next week, with a week to spare before the old agreement ends.

Working notes on switching payroll providers for the small studio, written over several evenings. I look after the admin side for my own consulting practice and for the two contractors who are on regular monthly pay, and the provider I have used for four years announced a price increase of 35 percent along with the loss of the tax filing feature. That was the trigger. I did not want to spend time on this, but ignoring it would have cost about 600 euros a year for a worse service, so it became a project.

What I need from a provider. Short list, written before looking at any product pages so that the marketing would not choose it for me: monthly payslips for three people, automatic tax and social contribution filing in Denmark, a way for Lena and Mattias to see their own payslips without asking me, export into my bookkeeping tool, and a fair price below 40 euros a month. Nice to have: holiday pay tracking, since the rules are fiddly, and a mobile app that does not feel hostile.

The candidates. I compared four. The first was the incumbent's new tier, which I ruled out immediately on price. The second, Lønvej, is a Danish service with a clear interface but no English support, and I am fine with that, though Lena is not. The third was a large international platform with impressive features and a pricing page that hides the real numbers behind a demo request, which I treat as a warning sign. The fourth, Paysmith, was newer, priced at 29 euros per month for up to five employees, with tax filing included. I booked a video call with Paysmith and a trial account with Lønvej.

The trial. I spent an evening entering Lena's and Mattias's data into both systems. Paysmith took about 25 minutes, with a good import from a spreadsheet; Lønvej took closer to an hour because of separate screens for pension, holiday and benefits. But Lønvej caught something Paysmith did not: Mattias's employment contract has a small allowance for home office costs, and Lønvej had a category for it while Paysmith wanted me to enter it as a taxable bonus, which is wrong. I emailed Paysmith support, and they answered within two hours with a workaround, which is a point in their favour. Still, the workaround requires a manual step each month, and manual steps are how mistakes enter.

Cost comparison over twelve months. Paysmith at 29 euros is 348 for the year, Lønvej at 34 euros is 408 for the year, and the incumbent's new price would be 62 euros a month, so 744. Any switch saves money. The gap between the two new options is 60 euros a year, which would not decide it. What matters more is which one I trust with tax filings, because a mistake there means penalties and awkward letters.

Talking to my accountant, Ingrid, helped. She uses Lønvej for several clients, said its tax filing is reliable, and warned me that switching in the middle of the year is fiddly, since year-to-date totals must be carried over. She recommended switching at a month boundary, importing the year-to-date figures as an opening balance, and running one parallel month, where the old system and the new produce the same payslips and I compare them. I liked that plan because it converts fear into a checklist.

I also checked the fine print on the things that hurt when they go wrong. Lønvej files the monthly tax report on the tenth automatically, but only if the employee data is confirmed by the fifth, and it sends me an email reminder three days earlier. Paysmith files on the same day but has no reminder, which I would have found out the hard way. Lønvej also stores payslips for ten years, matching the Danish bookkeeping rules, while the incumbent kept them for only five years and I have been saving copies by hand. When I asked Lønvej support about importing year-to-date totals, the answer arrived in English within a few hours, so the language gap seems narrower than I feared, and the person even attached a sample spreadsheet with the columns already labelled.

One worry remains, which is the holiday pay. Denmark's newer rules let employees earn paid leave as they go and take it in the following year, and Mattias started in September, so his balance straddles two systems. Ingrid said the safest route is to enter his accrued days as an opening balance, print the calculation, and keep the printout with the contract. I put that on the list as well, and it made me slightly happier to have a paper trail for the fiddly part, and I kept the calculation sheet in the payroll folder.

Decision and dates. I chose Lønvej, in the end, mostly because of the allowance category and Ingrid's confidence, and I accepted that Lena will need a translated guide, which I will write myself over a weekend. The first live payroll run is 27 March, with the parallel month in February so any discrepancy appears while the old provider is still active. I will give the old provider notice by the end of January, keeping in mind their thirty-day cancellation term, and I will save the final payslips and year-to-date reports from them as files before the account closes.

To-do list, in order. Export year-to-date totals from the incumbent on the first of February. Enter opening balances in Lønvej. Run the parallel month and compare each figure with Ingrid. Tell Lena and Mattias about the new login by email in early March, and remind them that the payslip layout will change. Cancel the old subscription the day after the second payroll has gone through cleanly, not before. I also put a reminder in my calendar to review the choice in a year, because the whole reason for this trouble was a provider that I stopped watching.

On-call log, the weekend of the disk alerts. I carried the pager from Friday at 18:00 until Monday at 09:00, which on our rota is the long straw and the short straw at once: two nights of being interrupted and a quiet Sunday in between. I keep a running log while on shift because the handover document is only useful if it is written while the details are fresh, and by Monday morning my memory of Saturday is always somewhat inventive.

Friday evening was calm. One alert at 21:40 for elevated latency on the search service, which resolved itself after eight minutes; I looked at the graph and found a deploy by the growth team a few minutes earlier, so I noted it and went back to my dinner. The second alert at 23:15 was for disk usage at 80 percent on the analytics volume, a warning threshold and not a page, so I made a note to look on Saturday morning. I set an alarm for 07:00, as I always do, but slept through the first ring.

Saturday morning, the volume had reached 91 percent, and the rate of growth was the interesting part. It was not a steady rise but a staircase, with steps every hour on the hour, each step around four gigabytes. Something was writing a large file hourly. I logged in to the host and listed the biggest directories, and the culprit was the snapshot directory of the reporting service, where each hourly job produced a full copy of the working data set and nobody had ever configured a cleanup. It had run quietly for eleven weeks, and the volume only filled because of a larger data load on Thursday.

I did not want to delete things blindly on a Saturday, so I asked in the team channel whether anyone knew what the snapshots were for. Kalinda, who wrote the job, replied within fifteen minutes from a bus in Tallinn: they were meant to be kept for two days and pruned, and the pruning step was commented out during a debugging session in the summer. She confirmed that anything older than 48 hours was safe to remove. I wrote a small script to list candidates first, checked its output by eye, and only then ran the delete. In total I freed 212 GB by deleting stale snapshots, and the volume dropped from 91 to 52 percent.

While at it, I restored the pruning line and opened a pull request with a proper retention setting of 48 hours, plus a metric for the age of the oldest snapshot. Kalinda approved it from her phone. I also asked whether the hourly frequency is really needed, and she said daily would do for most reports, but the finance dashboard uses hourly data on the first of the month, so we left it alone for now and added the question to Monday's agenda.

Saturday night was the noisy part. At 02:10 the pager went off for a failing health check on the mail relay. I got up, opened my laptop on the edge of the bed, and found that a certificate for the relay's internal endpoint had been rotated but the service had not reloaded it. A reload fixed it in under a minute. I wrote up the cause in two lines and could not get back to sleep until four, which meant that Sunday was largely wasted; I made pancakes, walked to the harbour and let the phone sit in my pocket, and it stayed silent until evening. On the walk I ran through what I would do differently: put a rotation line in every job the moment it is created, and make the alert text say which directory grew most, so the person at the keyboard at seven in the morning does not have to hunt.

Some numbers, for the record and for whoever is next. The analytics volume is 500 GB, with an alert at 80 percent and a page at 95. Before I started deleting, the two biggest directories were the snapshots at 268 GB and the raw event exports at 141 GB, so removing the snapshots alone put us well below any threshold. The snapshot names encode a timestamp, which made the age filter easy, and I confirmed the oldest one was from mid-June before touching anything. I also kept the three newest copies by hand, on the theory that a Saturday cleanup script deserves a safety margin.

Sunday evening brought one more alert, low free memory on a worker node, and the cause was a job that had been leaking slightly for weeks. I restarted the worker, watched the memory graph for half an hour, and filed a ticket with the graph attached. Monday morning I wrote the handover: three incidents, one cleanup, one open ticket, and a suggestion that the weekend rota include a short checklist for disk warnings so the next person does not have to rediscover the snapshot directory. Handover call at 09:00, and I handed the pager to Wenzel with a coffee-free apology for the mess I had made of the analytics volume, since it was, after all, partly my own team's oversight.

Support macro audit, first pass. Present: Avery, Blake, Colm, and Deepa from the support team, who joined for the second half. The purpose of the session was to go through every saved reply in our helpdesk tool, the ones agents insert with a shortcut, and decide which are still true, which are stale, and which are embarrassing. We had never done this properly. The library grew one tired Friday at a time, and when Colm exported it to a spreadsheet the total was 58 saved replies, some written four years ago by people who left long ago.

Some background on why now. Last month a customer forwarded us a screenshot of one of our replies with the line 'is this still true?' circled in red, and it was not. That message, a saved answer about export limits that was two versions old, sat in Marguerite's inbox for a day before she asked Blake to do something about it. Nobody owns the library; it belongs to everybody, which in practice means to nobody, and so the first decision of the session was to name Colm as the maintainer, with Deepa as his backup.

Method. Colm assigned each reply a row with its title, the number of times it had been used in the last ninety days, and the date it was last edited. We sorted by usage. The top five replies account for almost half of all uses, and they are about password resets, plan changes, invoice copies, cancellation and the standard apology for slow responses. Those we read aloud, sentence by sentence, because a mistake in a heavily used reply is copied hundreds of times a month.

What we found in the heavy hitters. The password reset reply referred to a menu item that was renamed last year. The plan change reply promised that the new price applies immediately, whereas since the spring it applies from the next charge date, which had already led to at least two confused customers. The cancellation reply was accurate but cold, with a sentence starting "Per our terms" that made Deepa wince. We rewrote all five and agreed that each new version should be tested by an agent who has not seen the change before.

The long tail. Below the top ten, usage drops sharply: thirty-one replies were used fewer than five times in three months. Some of these are for events that no longer exist, such as a reply about the migration from the old mobile app, a discontinued integration with a calendar service, and a holiday closure notice from two Decembers ago. Avery argued that a saved reply used twice a quarter has no business in the list, because every extra entry makes the search box slower and the wrong choice easier. Blake countered that rare replies are often the ones agents dread writing from scratch, such as data deletion requests, and that low usage does not mean low value. We agreed to keep the rare-but-sensitive ones and to mark them with a tag.

After sorting, the outcome was clear. We decided to retire fourteen of the 58 canned replies, merge nine others into three shorter ones, and rewrite the rest over the next month. Colm will archive the fourteen instead of deleting them, so that anyone who misses one can ask for it to be restored within thirty days. The merged replies were the fun part: three separate replies about failed card payments differed only in the decline reason, and Deepa proposed one reply with a short fill-in section that agents complete from the payment record.

Tone. A separate conversation took about twenty minutes, and I think it was the most valuable one. Blake read out three sentences from existing replies, and we asked whether a human would say it. "We apologise for any inconvenience this may have caused" fails. "I'm sorry this took so long" passes. The guideline that emerged: write as if speaking to a person you will meet next week, use the customer's own words when possible, and never open with the word "unfortunately". Deepa wrote these on a card and will put them at the top of the library.

Accuracy checks. Every saved reply that mentions a price, a limit or a date needs an owner and a review date. Currently six replies quote prices, and three of them are out of date. We agreed to replace hard numbers with a link to the pricing page wherever possible, since links do not go stale, and for the few that must quote a figure, the owner will be named in the reply's description so nobody has to hunt for who to ask.

Next steps. Colm archives the retirees by Friday. Deepa and Avery rewrite the top five and circulate them for comment, with a deadline of the following Wednesday. Blake takes the merged replies and tests them on his own queue for a week. We will meet again in one month to look at whether the average handling time has moved, and to see whether customers reacted differently to the new wording. Colm also proposed a quarterly cleanup, twenty minutes in the team meeting, and everyone agreed before he had finished the sentence. We closed the meeting with a small rule to keep the library healthy: a new reply is only added if the same answer has been typed by hand at least three times in a month, and the person adding it names a review date. Deepa will remind us at the next meeting.

Mentoring log for the first month with Sanne, our new junior engineer, who joined on the second of the month.
