I volunteered to be her onboarding buddy because I remember how alone the first weeks feel, and because my own buddy, years ago, wrote everything down and I have always wanted to do the same. This is a running document. I keep it short each day, but the pattern matters more than any single entry, and I share the file with her so it never feels like a secret assessment.

Week one, orientation. Sanne's laptop arrived a day late, which taught us that the setup checklist assumes a machine on day one. I gave her a spare on Monday and did the checklist together with her on Tuesday. The main point of the first days was to get the project running locally, and it took much longer than anyone would admit: two dependencies failed to install on her operating system version, and we spent an hour finding a note in the wiki last edited in 2022. She fixed the note herself on Wednesday, and that counts as her first contribution to the team even though it never went through a review.

During those first days I also tried to make the office less abstract. I introduced her to the people who answer support tickets, because our bugs come from them, and to Dario, who guards the deployment pipeline and will one day be her most important reviewer. We had lunch with the platform group on Wednesday, where she said almost nothing, but I saw her writing names on a napkin, and on Thursday she greeted three people correctly. Small social wins at the start matter more than any technical progress, and I treat them as part of the job.

I set her a small goal early: change something real, however tiny, before the end of the first week. We picked a wrong sentence in the billing help pages, where a screenshot showed an old menu. The first merged change landed on day six, a typo fix and a replaced image, and she was quietly delighted when the deploy notification named her. What mattered was that she went through the whole path, branch, pull request, review, merge, release, on something low-stakes, so that the process no longer felt like a wall.

Week two, reading code. I asked her not to write anything at first, only to trace what happens when a customer changes a plan: start at the button, follow the request, and find every table touched. She drew it on paper and it took her two days, and what she drew was better than our own diagram. She found a step that sends a confirmation email twice under one condition, which is now a ticket. I told her that this was a real finding, and that finding surprises in a system is what experienced people do all day.

Her questions. I keep a list of the questions she asks because they reveal what our onboarding lacks. Why are there two test frameworks? Who decides what goes into the release? Why does the staging environment have a different database version? Some of these I could answer, and others I could only reply "nobody remembers", which led to a good conversation about documenting decisions. I have started an entry page titled "Things we do and no one knows why", and she is the first author.

Week three, a real task. She took a small feature: showing the date of the last successful sync on the integrations page. It touched the backend, a database query and a bit of interface, the full stack in miniature. I paired with her for the first hour and then left her alone, sitting nearby in case, and she asked me only twice. Her pull request had a few problems, a query that would be slow for large accounts and a missing test, and I put my comments in as questions, asking what would happen with a million rows, rather than commands. She fixed both the next day without being asked to.

Feelings and pace. On Thursday of week three she said quietly that she worried she was slower than the others. I told her that nobody remembers speed, they remember reliability and questions, and that at her stage the most useful trait is asking early. I also told her about the week I once spent debugging a problem that a single message to a colleague would have solved in ten minutes. We agreed she would set a timer: after thirty minutes stuck, she asks someone.

Looking ahead. Week four is about on-call shadowing: she will sit with Wenzel during his shift and read the alerts without any responsibility. Next month, if all goes well, she owns a small service endpoint on her own. I will ask her at the end of this month what she would change about her onboarding, and then I will change it for the next person, and put the results on the wiki page where the broken note used to be. One more habit I want to record: every Friday afternoon we spend twenty minutes on what surprised her that week, no slides, and I write two lines in this log. Those two lines are what I will show my manager when she asks how the buddy arrangement is going, and they are more honest than any survey.

Planning notes for the pricing page experiment, written after two conversations with Nadia and one with Wenzel. The question we want answered is whether showing the annual plan first, with the monthly plan behind a toggle, produces more paid signups than the current layout, where monthly is the default. Everybody has an opinion. Marguerite is convinced annual-first will win, Blake worries it will scare off small customers, and I have learned to distrust every opinion held with that much confidence, including my own.

Current state. The pricing page gets about 2,600 visits a day, of which roughly 4.1 percent go on to start a trial, and about a third of those trials convert to a paid plan within thirty days. So the paid conversion from a page visit is around 1.4 percent, which is a small number, and small numbers make experiments slow. Wenzel pulled these figures from the analytics warehouse for the last eight weeks and confirmed that they are stable, without any obvious seasonal swings other than a dip around the national holiday.

Choosing the metric. The tempting one is clicks on the annual button, since that responds fast and we can see it within hours. But a click is not a payment, and I have seen experiments where a flashier layout increased clicks and reduced revenue. We agreed that the primary metric is trial starts, because it is frequent enough to measure, and that the secondary metrics are paid conversion after thirty days and the share of paid customers choosing annual. The thirty-day metric will only be read after the test ends, as a sanity check and not a stopping rule.

Design of the test. Two variants: control, the current page, and the treatment, annual first. Visitors are assigned by a cookie so that a person sees the same page every time, and assignment is fifty-fifty. Nadia wanted a third variant with a different headline, and I said no to it firmly; each extra variant multiplies the traffic we need, and mixing two changes in one treatment means we could never tell which one did the work. She accepted with a sigh and a note to try the headline next quarter.

Before the numbers, one more decision about who sees what. Returning visitors are the awkward group: someone who visited last month and saw the old page will be confused if the layout flips. Wenzel proposed to include only new visitors in the trial, defined as people without a cookie older than the start date, which cuts the traffic by about a third but keeps the comparison clean. I preferred to include everyone, since the returning visitors are the ones deciding whether to pay, but I lost that argument on merit: our measurement of trial starts is mostly about first impressions, and mixing in old visitors would blur it. So the plan is new visitors only, and the daily traffic figure drops from 2,600 to about 1,750, which changes the calculation, and I have redone it below with that lower count.

A second wrinkle is bots. Roughly six percent of pricing page visits come from crawlers and uptime checkers that never start a trial, and if they land unevenly in the two groups they add noise. Wenzel filters the known user agents and the office network, and will publish the filter rules alongside the plan so anybody can challenge them.

The calculation that shapes everything. We want to detect a relative lift of fifteen percent in trial starts, from 4.1 to about 4.7 percent, with a false positive rate of five percent and eighty percent power. Wenzel ran the numbers in a notebook and checked them with an online calculator that agreed. By that reckoning the experiment needs 9,400 visitors per variant, so roughly 18,800 in total, which at 1,750 new visitors a day means about eleven days. We rounded up to fourteen days so that every weekday appears twice, because our weekend traffic behaves differently, with more casual browsing and fewer purchase decisions.

What could spoil it. First, the marketing team plans an email campaign in the second week, which would send a burst of visitors who already know the product; Wenzel asked them to move it until after the test or to exclude those visitors. Second, a bug in the cookie logic could put people in both groups, so we will check the split on day one, and if the ratio is off by more than two percentage points, we stop and fix. Third, someone will be tempted to peek at the numbers every morning and stop when the result looks good. We agreed not to look at conclusions before day fourteen, though dashboards for the health checks are allowed.

Decision rule, written before the test begins. If the treatment improves trial starts with a confidence interval that excludes zero, and paid conversion after thirty days does not fall by more than ten percent relative, we ship it. If the result is flat, we keep the current layout, since it costs nothing to leave alone. If the treatment loses significantly, we drop it and record the finding on the team wiki so the next person can read why. Writing this down in advance prevents the argument we always have afterwards about what the result means.

Logistics. Wenzel builds the flag and assignment by Thursday. Nadia finishes the mock-up by Wednesday and sends it to Marguerite for a quick look. I will write the test plan as a one-page document, and Blake reviews it for the customer view. Kick-off is next Monday, with the two weeks ending on the Sunday, and we read the results on the following Tuesday. In the meantime I will resist the urge to draft the announcement before the data exists, though I admit I have already thought of the headline. Marguerite, when I showed her this plan, asked only one question: what would make me change my mind? I said a drop in paid conversion, and she nodded and left, which is her way of saying the plan is good.

Security patch rollout for the VPN gateway. Blake started the thread on Monday after the vendor published an advisory rating a vulnerability in the remote access appliance as critical: an unauthenticated attacker could run commands on the device. Since our gateway is exposed to the internet by design, this one is not optional. Avery joined on Tuesday to help with the plan, and this note combines both days into one record for the team.

What we run. Two gateway appliances in an active-passive pair, one in the Amsterdam facility and one in Frankfurt, serving about 160 people, mostly the support team working from home and the engineers on call. The firmware is version 9.2.4, and the vendor's fix is in 9.2.7. There is no workaround short of disabling the management portal, and we do need that, so patching is the only path. The advisory says exploitation has been seen in the wild, which is why we are not waiting for the usual monthly window.

Risk assessment. Blake read the advisory carefully and noted three things. The flaw is in the web management portal, not the tunnel service, so employees' connections are not directly affected. Second, the portal is currently reachable from the internet because Ines opened it last year for a remote support session and nobody closed it. Third, our logs show no unusual requests to the portal, but logs on a compromised device are a weak comfort. So the first action, on Monday afternoon, was to restrict portal access to the office address range and to two engineers' home connections, which reduced the exposure within an hour and gave us time to do the upgrade calmly.

Preparation. Avery downloaded the firmware from the vendor's site and verified the checksum against the value in the advisory, which matched. We exported the configuration from both units and stored the files in the encrypted archive with the passphrase kept by two people. We read the release notes for 9.2.5 through 9.2.7 and found two changes that matter: a new default for the session timeout, which will log people out after eight hours instead of twenty-four, and the deprecation of an old cipher that one legacy laptop still uses. Colm confirmed that the laptop belongs to a contractor who is finishing at the end of the month, so we will simply tell him.

Sequence for the change. Patch the passive unit first, since no user traffic touches it, reboot it and check that it rejoins the pair and reports healthy. Then trigger a failover so that the patched unit becomes active, watch the tunnel count for ten minutes, and patch the second unit. Finally fail back, verify, and lock the portal down again. Each step has a rollback: the previous firmware image stays on the device, and the exported configuration can be reloaded. Ines estimated fifteen minutes per unit for the upgrade and another twenty for verification. Avery noted that the vendor's own guide says a healthy pair should resynchronise within five minutes of a reboot, so any longer than that is a signal worth writing down.

Timing. When to do it was the subject of the most debate. Blake wanted the evening after the advisory, but the support team runs a late shift until eleven and the on-call engineers would be affected by the brief failover. Avery suggested weekend early morning, when almost nobody is connected. We checked the connection graph for the past month, and the lowest point is Sunday morning, with fewer than ten people connected. The maintenance slot is Sunday 04:00 to 05:30, which leaves a comfortable margin, and Blake will announce it to the company on Friday with a message telling people to save their work and expect one reconnection around four-thirty. Amsterdam and Frankfurt are in the same time zone as most of us, but Yusuf, who works from Lisbon, is an hour behind, and will be asleep either way.

Roles for the night. Ines does the upgrade, sitting at home with two screens. Avery watches the monitoring and calls if the tunnel count drops unexpectedly. Blake is the person who decides on rollback, and the rule is simple: if the second unit does not come back healthy within twenty minutes, we revert and try again at the next slot, with the exposed portal still restricted. Colm keeps the support channel informed in case anyone reports trouble.

Afterwards. We will review the logs of the portal for the last ninety days for anything odd, rotate the administrator passwords whatever we find, and add the appliance's advisory feed to the mailbox that the on-call engineers actually read. Blake also wants a standing rule that management interfaces are never exposed to the internet without an expiry date. It is a small rule, but this event began with a forgotten exception, and forgotten exceptions are how most of these stories start.

Budget request for a mobile testing pool, drafted over three evenings. For eighteen months our mobile app has been tested on whatever phones happen to be in engineers' pockets, which means a lot of recent flagship devices and almost nothing from the middle of the market, where a large share of our customers live. A bug report last month came from a customer with a four-year-old mid-range phone whose screen layout was broken in a way nobody on the team could reproduce. That was the last straw. I am writing the case for a small shared collection of test devices and want to keep the reasoning together in one place.

The evidence. Nadia pulled device statistics from the crash reporting tool for the last quarter. Of about 41,000 active mobile users, the top forty device models cover 78 percent, and seven of those forty are devices that none of us own. Six of the seven are from two manufacturers and run a customised version of the operating system with its own quirks for notifications and background work. The crash rate on those seven is 2.6 times the average, which is the number I will lead with in the request, since it turns a feeling into a cost. Fixing a defect after release takes on average two days of engineering time, while a device in a drawer costs a one-time fee.

Constraints from finance. Ilse told me that anything under 10,000 euros can be approved by Marguerite alone, while larger sums go to the monthly budget meeting, which would delay me by three weeks. So the request should come in below that limit, purchased in one order, and classed as equipment, which lets the company write it off over three years. She also reminded me that equipment should be recorded on the asset register with a serial number, and that means someone has to own the register. I volunteered, cautiously.

Before shopping I wrote down what a device in the pool is for, since a list of gadgets without a purpose becomes a drawer of dust. There are three jobs. First, reproducing bugs that customers report, where the exact model and operating system version matter. Second, checking every release candidate on a small set of old and slow phones before it ships. Third, trying new interface work on real screens instead of the emulator, which is kind to the eye and dishonest about performance. Anything that does not serve one of these three jobs is not on the list, and that rule cut four attractive candidates, including a premium tablet that nobody would touch after the first week.

I also spoke to Dario, who ran a similar pool at a previous company. His warning was blunt: pools die from neglect, not from cost. The devices go out of date, the batteries swell, somebody takes one home for a demo and it vanishes into a rucksack. He recommended a single named owner, a monthly ritual of updating all devices in one sitting, and a rule that the pool lives in the office cabinet and nowhere else. That is why I volunteered for the register, and why the cabinet with a lock is in the request even though it looks like an extra.

Choosing devices. Rather than buying every model, I chose by covering the categories: two manufacturers' mid-range phones from the last two years, two older devices on operating system versions we still support, one small-screen phone, one tablet, and two low-memory devices, since memory is the source of most of our unexplained crashes. I also wanted a phone with a notch or punch-hole camera, which affects the layout of the top bar. Wenzel checked the list against the crash data, and he added a ninth device, a foldable, because a large customer in the retail sector had mentioned that their staff use them.

The numbers. The shortlist totals 7,350 euros for nine handsets, with the foldable alone at 1,180 euros and the low-memory phones under 130 euros each. Adding a charging station for nine devices at 85 euros, a set of cables and a lockable cabinet at about 140 euros brings the whole request to 7,675 euros. I compared buying refurbished, which would have been about thirty percent cheaper, but the warranty is shorter and the condition varies, and for a pool that we want to rely on for years I preferred new units from a business supplier with a fixed delivery date.

Running costs. A pool is not free after purchase. Every device needs a data plan or access to office wifi, updates need to be applied so that devices do not fall out of date, and batteries degrade over about two years. I estimated 150 euros a year for replacements and accessories, and one hour a month of my time for maintenance, which Marguerite may or may not consider worth it. I suggested a shared spreadsheet for checking devices in and out, with a rule that anything not returned within a week gets chased by whoever runs the register.

Alternatives. The obvious one is a cloud device farm, where you rent time on real phones remotely. Its plans start around 200 euros a month, which is 2,400 a year, and it can cover hundreds of models. That is a sound option for automated tests, and I plan to use it later for regression runs, but for debugging a layout problem on a specific phone, holding the thing in your hand still wins. I will describe both in the request so that the decision is visible, and I will say plainly that the physical pool comes first for the reasons above.

Next steps. Ilse reviews the numbers on Thursday, then I submit the request with the statistics as an attachment and a one-paragraph summary. If Marguerite agrees, orders go out the same day, and delivery takes about a week. I will label each device with a number on a small sticker, install the app, and write a checklist of what to test on each. It will be satisfying to see a row of small screens lined up on a desk, each one an ordinary person's phone that we finally have in the room.

Preparing my self-assessment for the annual performance review. The form is due on Friday, the conversation with Marguerite is a week later, and I have a habit of writing the form the night before and regretting it. This time I am doing it properly, in pieces, and using this note as the raw material so that the final text is edited rather than invented on the spot. The company asks for three sections: what I achieved, where I grew, and what I want next.

Collecting evidence. Memory is unreliable and skewed to the last six weeks, so I went back through the pull request history, the incident log and my calendar for the past twelve months, and listed everything that felt significant. The list came to twenty-six items. Some are easy to name: the billing service migration in March, the redesign of the on-call rota, the new refund workflow. Others were nearly invisible at the time, like the six weeks I spent quietly answering questions from the support team, which reduced repeat tickets by a noticeable margin but does not show up in any tool.

Choosing what to include. Twenty-six is too many; a form full of items reads as noise. I sorted them by impact on customers or colleagues and cut to six. The migration stays because it removed a nightly failure that had cost the team about four hours a month. The rota redesign stays, because both Kalinda and Wenzel told me unprompted that their weekends improved. The refund workflow stays because it cut average refund handling from two days to about five hours. I left out things I enjoyed but that changed little, including a rewrite of an internal script that only I use.

A short note on tone, because I struggled with it. The company's form uses phrases like 'demonstrated ownership' and 'drove outcomes', and I find them hollow, so I wrote in ordinary sentences and then, at the end, swapped in a couple of the form's words where they fit. Marguerite has said more than once that she prefers plain writing, and I believe her. Each achievement is two lines: what I did, and what changed for someone else as a result.

Where I fell short. This part is uncomfortable, and I resisted writing it, but the form asks for it, and Marguerite will spot evasions. In the spring I took on too much and let two reviews sit for a week each, which blocked a colleague. I was slow to say no to requests from sales for one-off reports. And during the March incident I made a decision alone at midnight that I should have escalated; it worked out, but it worked out by luck. I wrote each of these in one plain sentence, with the change I made afterwards, since a weakness with a remedy reads as maturity and a weakness without one reads as a confession.

Growth. I spent a lot of time this year mentoring: two people joined the team and I was buddy to the second. I also gave a talk at the regional meetup in Aarhus about our refund workflow, which was terrifying and went better than I expected. Where I want to grow is leading larger pieces of work. So far my projects have been a month long, and I have never coordinated more than three people at once. I would like to run the export feature next quarter, and I will say so explicitly.

The pay conversation. The form has a box for compensation expectations, and I have avoided thinking about it for weeks. I asked two former colleagues what they consider normal, and looked at the salary bands that Marguerite shared last year. Given the scope I have taken on, and where I sit within the band for my level, which is near the middle, I concluded I should be asking for an eight percent raise, and I will present it with the evidence list next to it, which is more persuasive than a number alone. I would settle for six, and I have decided in advance that below five I will ask about a bonus or extra training budget instead.

Rehearsal. I practised the conversation aloud while walking along the canal on Sunday. The opening is straightforward, thanking her for the year. Then I state the three results that matter, the number I am asking for, and the reasoning, and I stop talking, which is the hard part. Silence after a request is uncomfortable, and my instinct is to fill it by apologising. Ilse, whom I told about this, laughed and said that everybody does that and that the trick is to drink some water.

Final steps before Friday. Trim the six achievements to two lines each. Ask Kalinda for one sentence of feedback I may quote. Print the form, since I edit better on paper. Sleep. And afterwards, whatever the answer, I will write down what she says within an hour, because that record is what I will need when the next cycle begins. I will also tell Ilse how it went, since she asked, and since telling one person makes the whole thing feel real rather than hypothetical, which oddly reduces the dread.

Synthesis of the customer interviews with warehouse managers, drafted by Avery and reviewed by Blake. Over three weeks Blake and I spoke to fourteen managers who use our stock-movement product, each for forty-five minutes, on video or in a few cases standing in their loading bays with a phone held up to show us the floor. This note keeps what we heard in the order we heard it, not as a slide deck, because the connections between comments are the useful part and slides cut them.

Who we talked to. Six run sites with fewer than twenty staff, five run mid-sized sites with a few dozen, and three run large distribution centres with over a hundred people per shift. They sell tyres, pet food, industrial fasteners, cosmetics, garden furniture and, in one case, wedding decorations. Locations range from Rotterdam and Gdansk to two managers in the north of England. We recruited them through account managers, so there is a bias toward happy customers, and I will say that plainly in the summary for Marguerite so nobody overstates the findings.

A day in the life. Almost every manager described the same rhythm. The morning starts with the overnight receipts, goods that arrived after closing and were left in the dock. Then comes the planning of the day's orders, followed by a rush between ten and noon, and a slower afternoon dominated by exceptions: damaged parcels, wrong quantities, an order changed at the last minute. Several said their whole job is exceptions, and the product is only ever opened when something goes wrong. That is a humbling thing to hear about software we think of as the heart of their operation.

Where the product helps. Nearly all praised the stock count screen, which lets a person walk an aisle with a phone and confirm quantities by scanning. One manager in Gdansk said that a full count used to take three people two days and now takes one person one day. Others liked the alert for items running below a minimum, though two said the alerts are too frequent and they ignore them. Ten of fourteen mentioned the barcode labels, which we print for them, as the feature they would miss most.

Integration pain. Six managers use their own accounting or carrier software, and the friction shows at the edges. Shipping labels have to be copied between systems by hand, and returns are logged in three places. Nobody asked for a grand integration; they asked for a plain file that another tool can read, which brings us back to the export work Marguerite has already prioritised. Two of the larger sites asked whether we offer an interface for direct connections, and we said we are considering it, without promising.

Pricing and trust. Managers were relaxed about price, which surprised Blake, who expected complaints. What worries them is downtime: a stoppage of an hour during the morning rush means a truck leaves late, and a late truck means a penalty. Three referred to an outage last spring, which had happened before either of us joined the interviews, and each recalled the date and the exact hour. Trust here is measured in incidents, and the memory is long. One manager in Rotterdam told us she keeps a paper log of every outage since she took the job, forty-one entries in six years, and reads from it before every contract renewal. Another said the honest answer to 'would you recommend us' depends entirely on whether the last month was quiet, which is a fair thing to hear and an uncomfortable thing to write down.

A word on method, since it shaped the answers. We asked every manager the same opening question, which was to describe the last time the system let them down, and we let them talk for ten minutes before showing anything. Blake kept a tally of the words people used for their own staff, in a notebook with a green cover. 'Pickers', 'the lads' and 'my team' came up far more than 'users', and we agreed to stop using that word in our own notes. We recorded each session with permission, took separate notes, and compared them the same evening, and the two sets disagreed less than I feared, which gives me some confidence in the themes below.

Where it hurts. The complaints cluster around the picking process, the step where staff collect items for an order. The screen assumes each picker carries a phone, but in many sites the pickers wear gloves, share a handful of devices, or work in cold rooms where touchscreens fail. Managers described workarounds that showed enormous inventiveness. One had taped a phone to a trolley handle. Another gives each picker a laminated card with a code. Several export the day's orders to a spreadsheet at six in the morning and run them through a printer, and this was the surprise that changed our thinking. Eleven of fourteen managers still print pick lists, even though the product has a mobile picking mode, and the reasons were not laziness. Paper does not run out of battery, does not need a signal in the freezer, and a picker can write a note on it.

What paper tells us. Blake pointed out that the printed sheet is a design in itself: it is sorted by aisle in walking order, it has a checkbox for each line, and it leaves room for scribbles. Our mobile picking screen sorts by order number, which makes sense for the database and none for a person walking. When we asked one manager what she would change, she did not mention a feature; she said she would love the product to print the list in the same order she walks. Two others said the same thing separately. That is the most concrete insight of the whole study, and it costs far less than a new mobile mode.

What we recommend. First, add a print layout for pick lists, ordered by location, and see how many people adopt it. Second, review the alert thresholds and offer a daily summary as an alternative to individual notifications. Third, invite two of the interviewed managers to try the new picking view early. Blake will write the interview transcripts into the shared folder with the names removed,.

Comparing three shared office spaces for a small team, written as a decision aid for myself and, in the end, for the other two people who would move in with me. After two years of working from home, the consultancy I run with Lena and Mattias has grown enough that we want a place to meet clients and a door to close, though not an actual lease with a landlord and a deposit and an argument about the radiators. So we are looking at coworking space in Aarhus, with a budget of about 1,500 euros a month for three people.

What we need. I wrote the requirements before visiting anywhere, because tours are designed to make you love the sofa. First, a meeting room we can book for at least six hours a month, with a screen and a decent camera, ideally not a glass box facing the open floor. Second, quiet: two of us are on calls for much of the day. Third, a month-to-month contract or at worst three months' notice, since we cannot predict our work beyond the spring. Fourth, twenty minutes or less from the station. And fifth, somewhere to store two boxes of equipment and a lockable drawer for each person.

Visit one, Ørsted Hub. Large, modern and slightly sterile, with about two hundred members across four floors. Flexible contracts, hot desks for 190 euros a month, dedicated desks for 380, and a well-equipped meeting suite. It also has a gym in the basement and a monthly breakfast. But it is at the edge of the city, twenty-five minutes from the station by bus, and the open floors are noisy. Mattias liked it because of the gym; Lena said she could not imagine having a private call there without whispering.

Visit two, Kvarter. A smaller place, twenty-five people, in a townhouse near the cathedral. It has the feel of a home: a shared dining room, a small yard with a bench, and rooms on two floors. The manager, Bent, told us frankly that they are almost full and that two desks together are available now, a third in about a month. The price is lower, 340 euros per desk per month with a one-month notice period, but meeting room use costs 18 euros an hour, and there is only one meeting room, shared with everyone. The phone booth situation is poor: one small room, always taken by eleven.

How I organised the tours. I booked all three in one week, on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, and always at eleven in the morning, when a shared office is at its most honest: people are in the middle of work, the phone booths are contested, and nobody has tidied for visitors. I brought Lena to the first and second, and Mattias came to the second and third, so each of us saw at least two places and two of us saw each one. On the way back from every visit we spent ten minutes in a cafe writing scores on a napkin before we could talk each other into anything. It sounds silly, but the napkins were the most useful documents of the week.

Money beyond the desk. Beyond rent, I asked each place about the extras that make a bill grow: printing, parking, a mailing address, guest passes, and the deposit. Deposits ranged from one month's rent to nothing, and one place wanted the deposit in cash on the day of signing, which I declined to discuss further. Several charge for a business address separately, around 25 euros a month, and one lets you keep your own boxes only for a storage fee. I noted every figure on a second sheet with a line for each extra.

Between visits two and three we stopped at a bakery near the station and did the arithmetic on commuting. Lena lives north of the city and takes a bus that adds fifteen minutes to any place on the harbour side, while Mattias cycles, and I walk, which is the point of caring about the station. I reminded myself that I have to be honest about my own reason for wanting a desk outside the flat: I get more done at a shared bench with strangers than at home with a full fridge. That is a fine reason, and I should not pretend it is only about clients, and I said as much to the others over the second round of tea.

Before the third tour Ragnhild sent a friendly message with a floor plan attached, and a note that the dedicated desks near the glass wall were already taken, which is the sort of gentle pressure I dislike and also, admittedly, works on me. I asked to try the desks by the pillar for an afternoon, and she agreed.

Visit three, Harbour Yard. A converted grain warehouse by the water, with brick walls, high ceilings and about eighty members. The host, a cheerful person called Ragnhild, showed us the dedicated desk area, a bright room with long shared desks, three phone booths and a lounge with a piano that no one plays. The meeting rooms are lovely and can be booked in the app. It is a ten-minute walk from the station. Harbour Yard asked 420 euros per desk per month for a dedicated desk, with meeting room credits of four hours included, and a six-month minimum term. That works out to 1,260 for the three of us before extras, which is inside our budget, and the term is longer than I wanted.

The scoring. We made a simple table with our five requirements and gave each place a mark from one to five, then added weights, with quiet and contract flexibility counting double. Harbour Yard scored highest on rooms and location and lower on flexibility. Kvarter did best on flexibility and price and worst on meeting rooms. Ørsted Hub was middling on everything except commute. The numbers came out close, which told me that the decision is not really about numbers, and that I should ask what each place does to the way we would work.

Talking it through. Lena pointed out that meeting rooms are the reason we want a place at all, and that eight hours a month at 18 euros is 144, roughly the gap in desk price. Mattias worried about the term at Harbour Yard, so I suggested asking for three months.

What I did next. I emailed Ragnhild that evening, and she offered a three-month minimum for a one-time set-up fee of 150 euros, which seems fair. Lena and Mattias confirm on Friday, and we start on the first.

Feature flag cleanup week, a log kept by me as the person who volunteered and the person who regrets it. Our codebase has, over four years, accumulated conditional switches for every launch and experiment, and almost nobody remembers which are still needed. Last month a bug traced to a flag that had been switched off in production and on in staging for two years, and the room went quiet in a way that made the decision for us. This week we clean up. The rules are simple: every flag is either deleted or given an owner and an expiry date.

Monday, taking inventory. Wenzel wrote a short script that scans the code for flag names and cross-checks the configuration service, and it found 52 flags. I put them in a spreadsheet with columns for name, created date, current value in production, current value in staging, the last time the value changed, and where it is used. The oldest was created in the first month of the project, and its comment reads "temporary". Fifteen flags had never changed value since creation, which is a strong sign they are permanent behaviour dressed as options.

Tuesday, classification. We sat together for two hours and sorted the flags into four kinds. Release flags, which hide unfinished work until it launches, should be deleted once the feature is on for everyone. Experiment flags should go as soon as the experiment ends. Operational flags, the kill switches we use during incidents, are legitimately long-lived and deserve documentation. And permission flags decide who sees a feature, and mostly belong in the product's access rules and not in a toggle. Twenty-nine flags were release flags for features launched more than six months ago, eleven were dead experiments, six were kill switches, and six were permission flags.

The archaeology. To decide about the older flags, I read the history of each. Some had clear stories: the flag for the new search ranking was created in a hurry before a demo and left in. Others were mysteries. One called new_checkout_v3 gated a code path for a checkout that no longer exists, and I had to search chat logs to confirm it. Kalinda remembered that another flag protected a workaround for a payment provider's bug, and asked us not to touch it until she checked whether the provider had fixed it, which they had, two years ago, so it went into the pile.

Wednesday, deleting. The technique is boring on purpose: for each flag, keep the code path that runs in production, delete the other branch, delete the condition, delete the tests of the losing branch, and remove the entry from the configuration service in a separate step after deploying. Doing the configuration removal last means that if something breaks, we can restore the flag value in a minute. I opened small pull requests, one flag each, since a change touching thirty flags is impossible to review. By the end of the day, I had twelve open and Wenzel had nine.

Some things we learned about the flags themselves along the way. Naming was a mess: some used camel case, some snake case, some included a date, and one was called simply 'fix'. A handful were negations, flags named disable_something with a default of false, which made every condition a double negative and every reader slow. When we deleted them we renamed nothing, since the flag was gone, but I wrote a naming convention in the guide for the ones that remain: positive names, an area prefix and a ticket reference. Kalinda pointed out that four flags refer to a ticket system we abandoned in 2023, so the reference is a dead link, and finding out what they were for took about an hour each.

Meanwhile the configuration service had its own surprise. Its audit trail shows who changed each value, and the most recent change to a flag called legacy_import_path was made by a person who left the company a year and a half ago, using an admin token that was never rotated. Wenzel revoked the token that same afternoon, before the tea was cold, and added token review to our quarterly checklist, along with a rule that admin tokens expire after ninety days. That was not part of the plan for the week, and I record it here because cleanup weeks tend to find the things nobody was looking for.

Thursday, the tricky ones. Three flags were tangled together, with nested conditions, and removing one changed the behaviour of another. For these, we wrote characterisation tests first, tests that record what the code does right now, so that we could delete conditions without changing outcomes. It took half a day and found one genuine bug: a case where two flags enabled at once produced a duplicate confirmation message. We fixed it in passing and felt smug for an hour.

By the numbers. By Friday afternoon, we removed 37 of the 52 flags, which is 71 percent, and the deployment went out in three batches with no incidents. The remaining fifteen are the six kill switches, which now have a documented purpose and an owner, four permission flags waiting for a change in the access model, three experiments that are still running, and two flags whose purpose Kalinda is investigating with the provider. We deleted about 1,900 lines of code and 640 lines of tests, and the build time dropped by about forty seconds, which no one had expected.

What we will do so this does not happen again. Every new flag needs an owner, a type and an expiry date in the configuration, and a scheduled job will open a ticket when a flag is past its date. Wenzel wants the check to fail the build for release flags older than ninety days, which is aggressive, but I think he is right, and Marguerite agreed after the weekend. We will repeat a smaller cleanup each quarter, since dust settles on any codebase.

Drafting the data retention policy, session notes. Blake, Avery and Ilse from finance met for two sessions, joined for the second by Fenna's colleague from the outside law firm, who kept her camera off and her comments sharp. Until now our position on how long we keep information has been a mixture of habit and accident: some tables never lose a row, others are wiped by a cron job somebody wrote in a hurry, and backups hold everything for a year without anyone having decided that. Two enterprise prospects have asked for a written policy in their security questionnaires, so it is time.

Principles first. Blake proposed three rules to guide the details, and we adopted them almost unchanged. Keep data only as long as there is a specific reason, and write the reason down. Keep what the law requires for as long as it requires, and no longer. And make deletion real, meaning that it reaches backups and search indexes in bounded time, because a promise to delete that leaves copies lying around is worse than no promise. Ilse added a fourth, which is that every retention period must be one that an engineer can implement with a scheduled job rather than a heroic project.

Categories. We listed what we store and grouped it. Customer content, meaning the records and attachments customers put into the product. Account data, such as names and login emails. Payment records, which include payment references and tax details. Operational logs, for debugging and security. And support conversations. Each category got a purpose, an owner, and a retention proposal. Ilse insisted that payment records be kept for seven years, which is what our tax rules require, and nobody argued with her; it was a relief to have one figure that was not negotiable.

The debate that took the longest was customer content after a customer leaves. Blake wanted a short period, thirty days, arguing that holding data for a departed customer is a liability without a benefit. Avery pointed out that customers frequently return, and that a mistaken cancellation, made by an intern on the wrong account, is a real occurrence in our history. Ilse noted that some large customers ask for a grace period in their contracts. After going around the loop several times we compromised: the account is locked but restorable for thirty days, then customer files are deleted 180 days after account closure, with the account record itself kept only as a minimal stub so that we can honour a request to prove a deletion happened. Backups age out within a further thirty-five days, and we will say so in the text.

Operational logs got a lighter discussion. Application logs contain identifiers and occasionally pieces of user content, which is unintentional but real, so we proposed thirty days for detailed logs and one year for the security audit trail, which contains no content. The lawyer suggested that we state plainly that logs are used for security and reliability and for nothing else, and Avery agreed since it is true and it is short.

Support conversations are a category that surprised us. They include screenshots that customers attach, and those screenshots often show more than intended: names, prices, once a passport page. Colm has been asked in the past to delete such images, and it currently takes him about ten minutes by hand each time. We agreed that support attachments are kept for two years and that customers can request earlier removal, with a target of five working days. We also want agents to have a button to purge an attachment, which goes on the product board as a small request.

What we need to build. Deletion after the retention period means scheduled jobs for at least four categories, plus a verification report for each so we can show that the jobs ran. Avery estimated about three weeks of engineering time overall, mostly in the backup process, which is the piece nobody has touched in a long while. Blake will ask Marguerite whether that fits before the end of the quarter, and if not, whether the questionnaire can honestly state a date.

Wording. The lawyer stressed avoiding absolute claims. Instead of 'all data is deleted', we write 'customer content is deleted within the periods stated, and backups expire on the schedule below'. She also asked for a short paragraph on legal holds, since a court order can require us to keep something we would otherwise delete, and we will record who decides in such a case. Blake will draft the text in plain language, Ilse will check the finance section, and the outside counsel will review before anything is published or sent to a prospect.

Negotiation notes with Ottilie Brandt, a freelance developer, about a statement of work for rebuilding the analytics screens in our reporting product. I was the buyer for this piece of work, and I wanted to write down how the conversation went because it was my first time hiring an outside contractor with real money attached, and I made a couple of choices I want to check against the outcome in a few months. Ottilie came recommended by Kalinda, who worked with her at a previous employer and said she is careful and blunt.

The brief. The current analytics area was built in a rush two years ago and is slow, hard to change and visually inconsistent with the rest of the product. It has six screens: an overview, a usage report, a cohort view, a retention chart, a list of top accounts and a settings page. I asked for a rebuild in the current interface framework, using our design system, keeping the same data sources, and with automated tests. I did not ask for new features, and I said so several times, because scope creep is the first way a fixed budget dies.

First call. We spoke for an hour on a Tuesday afternoon. Ottilie asked good questions before naming any figure: how many screens, what data volume, whether the design was ready, who would review her work, and how quickly I could respond to questions. That last one mattered to her; she told me that delays on the buyer's side are the main reason her projects overrun, and she offered to build a waiting cost into her rate if I could not promise a one-day reply. I promised a one-day reply and meant it.

Two pricing options. She offered either time and materials at 85 euros an hour, with an estimate of 100 to 130 hours, or a fixed price. Time and materials is honest but leaves me with the risk of an open bill. A fixed price moves the risk to her, and she charges for that in the form of a contingency. After some back and forth she agreed to a fixed price of 9,600 euros for the rebuild, payable in three parts: thirty percent at the start, forty percent when the first four screens are accepted, and the final thirty percent after the last acceptance and a two-week bug-fix window. That works out to slightly under her low estimate at her hourly rate, so I felt we had a fair deal.

What is in and out. We spent time on a written list, since the price only means something against a defined scope. In: the six screens, responsive layout down to tablet width, loading and empty states, keyboard accessibility, and tests covering the main flows. Out: any new charts, changes to the data pipeline, the mobile app, and translation into other languages. Change requests come in at the hourly rate, and each needs my written approval before work starts. Ottilie thought that was reasonable and added that she will tell me the hour count for a change before doing it.

Acceptance. I asked how we decide a screen is done, since 'done' is where contracts turn into arguments. We agreed on a checklist per screen: it matches the design at three widths, it passes the accessibility checks in our pipeline, the tests pass, and the code review comments are resolved. I have to review within two working days of each delivery, or the clock for that milestone stops. That last clause protects her, and I accepted it because it protects me from vague delays too.

Ownership and other clauses. All code belongs to us on payment, and she keeps the right to reuse general techniques but not our code. She will work in her own equipment and time, so no employment relationship arises, and she will sign our confidentiality agreement. She is not permitted to add third-party libraries without approval. Liability is capped at the total fee, and either side may end the contract with seven days' notice, in which case she is paid for accepted work plus hours to date on the current screen.

Next steps. Ottilie will send the statement of work within two days, I will read it against these notes, and Ilse will check the payment terms. If all is well, she starts on the first of next month, with a kick-off call to walk through the design system and the test setup. I will introduce her to Wenzel, who will be her main contact for code questions, and I will book my review slots in my calendar in advance so that the two-day promise is easy to keep. One last thought I want on record: I asked Ottilie what makes her clients difficult, and she said it is the ones who change their mind about the design after the code is written. I promised that the design is final and asked Nadia to sign off the screens in writing this week, before the first payment goes out, so that neither of us is tempted to test that promise.

Release day log for mobile version 5.8, kept by me as release captain. The plan was a staged rollout: five percent of users on Tuesday morning, then twenty-five in the afternoon, then everyone by Wednesday. I am writing this down as it happens because the story of a bad release is usually told afterwards as a tidy sequence, and it never was one. Present in the release channel: Wenzel, Nadia, Priya from support, Colm, and Dario watching the backend.

Morning. The build was signed off on Monday evening after the usual checks: the automated suite, two hours of manual testing on the device pool, and a review of the release notes by Nadia. The main change in 5.8 is a rewritten offline sync, which lets people keep working in a basement or a lift and merges changes later. It is the biggest change in the app for a year, and we knew it, which is why the rollout is staged at all. I submitted the release to the store at 07:30 and it was live for five percent at 08:15.

First checks. At 09:00 I opened the crash dashboard. The crash-free session rate for the new version was 99.2 percent, against 99.6 for the previous one. A small gap, though at only five percent of traffic the numbers are noisy, with about 2,100 sessions in the first hour. Priya reported two tickets from users who had lost drafts. I asked Wenzel to look into the first crash cluster while I kept watching, and he found a null pointer error in the sync code when a note has an attachment that failed to upload earlier.

Decision one, at 11:00. Do we proceed to twenty-five percent? Wenzel thought the null pointer was rare and fixable in a patch. Nadia was more worried about the lost drafts, which are the kind of thing that destroys trust. I proposed that we hold at five percent until noon, gather more data, and decide then. Nobody objected. I posted the plan to the channel so everyone knew the next decision time, because a vague hold gets forgotten.

By early afternoon the picture changed. At 13:00 the crash-free rate on 5.8 dropped to 97.9 percent, and Priya had nine tickets about lost drafts, two from the same customer, a project manager who had spent an hour writing meeting notes on a train. It became clear that the null pointer error was not a rare corner: it happened for anyone whose upload failed while offline, which on trains and in lifts is common. At 14:10 the rate touched 96.2 percent and the graph kept sloping down. We had agreed in advance a rollback threshold of 97 percent, which we had passed for ten minutes, and I made the call. The release was rolled back at 14:25 after crashes hit 3.8 percent of sessions, by halting the rollout in the store console and switching on the server-side flag that disables offline sync for version 5.8 users.

Why the flag matters. Store rollbacks are slow because users who already have the new version keep it. The flag lets us turn off the risky feature without waiting for a new build. Dario flipped it at 14:31, and within ten minutes the crash rate for 5.8 sessions was back to 99.1. Drafts already lost could not be recovered, but the flag stopped the loss from growing. Priya sent a short message to the affected customers acknowledging the problem and promising a fix, and Nadia drafted the apology in plain words.

Fix and recovery. Wenzel had a patch by 16:00: a guard for the null case, a retry for the failed upload, and a test reproducing the customer's scenario exactly, with the phone in airplane mode. I asked Dario to review it, and we agreed it would go through the full device pool again, not a shortened check, because shortcuts on the day of a failure are how second failures happen. Build 5.8.1 was submitted on Wednesday morning and reached five percent on Wednesday evening.

Lessons, for the record. The rollback threshold worked because it was set before we needed it, and nobody had to argue about feelings. The device pool testing did not catch the bug because we tested offline sync in airplane mode, but with attachments that uploaded successfully first. We will add a scenario for interrupted uploads to the release checklist. The retrospective is on Friday, and I will bring the timeline in this note so that it is the shared version of events. Personally, I also learned that I hold my breath during the first hour of a staged rollout, and that a printed list of the thresholds next to my keyboard, with the times of the decisions, calmed me down more than any dashboard. Wenzel has already sent me a photograph of the whiteboard from his desk where he wrote the rule about interrupted uploads, with a small drawing of a train, which made the whole team laugh at four in the afternoon on a hard day.

Review of the accounts payable process, meeting notes with commentary. Attendees: Ilse from finance, who owns the process, Blake as the sponsor, Avery, who joined to think about tooling, and Tomás, the part-time bookkeeper who does most of the actual work on Tuesdays and Thursdays. We sat around the big desk in the finance room with a printout of the last quarter's supplier bills, which Tomás had annotated in three colours of pen. The idea was to find out why suppliers keep sending us polite reminders, and whether anything can be done without hiring someone.

How it works today. A supplier bill arrives by email, sometimes to Ilse, sometimes to a shared mailbox, occasionally to whoever the supplier knew last. Someone forwards it to Tomás. He enters it in the bookkeeping tool, then asks the budget owner, usually a team lead, to confirm the work was done. Once the owner replies, Tomás schedules payment on the next weekly run, which goes out on Thursdays after Ilse approves the batch. In principle the whole path takes a week. In practice the notes on the printout tell a different story.

What the data says. Tomás counted the 212 supplier bills from the last quarter and measured the days from receipt to payment. The results were sobering: a quarter of the bills went out more than 55 days after arriving, and the median was well past the deadline printed on most of them. Late payment has not yet cost us a supplier, but two of them added a line about interest to their reminders, and our hosting provider sent a friendly note that read, to Blake, as slightly less friendly than intended.

Where the days go. Tomás split each bill's journey into stages using his coloured pens. Green stands for the time before it reaches him, which averaged nine days, because bills sit in inboxes of people who do not know what to do with them. Blue is entry and matching, only two days. Red is waiting for the budget owner to confirm, which averaged fourteen days and had the widest spread, from same-day to nearly two months. Black is the wait for the weekly payment run, three days on average. So the bulk of the delay is not in finance at all. It is in the people who commissioned the work.

Why owners are slow. We asked Blake and Avery what they do when Tomás sends a confirmation request. Both admitted that the emails look like every other automated message and get skimmed past, and that they lack the information to answer: which project was this for, what did we agree, is it the full amount? Avery said he often has to search his own mailbox to remember whether a supplier delivered. Tomás said that he is embarrassed to chase senior people, and that the third reminder is when things happen, usually because Ilse steps in.

Options discussed. Ilse's first idea was a strict rule: no confirmation within five days means automatic approval. Blake disliked that, as it would pay for work that had not been delivered. A gentler variant was accepted: the request goes out with the bill attached, the purchase reference and the amount agreed, and a two-click answer, 'delivered as agreed' or 'there is a problem'. Silence after five days escalates to the owner's manager instead of approving. Avery offered to build a small form to power it in a couple of days, using the existing bookkeeping tool's programming interface.

The front door. A second problem is that bills arrive in random places. We agreed to create a single dedicated inbox and to ask every supplier to use it. Tomás will send a short message to the active suppliers explaining the change, and Ilse will add the address to the purchase order template so new suppliers use it from the start. The shared mailbox forwards into the bookkeeping tool automatically, which cuts most of the nine days of green.

Targets. The baseline is the quarter just gone, when payments averaged 41 days against terms of 30. We set a goal of an average of 28 days within two months, measured the same way, and Tomás will publish the stage times monthly on a single slide. Ilse asked whether the Thursday payment run could become twice a week, and Blake said yes if approval stays with her. The next review is in six weeks. Meanwhile Tomás will send a personal apology, drafted by Blake, to the hosting provider and the two suppliers who mentioned interest, and Ilse will decide by Friday whether to pay any of the small amounts. Two further points came up after that.

One more thing came up while we were sketching the new flow: partial deliveries. Suppliers sometimes bill for a whole project when only half has arrived, and Tomás has no good way to record that. Ilse suggested a third answer option, 'partly delivered', which opens a short thread between the owner and the supplier and pauses the clock on our side. Blake worried that a pause option would become a place for bills to hide, so we added a rule that a paused bill is listed at the top of the Thursday meeting until it is resolved. Tomás said that a visible list would have saved him three uncomfortable phone calls last quarter, and I believe him.

Avery also wanted to know about early-payment discounts, since two suppliers offer two percent for payment within ten days. Ilse said that we have never taken one, because we are always late. Two percent for twenty days early is an excellent return compared with what the bank pays us, and Ilse will calculate whether it is worth prioritising those suppliers, of whom there are only a handful. The session ended in an hour and a half, and Tomás took the printout with the three colours of pen away to keep, saying it was the first time anyone had asked him what he thought of the process.

Planning how to tell our integration partners that the first version of the public interface is being retired. This is a communications problem more than a technical one, and the technical part is finished: the second version has been live for nine months, it does everything the old one did, and it is faster. What remains is persuading about 140 partners, some of whom wrote their integration years ago and have long since moved on to other projects, to change a few lines of code. I am writing the plan here before turning it into emails so that the reasoning survives the copy edits.

The audience. Wenzel pulled usage data from the gateway logs. Of the 140 partners who ever used version one, 88 called it in the last month. Of those, 51 also call version two, meaning they are in the middle of moving or run both. The remaining 37 use only the old one, and they are the ones at risk. Six of those account for more than sixty percent of the old traffic, and I will give them personal attention. For each of the 37, we also know the contact address that registered the key, though about a quarter of those addresses will bounce, since people change jobs.

Principles. My rules for the plan are these. First, give a date early and stick to it, because a moving deadline teaches everyone to ignore it. Second, make the migration as small as possible, with a document that shows the old call and the new call side by side. Third, warn more than once, through more than one channel, on a schedule set now, and write that schedule where partners can read it. Fourth, when the date arrives, do not switch off abruptly but degrade in steps, so that a partner who missed everything still gets a clear signal before a hard failure.

Channels. Email goes to the registered contact, addressed to a person and not to a role, since role addresses tend to bounce into a void, plus a notice on the developer page, plus a banner in the dashboard for accounts that have used version one in the last thirty days. For the six large partners, Blake or I will call, since a phone call takes ten minutes and prevents a week of confusion. I will also ask Priya to add a line to the support macro for integration questions, so that agents have a consistent answer if a partner writes in worried.

The announcement text. I drafted it in four short paragraphs. What is changing, in one sentence with the date. Why: the old version cannot be maintained securely, and the new one is faster and documented. What to do: switch to the new address, following the guide, and test using the sandbox. Where to get help: a named contact, not a generic address. Nadia read it and suggested moving the date into the subject line, which is obviously right, and I felt slightly foolish for burying it.

The schedule. Announcement today, seven months ahead of the end. A reminder at three months, one at one month, and one at one week, each shorter and more direct than the one before. In the last two months, responses from the old interface carry a warning header and a small delay of half a second, which is harmless but visible in logs. During the last week, one day in seven the old interface will fail on purpose for an hour, a brownout, so that any partner who ignores email will notice through a failure they can still recover from. And the old endpoint goes dark on 1 March, after which it returns a clear error message with a link to the migration guide, and does not simply vanish.

Handling objections. I expect two types. Some partners will say they lack the engineering capacity and will ask for an extension; for those with a real reason, I would offer a fixed extension of at most six weeks in writing, so it does not become open-ended. Others will ask for features that exist only in the new version, which is a good thing to hear because it means they see the benefit. Marguerite asked me to keep a list of the extensions granted so the sales team knows which relationships need care.

Measurement. Every Monday, Wenzel will send me a count of partners still calling the old interface, and I will plot it. The goal is fewer than five at the one-month reminder, and zero surprises on the day. If the count is not falling by the second reminder, I will escalate to a direct campaign by phone. I will post the date in the team channel, pin it, and put it in my own calendar with a note reminding me to be a bit nervous, because a deadline nobody worries about is usually one that nobody is meeting. I will also send Ilse a copy, in case a partner asks about billing during the change, and I will keep the final wording under version control so that every reminder repeats the same date.

Load test of the cart service ahead of the autumn sale. Every year the sale weekend brings roughly six times normal traffic in a few hours, and last year we discovered the limits of the ordering path the hard way, at eleven at night with the sales team watching. This year Marguerite asked for numbers in advance. I spent Thursday and Friday running a stress test against the staging copy of the service, with Dario watching the database and Wenzel keeping me honest about the test's design.

Goal and success criteria. Before running anything I wrote three targets. The service should sustain 1,200 requests per second, which is twice last year's peak, with a median latency under 150 milliseconds and the 99th percentile under 800. Error rate below 0.5 percent. And it must recover within two minutes after the load drops. I also wrote what I would not measure: browsers rendering the page, the payment provider's speed, and the search service, since those have their own tests and mixing them hides which part is slow.

Setup. The staging environment mirrors production at about half the size: four application instances instead of eight, and a database with half the memory. That makes it a conservative test, since if staging handles X, production should handle about 2X, though scaling is never perfectly linear, and I said so in the report. The load generator is a script that replays a mix of real request types from last year's sale: browsing the cart, adding items, applying discount codes, and placing orders, in proportions that match the recorded traffic. I ran the generator from three machines in the same region to avoid saturating a single network link.

Warm-up and tooling. A load test that starts cold measures the wrong thing: empty caches, unopened connections and a virtual machine still deciding how fast to run. So each run began with ten minutes at 100 requests per second before I recorded anything. I logged every request's latency with a timestamp to a file, and Wenzel wrote a short script to bucket it per second, which gave a graph that I could overlay with the database's own metrics. We also fixed the random seed of the generator so that a second run would replay the identical sequence of carts, since otherwise a difference between two runs could be chance in the mix of orders. Dario disabled the payment provider's live calls in staging, replacing them with a stub that answers in 120 milliseconds, roughly what the real one averages, and we agreed to say so in the report, since the real provider adds variance I cannot control.

Ramp. The test began at 100 requests per second and stepped up by 200 every five minutes. Up to 800 the graphs were boring, which is what one wants: median latency around 60 milliseconds, CPU on the application instances under forty percent, database connections steady. At 1,000 the median crept to 85 and the 99th percentile started to stretch. At 1,400 the database CPU touched seventy percent, and Dario noticed a single query, the one that checks stock for each item in a cart, dominating the load.

Finding the ceiling. I kept stepping up while Dario watched. At 1,800 the numbers were still inside the targets for latency, although errors were creeping to 0.3 percent. At 2,000 something snapped: latency at the 99th percentile jumped to nearly four seconds and errors reached six percent as the connection pool ran dry. Backing off to find the edge, we found that the service held 1,850 requests per second before latency broke, with a clean margin at 1,800. That is 54 percent above our goal on half-size infrastructure, which is a better result than I expected, and I checked the run twice because it seemed too good.

Why it broke. The stock query is not slow in itself, but each order runs it once per line item, and under load these small queries queue behind each other for connections. The application instances themselves were never above sixty percent CPU, so adding servers would not have helped; the bottleneck is the database connection pool, set at eighty. Raising it to a hundred and twenty only moved the wall to about 2,100 and raised database memory pressure, so I do not recommend it as a cure. The better fix is to fetch stock for all items in one query.

Recovery test. I dropped the load from 2,000 to 300 in one step and watched. Latency returned to normal in ninety seconds and errors vanished after about forty. That passed the criterion. However, the queue of half-completed orders took another four minutes to clear, and Wenzel pointed out that customers would see slow confirmations during that time, so we agreed to note it in the report even though it is inside the letter of the target.

Actions. Dario will change the stock check into a batched query this week, and I will rerun the test on Monday to see the difference. Wenzel will add a dashboard tile showing connection pool usage, since that is the metric that predicted the failure. I will also keep the raw request logs from both runs in the team folder for a month, in case someone wants to slice them differently. I will write the report with a graph of latency against request rate, the three targets, and a short paragraph of recommendations, and send it to Marguerite on Tuesday with a note that production should be tested at least once, briefly, on a quiet night before the sale.

Refund policy revision, working session. Avery, Blake, Colm and Ilse met with Marguerite for the last twenty minutes. The trigger was a pattern in support: over the past quarter, about one refund request in five came after the fourteen-day limit, and agents were making case-by-case exceptions with no shared rule, so the same situation produced different answers depending on who was on shift. That is bad for customers and worse for morale, since Colm's team feels they have to decide whether to be kind or correct every time.

The facts. Colm counted the requests in the last ninety days: 164 in total, of which 131 were inside the limit and approved without discussion. The other 33 were late. Of those 33, 19 were approved anyway as exceptions, and 14 were refused. The average amount refunded on exceptions was 96 euros, so the cost of the exceptions was about 1,800 euros a quarter, which Ilse said is small against monthly revenue but not nothing. What we did not know was how many of the 14 refused customers left and told others, and there is no way to measure that.

Why the limit exists. Ilse explained the history. The fourteen days were copied from a competitor's terms four years ago, when the product was simpler, and were meant to discourage people who sign up, use the service for a month, and then ask for the money back. But our data does not show much of that behaviour: only three of the 33 late requests came from accounts with heavy usage in the period. Most were people who never got around to setting the product up, or who were surprised by an annual charge on a card they had forgotten.

Options. Blake put three on the board. Keep fourteen days and formalise the exceptions. Extend to thirty days. Or make refunds depend on usage, with full refund if barely used and partial otherwise. The third is the fairest in theory, but Colm said it would be a nightmare to explain and to apply consistently, with each case turning into an argument about what counts as heavy use. We dropped it quickly. Formalising the exceptions would leave us with a policy that says one thing and does another, which Marguerite said she would rather not have on paper.

Marguerite asked what other companies in our space do, and Blake had done the homework the night before. Of seven comparable subscription products, two offer fourteen days, three offer thirty, one offers sixty and one says nothing at all. So thirty is the middle of the market, not a bold gesture. Ilse added that a refund period tends to matter more to customers before they buy than after: a longer one lowers the perceived risk of signing up, and on the pricing page it may do some of the work that a discount does at a fraction of the cost. We could not quantify that, and I said so in the notes so it does not turn into a claim later.

Colm raised the emotional side. Agents currently feel like gatekeepers, and the days after the limit are the worst, because a customer who is a week late and sincerely sorry has to be told no by someone who would prefer to say yes. He believes a clear thirty-day rule will remove more stress than any training could, and he asked that the wording tell agents exactly what to do when a request comes on day thirty-one: refuse politely, offer a partial credit once, and pass anything unusual to Ilse.

Decision. After some discussion of fraud risk, which Ilse considers low for a subscription product, we settled on a longer period. The refund period grows from 14 to 30 days for monthly plans, and for annual plans the full refund applies within 30 days too, followed by a prorated refund up to ninety days. Marguerite's condition was that the policy is stated in one clear paragraph, with no clauses that need a lawyer. Avery volunteered to write it, and Colm will translate it into a saved reply and a short entry in the help centre.

What could go wrong. The risk is that more people request refunds because the limit is longer, and Ilse ran a rough estimate: if the number of refunds doubled, which is pessimistic, the cost would be about 7,000 euros a year. If it does not change much, the cost is close to zero and we save time on discussions. We will track the monthly refund rate for six months and review the decision in the spring, with a threshold that triggers a rethink if refunds exceed four percent of new subscriptions.

Communication. Existing customers benefit too, so it applies immediately, including to customers who asked in the last thirty days and were refused; Colm will contact those fourteen people personally to offer the refund. Blake suggested that we say nothing in a big announcement, only quietly update the page, since a longer period can be read as a sign of weak confidence in the product. Marguerite disagreed, saying that a generous policy is worth advertising, and asked for a single sentence on the pricing page.

Who does what. Avery drafts the paragraph by Thursday, Ilse checks how it interacts with the tax rules for refunds, and Colm prepares the outreach to the fourteen refused customers. Blake will update the terms page once Marguerite approves the text, and we will note the change date so the policy in force on any given day is known. Marguerite closed the meeting by saying that a good policy is one that agents can explain in a single breath, and asked Avery to test the paragraph on somebody who has never seen our terms before publishing anything.

Ghent weekend diary, Saturday and Sunday. Mira had been nagging me for two years to see Ghent properly instead of changing trains there, so we finally booked two nights at a narrow guesthouse near the Patershol quarter. We left Brussels on the 08:12 train, which was half empty, and I spent the ride sorting the photos from the last trip so my phone had space for this one. The plan was loose on purpose: canals, a couple of churches, one proper meal, and no queueing for anything.

Saturday started with the castle of the Counts. The entry was thirteen euros each, and the audio guide was included, though Mira abandoned hers after the second chamber because the narrator kept whispering. I liked the torture museum wing more than I expected to; the guillotine was smaller than the one I pictured from school books. From the ramparts you can see the whole old harbour, and a man selling waffles from a hatch was doing better business than the museum shop. We each had one, with just sugar, and stood on the wall until the wind got cold.

After that we walked along the Graslei, where the old guild houses lean against each other like tired books on a shelf. A busker was playing a cello under the bridge and the sound carried surprisingly well over the water.
