We dropped a couple of coins in the case and moved on toward the Gravensteen side streets, looking for a lunch spot Mira's colleague had recommended. It turned out to be shut for a private event, so we ended up in a small place with a chalkboard menu and had a root stew with a poached egg on top. Nothing special, but warm, and the owner brought us a plate of pickled onions unasked.

In the afternoon I dragged us to the Saint Bavo cathedral for the Van Eyck altarpiece, the one with the lamb. There is a timed slot system, and ours was 15:40, so we killed an hour in a second-hand bookshop with a very grumpy cat. I bought a battered Dutch cookbook with handwritten margins for four euros, mostly for the annotations. The altarpiece itself was smaller than I expected but the detail is ridiculous: you can count the hairs on the beard of the figures if you lean in, and the guard let me lean in exactly as far as the rope allowed and no further.

Evening plan was a canal boat tour, which I had been sceptical about, but it was included in the city card we bought for the weekend. The guide spoke three languages in a row and made the same joke each time, in slightly different words. We passed under low bridges where everyone ducked, and saw the backs of houses that never appear in postcards, with laundry lines and potted herbs and one man practising the trombone on a balcony. Dinner was a fish soup at a spot on the Korenlei, and we split a portion of chips with a mayonnaise so heavy that Mira asked whether it was legal.

We had planned Sunday around the flea market at Bijloke, but it rained from before seven. Over breakfast at the guesthouse, the host, a retired ferry pilot named Jozef, explained that the tram network is much better than it looks on the map and that the day pass costs less than two single tickets. He also told us where to find the best hot chocolate in town, which he said with such gravity that we changed plans and went there first. It was worth it. The cup was nearly a soup bowl and the chocolate was made from a slab that a girl shaved by hand behind the counter.

The market was smaller under the rain, but the stallholders had tarps up and it felt cosy rather than miserable. Mira found a brass compass for eleven euros and haggled it down to nine, which she has been reminding me of ever since. I bought a set of old railway postcards, mostly for the stamps and the handwriting. One of them is from 1931 and says only that the sender will be late for supper, which struck me as the perfect postcard. We ate warm sausage rolls standing under an awning next to a man selling accordions, none of which he could play, he admitted.

Before leaving we had a couple of hours to spare, so we took the tram out to the Museum of Fine Arts and looked at the Bosch gallery, which is small but crowded with people who all seem to be looking for the same painting. The staff were friendly and let us leave our wet coats in a free cloak store. I sat for a while in front of a small saint and tried to sketch the hands, badly. Mira found a bench and read the guide to the following weekend's trip, which she has already begun planning, apparently without telling me.

Back at the station we had a small panic because the departures board did not list our train and a rail worker who barely looked up said only that the return leg left from platform eleven, not the usual number seven, because of maintenance. We ran, but it turned out to be no distance at all and we sat waiting ten minutes on a cold bench. On board I finally worked through my notes: total spend for the weekend was a bit under four hundred euros including the guesthouse, which is a decent number for two people and a lot of waffles.

Things to remember for next time. Book the cathedral slot in advance, since the walk-in queue on Saturday looked nasty. Bring a proper umbrella rather than the folding one that turned inside out at the market. Ask Jozef about the day trip to the coast, which he says is easy by train, and take the guesthouse recommendation for the fish restaurant near the Vrijdagmarkt. Also buy the second cookbook, the one with the ducks on the cover, because I keep thinking about it. Mira says I am allowed exactly one impulse purchase per city, and I have already used mine on the first one, so we will see.

Photos are in the folder labelled Ghent, about ninety of them after culling. The best is the cello player under the bridge with the boat passing behind him, and the runner-up is the compass in Mira's hand with the rain making everything in the background blurry. We will need to plan something with my sister in autumn, maybe Antwerp, which is even closer.

Repair cafe volunteer shift, Saturday at the parish hall. I signed up as a helper about six weeks ago after taking a broken desk lamp there and being impressed that a retired signal engineer named Lennart fixed it in eleven minutes while explaining what he was doing. This was my third shift as a proper volunteer, and the first where I was trusted with the intake sheet rather than just carrying boxes. The morning is organised so that visitors bring one item each, we write down what it is and what they think is wrong with it, and then it goes to the bench that suits it: electrical, textile, bicycles, or the general bench for everything else.

Set-up begins early because the hall is also used by a toddler group on Fridays and there is always a residue of foam blocks and small plastic animals to clear away. I arrived to find Marta, who coordinates the whole thing, already unstacking chairs and muttering about the heating. She hands out laminated cards for the tool benches so we can keep track of which screwdriver sets have wandered off; two disappeared last month and one was found in the toddler cupboard, which nobody could explain. I labelled the multimeters with coloured tape while she counted the extension leads, and then we tested every socket on the long wall, because one of them had tripped the breaker during the previous session.

The first visitor of the day was a woman with a hand mixer that only worked when held at an angle. Lennart opened it and found that the cord had frayed right where it enters the body; he cut, stripped, and re-crimped it in about the time it takes to boil an egg, and then gave her a short lecture about not wrapping the cord around the housing. She left with the mixer and a look of quiet triumph. I like how the volunteers never make anyone feel foolish. A man came with a radio from the seventies that he said his father had built, and the whole electrical bench gathered around it as if it were a very old cat.

By eleven we had a queue of nine people, and I was writing intake notes as fast as I could. The rules are simple: nothing with a mains capacitor bank that we cannot discharge safely, no gas appliances, no anything with a sealed battery that looks swollen. The swollen-battery rule came from an incident a year ago that Marta still refuses to describe. A teenager brought a scooter with a flat tyre and asked if we could fix it, and I sent him to the bicycle bench, where a woman called Ingrid had him patching the tube himself within a few minutes. She says the point of the exercise is that people leave knowing how to do it next time, not that we do it for them.

At the textile bench, an older man was sewing a zip into a jacket with a speed that made me feel clumsy. Three visitors came in a row with trousers needing hems, and the two women at the bench worked out a rota so nobody waited longer than fifteen minutes. There is a jar for donations on every bench, and the sums are counted at the end of the day and put towards new parts. This week the jar total was a hundred and sixty-two crowns, which Marta announced as if it were a record, though it is roughly average. The money pays for solder, fuses, tyre patches, and the occasional bag of biscuits for the volunteers.

I had a small triumph around noon. A visitor with a clock radio that would not turn on turned out to have a blown thermal fuse, and I had the correct replacement in the parts drawer because I had sorted that drawer the week before. Lennart let me solder it under his supervision, and I only burned my thumb a little. The radio played a crackly local station immediately, and the owner laughed and asked whether we took requests. There is something very satisfying about a repair that takes two minutes but rescues an object which would otherwise have gone in the bin. Mira says I talk about nothing else after these Saturdays.

After the last visitor left we did the closing routine: count the leftover parts, write down what needed ordering, sweep the floor, put the foam blocks back for the toddlers. Marta had a short meeting with the six of us in the tea corner and explained that the shift started at nine thirty for everyone on the next date, an hour later than before, because two of the electricians can no longer manage the early start after switching jobs. I said that suited me fine. She also asked me to bring my own soldering iron tip, since ours has been showing signs of giving up.

The list of things we could not fix this time was short: a vacuum cleaner with a cracked motor housing, a very old toaster with no available element, and a pair of headphones whose cable was internally broken in three places. We explained to each visitor honestly what was wrong and where they could find a specialist. One man asked whether there was a way to at least recycle the toaster, and Ingrid found him the address of the nearest collection point on the back of a leaflet. He went away satisfied, which I think is the actual aim.

Afterwards, a few of us went for a bowl of soup around the corner, and Lennart explained how he trained as a signal engineer on the railway in the eighties and why he thinks modern appliances are built to be thrown away. I asked whether he was pessimistic and he said no, just tired of glue. I walked home with a new appreciation for screws. Next shift I intend to shadow the bicycle bench for an hour, since Ingrid offered to teach me how to true a wheel.

Orienteering afternoon, team outing write-up. We held the outing at the forest park north of the city on the last Friday of the month, and it was organised by Blake and me with help from Tove in operations, who booked the bus, since the little car park at the forest entrance holds barely a dozen cars and nobody wanted to shuttle. The idea came out of the retrospective last quarter, when several people said they wanted a day that was physical without being a competition among departments. We settled on orienteering in mixed teams of five, with maps printed on waterproof paper and a set of control markers borrowed from a local club that let us use them for a donation.

Preparation took about three weeks. Blake walked the course twice with the club instructor, a patient man named Halvard, and they placed fourteen markers in total, with different point values depending on difficulty. The easy ones were on the main tracks and worth ten points; the hard ones sat in a boggy area or up a rocky slope and were worth thirty. We printed the maps on the plotter after checking scale against the official grid, and Tove laminated the score cards. I wrote a short safety briefing that covered whistles, emergency numbers, and the rule that nobody leaves the marked area, with the club's advice to turn back if you are unsure.

The bus left the office at 11:30 and arrived at the car park around noon. It was cold but clear, about four degrees, with frost still holding in the shadows. Halvard gave a ten-minute demonstration of how to read the map, how to orient it with the compass, and how to use handrails, which are linear features like fences and streams that guide you between points. Several people had never held a compass before, and there was some enthusiastic misuse of the mirror flap. We split into six teams by drawing names from a hat, making sure that each team had at least one person who had done this before, even if only as a child.

The first hour was pure chaos in the best way. Team Three went the wrong direction along the ridge and reappeared at the start point twenty minutes later, cheerful and completely lost. Team Five found the boggy markers first and came back with wet boots and considerable pride. Someone on Team Two discovered that the map had a small printing error where a path was drawn slightly off, and we later agreed to correct it for future use. I ran between the checkpoints with a radio and a thermos and stood at the halfway point handing out cocoa, which was the most popular thing I have ever organised.

Around two o'clock we regrouped by the big fireplace shelter, where Tove had set up a soup station with two large pots: a lentil one and a chicken and barley one. People kept their gloves on while eating. We tallied scores on a whiteboard propped against a birch trunk. The winning team, Team Four, collected two hundred and ten points and included Ana from finance, who turned out to be a fearsome navigator. She said she grew up in a village with no signal and learned to read terrain out of sheer necessity. The losers earned the traditional prize, a bag of dried fruit, which they declared a victory.

Feedback was collected over the soup and via a short form afterwards. The response was very positive. People said they liked being outdoors, they liked the mixed teams, and several said it was the first time in months they had talked to colleagues from other departments about anything other than deadlines. Two complaints: the bus was late back to the city because of traffic on the ring road, and the soup ran out slightly early. There was also a request for a longer course, and one from Ana for a night version, which Halvard said he would consider if we pay for the head torches.

Decision points from the debrief on Monday. We agreed to repeat the outing next year, probably in autumn when the colours are better. Budget was about nine hundred euros in total, of which the bus was the largest share and the club donation the smallest. Blake suggested rotating the organiser role so the same people do not do all of it. I noted that the sunrise start was set for six forty for the next event, a proposal from Halvard who wants us to try a dawn session with a proper breakfast afterwards, and it will be optional for anyone who would rather sleep.

Action list. Tove will send thank-you notes to the club and the bus company. Blake will update the map with the corrected path and file the digital copy on the shared drive. I will write up the safety briefing as a reusable template and add a section on cold weather clothing. Everyone will get a small certificate; Ana has already asked for hers to be laminated. We also agreed to check whether the club would sell us a starter set of compasses at a discount, since about half of them came from staff personal collections and some had bubbles inside.

Personal note. I finished the day with cold ears, a ruined pair of trousers, and the strong sense that this was the best team event we have run in a long time. Halvard stayed after everyone left to collect the markers, and Blake and I helped him carry them to his van. He said the team was better than most school groups, which from him counts as high praise.

Bookbinding evening course, week one to week four, combined notes. I enrolled in the Thursday course at the craft school after seeing a finished sewn notebook at Mira's cousin's flat and realising I could make one myself. The course is six evenings, three hours each, in a workshop with high ceilings, two large presses, and a smell of glue and old paper that I found immediately calming. Our teacher is a woman called Sigrid who has been binding for thirty years and mends the collections of two local libraries. There are eight of us in the group, including a retired surveyor, a nervous student, and a couple who came together because the husband had won the place in a raffle.

The first evening was mostly about vocabulary and tools. A signature is a folded group of sheets; a text block is the collection of signatures; a spine is the spine. We learned to fold with a bone folder, using the pressure of the flat side rather than the edge, and to cut paper against the grain so the fold stays crisp. Sigrid showed us how to test the grain direction by bending a sheet gently in both directions and feeling which way is stiffer, which I would never have thought of. We each folded twenty-four sheets into six signatures, and mine came out unevenly. She kept a drawer of ruined attempts from previous years as reassurance, and I spent a happy ten minutes looking through them.

Week two was sewing. We used a kettle stitch on waxed linen thread, working from the first signature to the last and linking each to the previous at the head and tail. I tangled the thread four times and broke it once. The surveyor next to me was quietly excellent and produced a spine so even that Sigrid held it up as an example. She corrected my tension twice and explained that most beginners pull too tight, which puckers the folds. By the end of the evening I had six signatures joined and a strange feeling of pride in a pile of paper that could not yet be called a book. The wax on my fingers took two days to wear off.

The third week was about the cover. We cut greyboard to size, allowing three millimetres of overhang at the top, bottom and fore-edge, and covered it with cloth glued with a wheat paste that Sigrid cooked herself in a small pot on the workshop's hot plate. My cloth was a deep green with a faint weave, chosen because it reminded me of an old atlas I had as a child. Gluing cloth is trickier than it looks; it stretches, wrinkles, and sticks to everything, including sleeves. I managed to get one bubble under the front board which I could not smooth out, and Sigrid said it was a feature that gave the book character, which is the kindest thing anyone has said about my mistakes.

On the fourth evening we attached the text block to the covers with endpapers and left everything under the presses for an hour. During the pressing time, Sigrid gave a talk on the history of the codex and passed around a sample of a sixteenth century vellum leaf, thin and faintly greasy to the touch. She let each of us hold it for a moment; the student almost cried. Someone asked about repairing a book with a broken spine, and she spent twenty minutes explaining how she would rebuild one with new cords, which turned into an unplanned masterclass. We stayed late and she locked up around ten with the couple still arguing about the colour of their thread.

Cost tracking, since I always forget. The tuition came to fourteen hundred kronor, materials included, with an extra fee of sixty for the cloth I chose. I also bought a bone folder and a small awl in the school shop, because I liked them, and a bottle of wheat paste starter that is apparently not needed. Travel is negligible, since the school is a twelve minute walk from home. Mira's view is that this is the cheapest hobby I have ever taken up, because the only expensive thing is the temptation to buy paper. She may be right, given that I already own three sheets of marbled paper I do not know what to do with.

What I learned so far. Precision matters less than consistency; a slightly wrong fold, repeated across all signatures, still produces a decent book. The glue must be applied thin and fast, because thick layers dry lumpy. I should always test cloth on a scrap before committing. And the best thing about the class is the workshop, which feels like a place where nothing has to be hurried. Even the nervous student has relaxed by now, and yesterday she brought a plate of cardamom buns for everyone, which Sigrid promptly incorporated into the lesson as a reason for a break.

Plans for the last two weeks. Week five is a Japanese stab binding, which uses a single needle and a decorative stitch across the spine edge. Week six is an open studio, where we can finish personal projects with help. I want to bind a small notebook for Mira's birthday, with her initials stamped in gold foil if I can borrow the equipment. Sigrid has hinted that there is an advanced course in the spring focused on leather, and I have quietly been saving for it. I have already promised myself that I will not buy leather tools until I have finished the first three books properly.

Kimchi experiment notes, first batch. The idea started when my neighbour Dagny gave me a jar of her own and I ate it straight from the fridge, standing in the hallway like a person possessed. I decided to try making it myself, following a Korean home-cook video with the subtitles set to slow, and to keep detailed notes so the second batch could improve on the first. I ordered a bag of coarse sea salt and a jar of gochugaru flakes from the Asian grocer at Odenplan, a place that also sells the best pickled radish I have ever had. The napa cabbage came from the market on Saturday, two medium heads weighing about two and a half kilos together.

Preparation began on Sunday afternoon. I quartered the cabbages lengthwise, cut them into large squares, and sprinkled them layer by layer with salt in the biggest bowl I own. The video advised turning them every thirty minutes for two hours, so I set the oven timer as a reminder and pretended I was not bored. While the cabbage sweated, I made the paste from glutinous rice flour, water, and a spoonful of sugar, cooked gently until it turned translucent and sticky. The recipe called it a porridge, and it did look like a small, smug bowl of wallpaper glue. I stirred until my arm hurt and then left it to cool on the balcony.

The seasoning was the fun part. I grated a whole head of garlic, about forty grams of ginger, and half a sweet apple, then mixed them with fish sauce, a little shrimp paste, and the gochugaru. The colour was a startling orange-red, and it stained my gloves, my sleeves, and one of my eyebrows. I added sliced spring onions and a handful of julienned radish, and stirred the paste in until it was smooth. Tasting the raw paste made my eyes water. Dagny came over when she smelled the garlic through the wall and offered some guidance, mostly to say I was being too timid with the chilli and too generous with the sugar.

After rinsing the cabbage three times, the important step is checking the salt level. It should taste pleasantly salty, like the sea on a calm day, but not harsh. I squeezed a piece and tasted it, and it was a little too mild, which Dagny confirmed by tasting. She said the correct salinity is about two percent by weight of the finished mix, so we weighed the drained cabbage and the paste together and worked it out; the whole jar went in at two percent salt after I added another spoonful of coarse crystals dissolved in a little water. We massaged the paste into every leaf with gloved hands, which took a good twenty minutes and felt oddly meditative.

Packing the jar was harder than I thought. The cabbage wants to spring back and trap air pockets, which invite mould, so I pressed each handful down with a spoon until the brine rose above it. I left three centimetres of headspace because the mixture will bubble as it ferments. On top I placed a small ceramic saucer weighted with a clean stone from Dagny's shelf, and I covered the whole thing loosely with a cloth held by a rubber band. It is now sitting in the cupboard under the stairs, which stays at about eighteen degrees. I photographed it and wrote the date in permanent marker on masking tape.

Day two checkpoint. No visible bubbles, but the smell has changed from raw garlic to something more complex and slightly sour. On day three there were small bubbles and the liquid had gained about four centimetres of brine. I pressed the cabbage down with a clean spoon and tasted a leaf; it was crunchy, tangy, and a bit spicy, with a hint of sweetness from the apple. The recipe says to move the jar to the fridge once it reaches the sourness you like, and I decided to give it two more days at ambient temperature. Mira, who has been treating the cupboard with suspicion, now peeks in every morning and says it smells like a nice restaurant.

Lessons and adjustments for batch two. Use less sugar, and consider replacing the apple with a pear. Check that the jar is sterile before packing, because I found a small speck on the rim that I hope was only paste. Buy a proper fermentation weight; the stone works, but Dagny says it is not how a serious person does it. Make the batch smaller, since one and a half kilos would have fit in the jar with space to spare and I would not feel obliged to give away half. And do not, under any circumstances, taste the paste with a bare finger while wearing contact lenses.

Final thoughts on this experiment. On day five I moved the jar to the fridge, and on day seven I opened it and served it with rice and a fried egg. It was better than I had any right to expect, sharp and crunchy with a warm chilli glow, and Mira ate three helpings. I gave a small jar to Dagny for judgement, and she has not yet responded, which I choose to interpret as respectful silence. I plan to make a second batch next weekend, this time with pear, less sugar, and radish chunks, and to keep a chart of days against sourness.

Food bank sorting day, volunteer notes. Six of us from the team spent Thursday morning at the regional food bank warehouse in the industrial estate east of the ring road, as part of the volunteering days the company agreed to fund. I organised the sign-up, Avery drove the van with the folding trolleys, and the rest were volunteers who put their names on the sheet in the hallway. The warehouse manager, a brisk woman called Kerstin, met us at the loading bay at eight and gave us hi-vis vests, hairnets for anyone with long hair, and a very clear speech about what we were and were not allowed to touch.

The first hour was induction. Kerstin walked us through the layout: a chilled store for dairy and cooked meals, a dry goods hall with racking to the ceiling, and a small area at the back for damaged packaging. Every donated item has to be checked for date, seal and dents before it goes onto a pallet. Anything past its use-by date goes in the grey bin, but items that are past best-before and still sealed can be distributed if they are labelled. She showed us how to read the codes printed on tin lids, which none of us had ever paid attention to, and told us that the most common reason for rejecting a tin is a dent along the seam rather than on the body.

We were split into three pairs. Avery and Tove took the incoming donations from a supermarket chain, which arrived on two pallets wrapped in plastic film so tight that it took a knife and considerable patience to open. Ana and Joel went to the packing line, where boxes are assembled for families according to size: a standard box for a household of one or two, a large box for four or more. I worked with Marit, a long-term volunteer who has been coming every Thursday for nine years, and who taught me the rhythm of sorting without looking at my watch.

Halfway through the morning the mood shifted from cautious to competitive. Joel started keeping count of boxes packed by each pair, and it turned into an unspoken race. Kerstin noticed and quietly moved the scoreboard from the wall to the office, saying that the speed of packing matters less than whether each box has the right number of items. It was a fair point. We slowed down, checked the lists, and caught two boxes where someone had swapped pasta for rice. There was a short break at ten with tea and small cinnamon rolls that one of the regulars had baked, and Marit told us stories about the winter when the warehouse flooded.

Around eleven a truck arrived unexpectedly with a large late donation from a wholesaler that was closing a line of products. It took all of us to unload it. The delivery included fruit cups, two dozen bags of oats, and a surprising amount of baby formula, which Kerstin greeted with obvious relief because the shelves for that had been nearly empty. We logged every item on a handheld at the loading bay, entering weights and best-before dates while Ana read them out. It was the first time I had realised how much administration is hidden behind a full shelf. Each entry has to match what the driver says, and Kerstin corrects discrepancies with a sharp pencil.

The dry goods hall was where I spent the rest of the morning. My job was to carry the sorted tins to the racking and stack them by type, which sounds simple until you notice that the tins are heavy and the aisles are narrow. I counted, in the end, forty-one crates of tinned tomatoes that we shelved on the third rack from the entrance, which Kerstin said would last the canteens they supply about a fortnight. Joel pointed out that this was probably more tomato than any of us would see in a year.

Lunch was provided, and it was surprisingly good: a lentil curry made by the meal service next door, with rice and flat loaves. We ate together on stackable chairs in the loading bay with the doors open, since it was a mild day. Kerstin joined us for ten minutes and told us that requests for boxes have risen by about a third over the past two years, driven mainly by families rather than single people, which surprised most of us. She is clear-eyed about it; she does not want gratitude, she wants more volunteers on weekday mornings, when most people are at work. We agreed to raise it with management.

In the afternoon we did a final sweep. The warehouse floor was cleaned, pallets were relabelled, and the damaged goods area was emptied into the correct bins. Kerstin gave each of us a short evaluation, which involved a lot of kindness and a few practical tips about lifting. She asked whether we could send a team again in the spring, and I promised to check the budget. Avery drove the van back with the remaining trolleys and a box of misshapen apples that Kerstin insisted we take home, which ended up as a shared crumble in the office on Friday.

Follow-up actions from the team. I will submit the volunteering hours to the finance system by Monday so the sponsorship match is triggered. Tove will write the intranet post with photos, checking first that nobody in them minds. Joel wants to suggest that we run a food drive in the lobby, with a tin collection point, and I will talk to facilities about placing a bin near the entrance. Ana asked whether we could add a standing volunteer slot every quarter, and there was agreement in principle. I will bring the idea to the leadership meeting next week, along with Kerstin's note about weekday mornings.

Reflections. Nobody complained about the physical work, and several of us noticed how different the morning felt from a normal day at a desk. There is a kind of quiet satisfaction in filling a box and knowing precisely who it is for. Marit said something on the way out that I keep thinking about: that the shelves never really fill up, but that is not the point of stacking them. I think Blake at his desk would have said the same about backlog. Either way, six tired colleagues went home with sore backs and something to talk about at lunch for weeks.

Learning to surf in Peniche, the first two days. I booked a four-day beginner package after Mira sent me a photo of a friend standing on a board in Portugal, and I decided that being clumsy in warm water sounded better than being clumsy in a cold lake. The flight from Stockholm to Lisbon was quick, and the bus to Peniche took about an hour and a half through fields of low scrubby vegetation and windmills. The surf school was just behind the beach at Supertubos, a low white building with a rack of boards outside and a hand-painted sign that said, in three languages, that no experience was needed but a sense of humour was.

Day one started at nine with a briefing on the sand. Our instructor, a lean, sun-browned man called Tiago, gave a short lecture on rip currents, wave types and etiquette, in English so precise that I suspected he had taught it many times. There were nine of us in the group, from Germany, Brazil, Australia, and me. He drew a diagram in the sand with a stick that showed where waves break, where the safe zone is, and why you should never turn your back on the ocean. Then came the practice of the pop-up, lying on a board on dry sand and springing to your feet in one motion. I fell over sideways on my first attempt, and the Australian, Kelsey, said it was the most elegant collapse she had ever seen.

We spent about forty minutes on the pop-up alone, and Tiago corrected everyone individually: chest up, back foot across the tail, eyes on the horizon rather than on your feet. By the time we got into the water, my knees were already tired. The water was around seventeen degrees, cold enough to be a shock for the first minute, and the wetsuits we had hired were thick and slightly damp inside from previous users. I struggled into mine with the help of another student, and we both agreed that surfing begins and ends with wrestling neoprene. The wetsuit rental was thirty-five euros for the four days, a bargain compared with what I had feared.

In the whitewater, on the inside of the beach, Tiago pushed each of us into small broken waves and shouted instructions from behind. I managed to stand for about two seconds on my third attempt, and then fell backwards with a satisfying splash. The feeling was ridiculous: pure delight mixed with cold, salt, and a small amount of panic. After ninety minutes we came out shivering and were rewarded with sweet tea from a flask and slices of orange. My shoulders burned in a way I had not experienced since my rowing days, and I understood that paddling is the real workout, not standing up.

Lunch was fish grilled over charcoal at a place on the harbour, a whole sea bream with boiled potatoes and a salad dressed in too much vinegar. I sat with Kelsey and a Brazilian couple, Rafa and Luana, who have surfed for years but wanted a lesson to fix their timing. They talked about tides and swell periods like people discussing the weather in their home town, and I nodded gravely at things I barely understood. In the afternoon, we had a theory session about reading waves, and Tiago showed us a chart of the swell forecast on his phone, pointing out how a long period means more energy. We were told to rest, drink plenty of water, and rub something on our sunburnt noses.

Day two brought bigger waves and better technique. The morning started with stretching on the sand, and then a run along the shoreline to warm up. The forecast was for a metre and a half of swell, which Tiago called generous, and the school moved us a little further down the beach to a spot with a gentler slope. I got up on my fourth attempt and rode a wave all the way to the shore, arms out like a nervous tightrope walker. Kelsey filmed it and later sent me the clip, which I have watched more times than is reasonable. The thing that no one warns you about is how much water gets up your nose.

After the lesson I was completely exhausted. I lay on the beach for an hour, ate a pastel de nata, and fell asleep with my hat over my face. When I woke, a dog had settled next to me and was watching the waves with the same solemn expression as Tiago. The evening was quiet: a walk along the cliffs to the old fortress, where the light turned everything gold, and a simple dinner of grilled sardines and green wine. My hands were shaking slightly from the effort, and I made notes of what I needed to improve before day three. Mira messaged to ask whether I was still alive, and I sent her a picture of the sea in reply.

Notes for the next two days. Get a rash vest, because the wetsuit chafes at the neck. Bring more sun cream and reapply it after every session, since Kelsey says the reflection from the water is worse than direct sun. Use the school's lockers rather than trusting my bag to the sand. Practise the pop-up in the hotel, quietly. Ask Tiago about a next-level lesson, since he hinted that I might be ready to try a slightly bigger board. And remember to bring back a small gift for the neighbour who is watering my plants, perhaps a tin of the local sardines, which they sell in beautiful boxes with lighthouses on them.

Croissant lamination trial, three attempts over one weekend. I have wanted to try laminated dough for a year, ever since Mira and I ate a truly flaky croissant in a tiny place near Gamla Stan and I spent the rest of the day trying to describe the sound it made. This weekend I cleared the schedule and committed to three batches, with the aim of comparing hydration, resting time, and fat temperature. I bought good butter with a high fat content, a bag of strong flour, fresh yeast, and a marble slab that I found on sale at a homeware shop, because everything I read says that a cold work surface makes a difference.

The recipe I followed was adapted from a pastry chef's video. The dough, called the detrempe, is made from flour, cold milk, a little sugar, salt, and yeast, kneaded briefly, and left overnight in the fridge. The butter block is a separate operation: two hundred and fifty grams of butter beaten between sheets of parchment into a flat square about the thickness of a finger, then chilled until firm but pliable. The trick is to get the dough and the butter to the same consistency, so that they roll together without the butter cracking or squeezing out at the edges. I spent a ridiculous twenty minutes on Friday evening getting the square exactly right with a ruler, then wrapped it in cling film and put it on the coldest shelf, next to a jar of pickled beets that Mira insists is a family heirloom. I also read three more guides that night, and each one disagreed with the others about how much sugar the dough deserves.

On Saturday morning I rolled the dough into a rectangle and enclosed the butter block like a parcel being folded shut, sealing the edges with my fingertips. Then began the rolling and folding, which the video called turns. A single turn is a fold in thirds, which gives three layers; another turn gives nine; and so on. The dough must rest in the fridge for thirty minutes between each turn to relax the gluten and firm up the butter. My first batch went smoothly for two turns and then the butter broke through in a streak on the third, leaving a greasy patch. I patched it with flour and carried on, but I knew it would show in the final layers. Mira wandered in at that point, looked at the greasy sheet, and asked whether it was supposed to look like that; I said yes, confidently, and she went away unconvinced. The video's host makes the same mistake look charming, which is annoying.

While the first batch rested, I prepared the second with a different approach: chilling the flour in the freezer for an hour and using a cooler water temperature. I also slowed down the rolling and used a lighter touch, letting the rolling pin do the work rather than pressing hard. The dough felt different, silkier and more forgiving, and there were no breakthroughs. I noticed that the galley was much warmer than I had assumed, since the oven had been running for most of the morning for the first batch tests, and this partly explained the trouble with butter. I opened the balcony door and put a bag of frozen peas on the slab to cool it, which felt like cheating but worked.

The first batch went in the oven at two in the afternoon after shaping and a long proof. I cut triangles, rolled them up from the wide edge, and set them on trays lined with parchment, where they proved for about ninety minutes until they were puffy and wobbled when nudged. Before baking I brushed each with beaten egg, and the smell of the oven filling up with butter and yeast was outstanding. They came out a deep golden colour, with a decent rise, but the interior was doughy and dense, without the honeycomb structure I had hoped for. Mira ate two anyway and said they were lovely, which is exactly what a supportive partner would say.

The second batch, baked on Sunday morning, was better. The layers separated in thin, crisp sheets, and when I cut one in half the crumb was an open network of air pockets. It shattered when I bit into it, sending flakes all over my jumper. Even so, I could see scope for improvement; the ends were slightly under-proofed and the shaping was uneven. I kept notes on each tray and wrote down the oven temperature, which I dropped from two hundred and ten to one hundred and ninety midway through.

The third batch was baked on Sunday evening for a small audience: Mira, her brother Elias, and our neighbour Dagny. I served them warm with apricot jam, and there was a moment of silence at the first bite, which I have decided to treat as a compliment. Elias, who is a pastry sceptic, admitted that it was better than the one from the bakery on his corner, and Dagny asked for the recipe. I promised to write it up once I had tested it again. We finished the plate and then, embarrassingly, the leftover first batch as well, since the dense ones were fine dunked in tea. For the record, the third dough needed nineteen turns of the rolling pin in total, since I switched to a longer sequence of shorter rolls to keep the butter even. It was the best croissant of the weekend.

Lessons for the next attempt. Keep everything cold, including my hands, which I tried to cool under running water between turns. Do fewer and shorter rolls rather than heavy ones. Weigh the dough blocks precisely, and note the ambient temperature at each step. Shape a bit tighter, and proof in a slightly cooler place so the butter does not soften. I want to try a version with a little rye flour for flavour. I also need a better ruler, because the plastic one I used has a warp that I discovered only at the end of the second day. The marble slab was worth every krona, and I have already offered it to Dagny for her next pastry experiment.

Launch party planning, working notes from the three sessions. Blake and I were asked to organise a small celebration for the release of the new mobile app, mostly for the team, partners who helped test it, and a handful of early customers. The brief from leadership was one line long: warm, not corporate, and cheaper than last year's dinner. We started with a session on Monday in the small meeting hall, with a whiteboard, a bag of clementines, and a shared spreadsheet that quickly grew tabs for venue, food, music, invitations, and something Blake called contingencies, which was mostly rain.

Venue was the first decision. We looked at four places: a converted boat moored by the old shipyard, the upstairs hall of a neighbourhood brewery, a gallery with a courtyard, and our own office atrium. The boat was charming but the capacity was a hard cap of sixty, and the gangway worried the insurance person. The brewery gave us a friendly quote but no way to control the volume of the downstairs crowd. The atrium was free, which mattered, but Tove pointed out that nobody wants to celebrate in the place where they spent the week. We settled on the gallery, whose manager, a soft-spoken man called Ibrahim, offered the courtyard with a pop-up awning and heaters on a Thursday evening, for a flat fee.

Food came next. I had strong feelings about avoiding the usual tray of sandwiches. After tasting sessions at two caterers, we chose a small local outfit that makes a menu of shareable plates: roasted roots with herbs, marinated funguss, flat loaves with spiced lamb, and a big salad with pomegranate. For vegans there would be a chickpea stew and a coconut rice. The caterer, a cheerful woman named Solveig, brought samples in reusable tins and stood over us while we ate, which was slightly intimidating, but her sauces won us over. She recommended three plates per person to start, plus a dessert of small lemon tarts. Blake insisted on pickles, and we agreed.

Drinks were simpler. We negotiated a fixed price for two glasses of wine or beer per guest, with unlimited soft drinks and a non-alcoholic cocktail that Ibrahim's bartender designed with ginger, lime, and cucumber. There was a short debate about whether to serve anything stronger, which ended when Ana from finance reminded us of the budget and the events policy. We agreed to put a signature drink on a small chalkboard and provide sparkling water in glass bottles. I worked out the quantities on a scrap of paper: roughly one bottle of wine per three people, two crates of beer, and a large tub of ice that Solveig promised to deliver.

Music was where we spent far too long. Blake wanted a live band, I wanted a playlist, and Tove suggested a middle way with one local duo playing for forty-five minutes at the start and a curated selection afterwards. The duo, two sisters who play guitar and cello, quoted a reasonable rate and sent a video of their set that made everyone in the hall go quiet. We asked them to include a couple of familiar covers, to make it easier to talk over them. I built the playlist from suggestions the team dropped into a shared list; the strongest contender for last song was a slow tune everyone agreed on but nobody could name.

The invitation list was the most sensitive part. We started with the internal team, sixty-two people, and added partners, testers, and family members of the core team, which pushed the number up quickly. Each name needed a short line and an RSVP by the following Wednesday. I drafted the invitation in plain language, with a small illustration of the app icon drawn by Joel, and sent it via the events tool. Replies came in slowly and then all at once; by the deadline the count had climbed past what we planned for and forced a recalculation of the food order and the number of heaters.

On the Thursday itself, the setup started at three. Ibrahim's staff put out long trestles and strung lights across the courtyard, and Solveig's team arrived with insulated boxes at four thirty. The duo did a soundcheck and Blake tested the microphones for the short speech by the head of product. The wind picked up around five, and the awning started to flap, so we asked Ibrahim for extra weights. By six the first guests arrived, and the courtyard filled with the low hum of people finding friends.

The evening went well. The speeches were short, the duo was warmly applauded, and the lemon tarts disappeared within twenty minutes. A tester from one of our partner companies said it was the first launch party she had attended where she could actually hear the person next to her. Blake worked the hall with a tray of the ginger cocktails and reported that the bartender had run out of limes by eight, which was fixed by a runner sent to the corner shop. The heaters were adequate, though people near the far wall wore their coats.

Post-event notes. By the reply deadline one hundred and forty guests were confirmed, against the hundred we first budgeted for. Actual cost came in about eight percent under budget, mainly because fewer people drank the second glass than we assumed. The caterer left a small amount of food, which we boxed for the cleaning staff and for the shelter around the corner. Feedback so far is positive; two people asked for more seating and one asked for a quieter corner. For a future event we should rent extra benches and keep the number of guests closer to a hundred. Ibrahim has offered a discount if we book the courtyard again in the spring, and I have added it to the shared calendar as a maybe.

To do list. Send thank-you messages to the duo and to Solveig. Post the photos in the team channel, checking first for anyone who prefers not to appear. Close the budget sheet and file receipts with Ana by Friday. Ask Joel whether the illustration can be used for the next release notes. And thank Blake for the pickles.

Winter offsite in the mountain hut, trip report. We spent three nights in a hut above the tree line in early February with the whole product team, twelve people in total. I organised the logistics with Avery, who booked the trains, and the idea was to combine planning with a stretch of time away from screens. There is no mobile signal above the second lift station, and that was precisely the point. The hut belongs to a mountaineering association and sleeps twenty-four in bunks, with a wood stove, a generator that runs for four hours each evening, and a warden called Petra who has kept it for eleven winters.

Travel took most of the first day. We met at the central station at seven, boarded a regional train to the valley, and then a small yellow bus that wound up a road full of hairpin bends. Ana turned slightly green on the second bend and was rescued by a peppermint. From the last village we skied up on rented touring equipment for about two and a half hours, dragging sledges with food and gear behind us. The sun was low and golden by the time the hut came into view, sitting on a shelf of rock with smoke curling out of its chimney. It felt like arriving in an illustration for a children's story.

Petra met us at the door with a pot of hot tea and a stern lecture about boots. Wet boots stay in the drying closet at the entrance, slippers are provided, and nobody touches the stove without permission. We were shown the sleeping loft, the dining hall with its long wooden benches, and the small storage nook with a rack of board games and a shelf of worn paperbacks left by previous guests. The bunks were cold until the stove warmed up, and we slept with our jackets on the first night. Joel unpacked a bottle of plum brandy that he had promised to bring, and Petra confiscated it politely until after supper.

Planning sessions ran in the mornings, on the theory that people are sharpest before lunch. We had three questions to answer: what to build in the next two quarters, how to split the team into smaller groups, and how to reduce the load of urgent requests. We wrote everything on large sheets of brown paper taped to the wall and stood in a circle around them. The absence of laptops changed the tone; people listened more and interrupted less, and the sheets filled with sketches and arrows rather than bullet points. By lunch on the second day we had a draft plan and a list of disagreements, which felt about right.

Afternoons were for the mountain. On the first full day, Petra led us on a short tour to a nearby ridge, warning us about wind slabs and pointing out tracks left by hares and foxes. We practised using avalanche beacons in a snowy field, hiding one in a rucksack and searching for it with the receiver. Tove found hers in under a minute and looked unbearably pleased. I was slower and got a lecture about grid patterns. Later we built a large snow bench outside and sat on it with mugs of tea, watching clouds drift below us like slow smoke. It was the quietest I have felt in years.

Evenings had a rhythm too. The generator started at six, and we cooked on a large stove in the hut's galley, taking turns: a lentil soup on the first night, pasta with a rich tomato sauce on the second, and a pot of dumplings on the third, made by Ana from a recipe from her grandmother. We ate at the long benches, played cards, and told stories. There was one evening game where each person had to describe a project that failed and what they learned from it, and the stories were funnier and more honest than any retrospective I have run.

The second night was cold, minus eighteen outside, and the wind found every gap in the boards. We piled on blankets and someone kept feeding the stove until morning. I woke to the sound of Petra sweeping ash and the smell of porridge, and went outside to see the peaks turning pink. The sky was completely clear, and stars were still visible over the western ridge. We ate breakfast standing on the porch, wrapped in blankets like a small refugee camp of the well-fed. Someone remarked that in all their years in the office they had never seen the sun rise on a workday.

The final morning was spent finishing the plan. We agreed on two priorities for the next quarter and a new way to handle urgent requests: a rotating owner each week, with a written rule that nothing interrupts a focus block unless it involves customer data or safety. We wrote the decisions on a single sheet, and everyone signed it, half as a joke and half not. Then we packed, cleaned the hut, swept the loft, and paid our bill to Petra in cash. The ski down took only forty minutes, and we were back in the village by noon, eating soup in a low-ceilinged inn while our legs slowly remembered the ground.

Practical notes for next time. The bunk allocation put eleven people in the loft and one, by choice, on the dining hall bench, since Joel snores. Book earlier, since the hut fills up by November. Bring more spare batteries for the headlamps and two extra pairs of dry socks each. Pack the food in smaller crates, which are easier to strap onto sledges. The total cost was about three hundred and ten euros per person, including transport, lodging, and food, which we felt was fair. Petra said she would happily host us again and even offered to keep the sheets from the wall, which I have asked her to send by post. Feedback from the group was overwhelmingly positive.

Birdwatching morning at the wetland reserve, field notes. I got up at five, which is an hour I usually only see from the other side, and drove out to the reserve on the plain south of Uppsala with a flask of tea, a borrowed pair of binoculars, and a thin notebook I bought for exactly this. Mira had declined the invitation, and made me promise to text her a photo of any owl, saying that anything requiring silence before eight was a personal insult. The car park was empty except for a rusty estate car belonging to Gunnel, a retired teacher who leads the Sunday walks and who had offered to show me the good spots before the group turned up.

We started at the tower hide, a wooden structure on stilts with a ladder and a small sign warning about wasps. From the top you look across a wide shallow lake fringed with reed beds, and in the early light the surface was smoking with mist. Gunnel set up her telescope, a battered old thing held together with tape and obvious affection, and told me to lower my voice, put my elbows on the rail, and simply look for a minute without naming anything. That turned out to be excellent advice; I had spent years walking past exactly this kind of place with my head down, listening to podcasts, and had never once heard how loud a reed bed is at dawn. Shapes resolved slowly, the way a photograph does in a developing tray: heaps of grey that were geese, dark specks that were coots, a pale bar on the far shore that was a resting flock.

The first thing she taught me was how to count. You do not count birds one by one; you count a block of ten, then estimate how many blocks fill the flock. She swept the scope across the far shore, tapped the numbers into a small tally counter, and gave me a count of ninety-three whooper swans, with a note that several were young ones in dull grey plumage still travelling with their parents. She said the flock had grown by about a dozen since last week as migrants arrived from the north. I wrote the number down and underlined it, feeling like an official of some very quiet ministry.

The second half hour was the good bit. A marsh harrier drifted low over the reeds, tilting its wings in a shallow V, and every small bird in the vicinity went silent. Then it was gone and the chatter came back, first cautiously and then all at once. Gunnel pointed out a bittern's boom in the distance, a sound like someone blowing across a very large bottle, which I would not have noticed had she not said. A pair of cranes walked out of the mist along the shore, stately and slightly ridiculous, and stood there like two tall people who had lost their party. I forgot to breathe for a while.

We moved to the meadow trail, where the ground was soaked and the grass heavy with dew. My trainers were wet within minutes. Gunnel wore rubber boots and gave me a pair of plastic bags to pull over my socks, which was ridiculous and effective. Along the path she showed me how to identify small brown birds by shape rather than colour: the fat tail of a wren, the upright posture of a redstart, the constant flick of a wagtail. I kept a list of all the species I could confirm, which reached twenty-six by the time we reached the wooden bridge, including three I did not know existed.

At nine, the Sunday group began to arrive, about fifteen people of all ages with matching enthusiasm and mismatched hats. A boy of maybe eight showed me his life list, written in careful pencil in a school exercise book, and it was longer than mine by a factor of ten. I was slightly humbled. The group leader gave a short talk about etiquette: keep noise low, never use playback of calls, stay on the path, and share your sightings openly, because a rare bird spotted by one person belongs to everyone. Someone passed round a plate of cardamom biscuits, and I ate three before I realised they were meant to be shared among fifteen.

We took a break at the reserve's visitor hut, where a volunteer sold hot chocolate and small bags of sunflower seeds for the feeders outside. The feeders were busy with tits, finches and a single, tremendously bossy nuthatch. I sat on a bench with my notebook and tried to sketch a chaffinch, and produced something that looked more like a potato with a beak. Gunnel looked over my shoulder and said that the first hundred drawings are always bad and I should just keep the potatoes coming. She invited me to join the monthly walks and said the club has a loan library of field guides.

On the way back to the car park we walked through a birch wood, where woodpeckers were drumming somewhere out of sight. I learned to distinguish the sound of a great spotted from that of a black woodpecker by the length of the roll. It was nearly noon and the sun had burned off the mist, leaving the whole plain glittering. I took a last look across the lake with my binoculars and noticed that the swans had all lifted their heads at the same time, as if hearing a bell. Then, one by one, they folded them back under their wings and returned to sleeping.

Final tally for the morning: thirty-eight species, which Gunnel called a decent day for the season, including my first bittern by ear and my first harrier by sight. I have decided to buy a proper field guide, a small waterproof one, and to join the group on the third Sunday of next month. Mira asked me at lunch what I had seen and I read her the list in order, which took a while. She listened politely and then asked whether the swans were considering coming to the city for the winter.

First aid course, Saturday and Sunday, notes for the certificate renewal. My workplace certificate had expired in the spring, and after seeing a man collapse at the bus stop last month and realising that I stood there like a statue, I decided to book a full two-day course instead of the shorter refresher. It was run by a local ambulance charity in a rented loft above a sports hall, with eleven participants, a dozen plastic mannequins, and a very tall instructor named Bertil, who introduced himself as a paramedic with thirty years on the road and a low tolerance for mumbling.

Bertil began by asking us what we were afraid of, and the answers were revealing: blood, doing harm, not remembering the steps, being sued. He said that the greatest danger in an emergency is standing still, and that the law protects people who try in good faith. The course would be built around a simple sequence: check for danger, check for response, shout for help, open the airway, check breathing, call emergency services, and start compressions if there is no normal breathing. He made us chant it three times, like schoolchildren, and then made us do it on the mannequins, so that the words became movements.

The first session was about the recovery position and choking. I had done this in the past but had forgotten small details, such as rolling the person towards you so that their head is supported by the upper hand. For choking we practised back blows, five sharp ones between the shoulder blades with the heel of the hand, followed by abdominal thrusts if needed. Bertil demonstrated on a volunteer, who was a very good sport, and I noticed that nobody in the hall could quite manage the sharpness he asked for. A woman called Sanna cracked a joke about apologising to the victim, and Bertil said that sorry is a perfectly good word if you say it after the sausage has come out.

Saturday afternoon was the long block on cardiac arrest. We knelt beside our mannequins and learned the rhythm of compressions: the centre of the chest, arms straight, about five to six centimetres deep, at roughly a hundred to a hundred and twenty a minute. Bertil played a playlist of songs at the right tempo, which included a disco classic, and we rehearsed with sweat on our foreheads. My arms ached after two minutes. He explained that two people should swap every two minutes, and that compressions alone are a fine choice for anyone who is untrained or unwilling to give breaths. We also used a trainer defibrillator, a small box that speaks in a soothing voice and tells you exactly where to put the pads.

There was a written test on Sunday morning, thirty multiple choice questions, along with a practical assessment. The pass mark was eighty percent, and Bertil had warned us that people usually lose points on the questions about burns, because everyone has a home remedy involving butter. I sat in the back next to Sanna and we shared a pencil. The practical assessment involved a scenario in which a worker collapses in a warehouse, and each of us had to lead the response while the others played bystanders. Mine went reasonably well until I forgot to say the address aloud, and Bertil pretended to be the emergency dispatcher and asked, deadpan, where I thought the ambulance should go.

The rest of Sunday covered wounds, bleeding, burns, fractures, and shock. We learned to press firmly with a clean cloth on a bleeding wound and not lift it to check, to cool burns under running water for twenty minutes, and to immobilise a suspected broken limb without straightening it. We practised bandaging each other, wrapping wrists in figure-eights and slings from triangular cloths, and I discovered that my partner had ticklish elbows. A section on strokes introduced the mnemonic of the face, arms, speech and time, and Bertil showed a short video of an actual patient before and after treatment that made the whole hall go very quiet.

Lunch on Sunday was in the sports hall's cafeteria, where a group of children in football kits shouted about pizza. Bertil sat with us and told stories, carefully leaving out names. One was about a woman who performed compressions on a stranger at a train station for eleven minutes with nobody helping and who was, months later, thanked by the man's daughter over a cake. Another was about a mistaken call that turned out to be a stubborn hiccup. He said the hardest thing about the job is not the blood but the silence afterwards, and that the certificate is really about learning to be brave in small steps.

Results were announced at the end. All of us passed; I scored twenty-seven out of thirty, missing two questions on burns, exactly as predicted, and one about the correct dose for a child's compressions. The certificate is valid for three years, and the charity offers a free half-day refresher every twelve months, which I have booked in my calendar. The cost of the course was nine hundred crowns, covered partly by my employer. I walked home with my certificate in a plastic sleeve and a stiff neck. On Monday, I ordered a proper first aid kit for the flat and a small pouch for my rucksack, because Bertil would be disappointed if I did not.

Planning Mum's seventieth birthday, working notes. Her birthday falls on a Sunday in late June, and my sister Elin and I have been plotting a surprise for two months, which is longer than either of us has ever kept a secret. The rules we agreed: no lies that could be traced, no group messages that Mum might see on her phone, and no involving Dad's cousin Roland, who cannot keep a secret for longer than a lunch. We decided to hold the party at the lake cottage that belongs to Uncle Sten, a red wooden house with a jetty and a smoke sauna, where Mum spent most summers as a child.

The guest list went through several drafts. Elin started with sixty names and I cut it to forty-five, based on a strict rule of who Mum would actually like to see rather than who would feel offended. We ended with forty-two, including her three sisters, her old friends from the choir, two neighbours from the building where she raised us, and a former colleague from the school who has moved abroad and promised to fly in. Dad kept adding people by phone, and each time we quietly wrote them in and worried about the capacity of the cottage. The invitations, sent by post to preserve the secret, included a small map drawn by my nephew.

Food was the second big question. Mum does not like fuss, but she loves a proper spread, and Elin wanted to honour the dishes of her childhood: cured salmon with dill and mustard sauce, boiled new potatoes, pickled herring in three flavours, a dark rye loaf, and a strawberry cake with whipped cream. We asked Aunt Britta to help cook, which meant we would be told what to do, and she immediately began a list on the back of an envelope, crossing out and rewriting quantities as though the guests were a small army. She also vetoed the cream sauce I proposed and said that a seventieth needs butter, not fashion. The cake had to be ordered by the ninth, since the baker in the village is booked solid for weeks around midsummer and Britta had sworn that no other bakery would do. I called and left a message that got a short curt reply and a confirmation with a price of eight hundred kronor.

Transport was the tricky part of the plot. Mum believed she was going for a quiet lunch with Dad and me at a restaurant in town, and Dad was supposed to steer the car by the lake road under the pretext of showing her the new bridge. The problem is that she gets carsick and insists on driving herself. After a long call, we agreed that Dad would say the car was in the garage and that she should let me pick them up. Elin worried that Mum would notice my bag full of balloons, so I stashed everything at Uncle Sten's the day before, together with a heavy speaker, bunting, a large banner, and a box of candles sized for a very long cake.

The programme took a whole evening to draft. Guests would arrive between noon and one and wait on the porch, hushed, while Elin kept watch on the road. When the car pulled in, everybody would come out with a song, which we had rehearsed by video, though most of us are hopelessly out of tune. There would be a welcome speech from Dad, then lunch, then a slideshow of photographs from her life, which I had spent evenings compiling from albums in Dad's attic. The slideshow was the hardest part; I found pictures of Mum at eighteen wearing a hat that should be illegal, and a shot of her with a giant fish, grinning.

Gifts were another topic. Instead of buying yet another scarf, we proposed a joint present: a small watercolour of the cottage painted by Elin's neighbour, an artist, from an old photo, plus a voucher for a spa weekend that Mum will pretend she did not want. Everyone contributed what they wanted, and I collected the money in a shared account. There was a small argument about whether to include an album with handwritten notes from each guest, resolved by Britta, who said that if there is a choice between more paper and less paper, choose more. So I ordered a plain linen-bound book and a stack of cards.

There were, inevitably, moments of near disaster. Roland got wind of the plan and rang Mum to ask whether she was looking forward to the weekend, which produced an interrogation at the breakfast bench that Dad had to defuse with a story about a fishing trip. Elin's daughter almost posted a photo of the bunting on her account, and I had to talk her out of it with a bribe of ice cream. The weather forecast changed every day, from sun to thunderstorms and back, and Sten offered to put up a big tent by the jetty as insurance. We accepted, and he claims to have an old army tent big enough for sixty.

Checklist for the final week. Confirm the cake pickup with the baker and rent a cool box for the fish. Collect the borrowed chairs from the community hall and test the speaker. Print the songbooks so nobody has to guess the second verse. Ask Sten to check the sauna heater and cut the grass around the jetty. Pack a small first aid kit and a spare set of car keys. And finally, write a short speech of my own, which I have been avoiding since April. Elin says I should just tell the story about Mum and the fish, and I think she may be right.

Charity relay entry, planning log. When the Harbour Run announced its twenty-fifth edition with a corporate relay category, Blake spotted the post in the team channel and asked who would be up for entering a team of five to raise money for the children's hospital fund. Within an hour eleven people had replied, three of whom had never run further than a bus stop. I offered to coordinate and to find a fair way of choosing. After a short poll we decided that the first five to sign up would run, with the rest forming a support crew, and that everybody would take part in the fundraising.

The relay format works like this: five legs of about eight kilometres each around the harbour and the old town, with a baton exchange at marked zones. Each runner has to finish within a time limit, and the team's overall time is the sum. A team can also enter an unofficial category for costumes, which was Tove's suggestion and immediately became the most popular idea. Registration opened on a Tuesday at noon and, as expected, filled quickly, so I set an alarm and completed the form within the first five minutes. The fee, race shirts and a small team banner were all covered by the company.

Deciding who runs which leg took a full meeting. Leg one is flat and fast and suits someone who likes a strong start; leg two has a steady incline through the old town; leg three runs along the water and is exposed to wind; leg four includes the cobbled streets, which are punishing; and leg five is the anchor, with a cheering crowd at the finish. Ana volunteered for the first leg, since she runs marathons and does not mind being ahead of the pack. Joel took the cobbles, saying that he was used to pain from his desk chair. I chose the second leg, and Blake, who had not run since university, gamely accepted the wind.

Training began three weeks out. We agreed on two group runs per week at lunchtime, starting with a shared warm-up and a ten-minute jog for the beginners, and building up to longer distances. Ana wrote a simple plan and posted it on the wall by the coat hooks. Some days we ran through the park behind the office, other days along the canal. On the third session Blake pulled a calf muscle and had to swap legs with Tove, who took the wind and said she would treat it as a facial. We debated the wisdom of running so soon after lunch and moved the sessions to the late afternoon.

The fundraising page took a weekend to set up. We wrote a short description of the fund, uploaded a team photo of us in mismatched shorts, and set a target of three thousand euros. Joel drew a logo of a running sneaker with wings. The finance team offered to match donations from employees up to a limit, which spread the word better than any email. We also held a bake sale in the lobby, where Ana's cardamom buns sold out in twenty minutes and a plate of very dry brownies was left to the end. By the week before the race the page showed two thousand two hundred euros, and the target felt within reach.

Race weekend logistics were more complicated than expected. Packets had to be collected at the sports hall on Friday between four and eight, showing photo identification, and each runner received a bib, a chip for the ankle, and a coupon for a free sports drink. The support crew met on Saturday morning to divide roles: two drivers to shuttle runners between the exchange zones, two people with bicycles carrying spare water, and one photographer with a very long lens. The entry fee was thirty-eight euros per runner, and the fee also covered the shirts. Tove printed a laminated map with the timings for each leg, marking the exchange zones in bright pink, and we agreed to meet at the finish for a picnic.

On race day, the weather held. It was eleven degrees, grey but dry, with a light breeze off the water. Ana set off at nine sharp and returned in thirty-nine minutes, well ahead of her estimate, and passed the baton to me at the zone by the old fish market. I remember the first kilometre as a blur of elbows and the second as a slow realisation that I had started too fast. The incline through the old town was steeper than on the practice run, but a band was playing on a balcony and the crowd cheered every runner, including the slowest. I handed on to Tove in fifty-one minutes, and collapsed against a lamppost.

The rest of the relay went as such things do: Joel arrived at the cobbles grinning and left them limping, Tove gained a place on the wind, and Blake finished the anchor leg to a roar from the crowd, wearing a cape made from a bin bag. Our overall time was three hours and forty-four minutes, ranked in the middle of the corporate field, and we won the costume prize for the winged sneakers. We ate our picnic on the grass afterwards with medals around our necks. The fundraising total reached three thousand four hundred euros after the match, and the hospital fund sent a warm thank-you message with a photo of the ward's new play corner.

Ramen from scratch, a long weekend project. It began with a documentary about a small noodle shop in Fukuoka where the owner stirs the same pot every day for fifty years, and by the end I was determined to make a bowl of tonkotsu that would not embarrass me. Mira reminded me that I had also made this promise about sourdough and hollandaise. Undeterred, I spent Thursday evening writing a shopping list: two kilos of pork trotters, a kilo of pork neck bones, chicken carcasses, kombu, dried shiitake, ginger, leeks, and a small mountain of garlic. The butcher in the market hall asked whether I was opening a restaurant, and I said I was opening a hobby.

The broth is the heart of the thing, and it is unforgiving. On Friday evening, I blanched the bones in a huge pot to remove impurities, boiling them hard for ten minutes and then rinsing each one under the tap, scraping away dark scum with a spoon. This is not glamorous work. The trotters had to be split with a cleaver, which I borrowed from Dagny with a stern instruction to bring it back with all its fingers. I put the cleaned bones back into the pot with cold water, brought them to a rolling boil, and left them there with the lid ajar, which is the key to emulsifying the fat and collagen into a milky broth.

Ideally you keep the boil going for a very long time and top up with hot water as it reduces. I started at eight on Friday night and set an alarm every two hours to check on it, which meant that I slept badly and dreamed in pork. By three in the morning the whole flat smelled like a warm, savoury cloud, and Mira came into the galley in her socks to ask if there was a fire. At seven, the broth had turned a pale cream colour. I skimmed it, added aromatics, and let it continue. When I finally decided it was done, there was a sticky layer of collagen on the spoon and a rich, slightly sweet aroma.

Meanwhile, I prepared the other components. The chashu, braised pork belly, was rolled tight with string and simmered in a mixture of soy sauce, mirin, sake, sugar, and ginger for two hours, then left to cool in its liquid overnight. I made the tare, the seasoned base that goes into each bowl, from soy sauce, salt, and a splash of the chashu liquid. Eggs were boiled for exactly six and a half minutes, peeled under cold water, and marinated in a mix of soy and mirin. The peeling took longer than the boiling, and I lost three eggs to the sink. For toppings I sliced spring onions, toasted sesame seeds, and prepared a small dish of chilli oil.

The noodles were a step too far, or so I thought. I had read that alkaline noodles need baking soda baked in the oven to raise its pH, and that the dough is stiff and dry. I did it anyway. The dough was crumbly, almost like wet sand, and I had to knead it with my whole body weight for ten minutes. After resting under a damp cloth for an hour, I rolled it through a pasta machine, folding and re-rolling until it was smooth and elastic. Then I cut the sheets into thin strands and dusted them with starch. The strands looked oddly professional, thin and curly, and I held one up to Mira as if I had built a cathedral.

By Saturday evening, everything was ready. I heated the broth until it steamed, warmed the bowls in the oven, and set out the toppings in little dishes. We invited Dagny and her husband over as a reward for the cleaver. I cooked the noodles for ninety seconds, drained them, and assembled the bowls: tare at the bottom, broth poured over, noodles folded in, then chashu, egg, spring onions, and a swirl of chilli oil. The first sip was a shock; the broth was velvety and deep, with a savoury sweetness that clung to the lips. For the record, the broth simmered for exactly fourteen hours before it reached the bowls, and I would not shorten it. Nobody spoke for a couple of minutes, which I took as the highest form of praise.

Feedback from the panel of three. Dagny said the broth was better than most restaurants, but the noodles were slightly too firm and could do with less time. Her husband said everything was perfect and asked for seconds twice. Mira, ever honest, said the chashu was a little salty and the egg a little firm, and that she loved it anyway. I agreed with all of it. Salt is an easy fix; next time I will reduce the soy in the braise and cut the egg time by thirty seconds. The noodle thickness is a matter of taste, but I think I will roll them one notch thinner.

Cleanup took an hour. The pot was so greasy that I had to fill it with soapy water and leave it overnight, and the flat smelled of pork for two days. Mira suggested that the next time I do this I do it at Dagny's, which was gracious of her. I froze the remaining broth in six containers, each enough for a bowl, and put the leftover chashu in the fridge for sandwiches. I made a note in my cooking journal: ramen is not a dish, it is a weekend. And if anyone wants the cleaver, it is on the drying rack and has all its fingers.

Overnight bikepacking trip, Vadstena to Motala and back. The idea was to test my new frame bags before the longer tour planned for August, so I picked a route I could bail out of at any station: eighty kilometres one way along the eastern shore of Lake Vättern, sleeping wild somewhere in the middle. I packed the night before, laying everything out on the sitting-area floor like a crime scene: a two-person tent that I use alone, a down bag rated to five degrees, a stove the size of a fist, a titanium pot, a small tool roll, spare tube, two bottles, and food for one dinner and two breakfasts. Mira watched me weigh the bag on the bath scale and asked whether I planned to cross a desert.
