The train from home to Vadstena left at 8:41 on Saturday, with a special carriage for bicycles that was already half full of people in lycra and slightly nervous parents with children in trailers. I hung my bike from the hooks and stood next to it for two hours, reading the map on my phone and eating a cinnamon bun. The conductor, a young man with a moustache that seemed borrowed, warned me that the rack was built for lighter bikes. It held. At Vadstena I unloaded, checked the tyres, and rolled down to the castle, which stands in the water like a stone ship, for a first photo and to buy a second bun.

The first stretch followed a cycle path along the shore, flat and sheltered by tall trees, with the lake occasionally flashing through gaps. I settled into a slow rhythm, breathing through my nose and counting telegraph poles, about seventeen kilometres an hour, which is the speed at which a loaded bike feels steady and the mind starts wandering. I passed yellow rapeseed fields and a farm stall selling strawberries on the honour system. After about an hour I hit a gravel section, and the bags began to rattle; I stopped and re-tightened the straps, which stopped the noise but not the doubt that I had brought too much.

Lunch was on a small jetty near Borghamn, where a group of teenagers were jumping into the water and screaming. I boiled water for a pouch of instant noodles, added a stock cube and a handful of frozen peas I had hidden in a side pocket, and ate them sitting with my legs dangling. The water looked so clear and cold that I took my shoes off and waded in to my knees. It was, I estimate, about twelve degrees. My feet went numb in about ten seconds, and I stood there grinning like an idiot until the teenagers applauded. A woman walking a dog looked at my bike and said that I looked like a snail carrying its home, and I said that snails have better route planning.

The afternoon was harder. The path left the shore and climbed through forest on a road with no shoulder, and a headwind picked up, pushing against me on every open stretch. I ate a bar of dark chocolate and thought bad thoughts about my choice of gear ratio. Around four I passed a little church with a graveyard on a hill, and I stopped for water at a tap that had a sign saying it was not for drinking, but everybody seemed to drink from it. I sat for ten minutes under a lime tree and felt my legs come back.

I made a detour into Motala harbour, partly to see the canal locks and partly to check the price of the summer boat along the canal, since I am considering it for the August tour. The excursion boat cost 289 crowns for an adult with a bicycle, according to the noticeboard by the harbour office, which is a lot cheaper than I had feared.  A man in a peaked cap explained that booking early gets you a slot on the cycle deck. I left with a leaflet and a slightly guilty feeling of planning the next trip before finishing this one.

Camp was on a headland a few kilometres north of Motala, a piece of open ground with a fire ring and a view of the water. I put up the tent in twenty minutes, fighting the wind for the fly, and cooked pasta with a tin of tuna and a lot of olive oil. As the sun sank, the lake turned the colour of hammered pewter and a heron flew low across the bay, with slow, deliberate beats of its wings. I had planned to read, but I only stared. The temperature dropped fast, and by nine I was in my bag with my hat on, listening to the water lap on the stones and a distant motorbike.

The night was cooler than promised, and I woke twice with cold feet. Around four, a chorus of birds started so loudly that I gave up on sleeping and lay listening, identifying nothing. At six I crawled out to find the whole headland wrapped in mist, with dew beaded on the tent like small glass beads. Breakfast was porridge with raisins and a splash of the last of my milk. I packed in an efficient forty minutes, which for me is a record, and was on the road by half past seven. My knees complained for the first three kilometres and then stopped, as they do.

The ride back followed the same path, and it seemed shorter, as it always does. A Sunday morning cyclist on a race bike overtook me and shouted good morning, then slowed down to chat about my bags, and we rode together for a while talking about tyres and pressure. He told me about a bikepacking route through the Norwegian mountains that had me taking notes at speed. At Vadstena the train left in twenty minutes, and I spent them buying a bottle of cold milk and a packet of biscuits, which I ate on the platform like a starving man. Home by three, tired, sunburned on my forearms only, and strangely happy.

Lessons learned. Pack less: I carried a spare jersey I never wore and a book I never opened. Move the heavy stove to a lower position on the frame to improve handling. Get a better sleeping mat, since mine is thinner than the brochure implied. The trip proved that the whole system works, which is what I wanted to know before the long tour. I also found out that I like being alone with the lake more than I expected, and that a strawberry bought from a tin on the honour system tastes better than any supermarket one.

Midsummer at the lake, the whole day. Every year the village association organises midsummer on the meadow behind the old dairy, and this year I promised to volunteer for the morning and then join the party. I arrived at nine with Mira, who had agreed to help provided she was not asked to climb anything. The meadow was already alive with activity: a tractor dragging the last of the chairs, two men wrestling a large pole onto a trailer, and a group of women in aprons carrying trays of pickled herring in the direction of the tents. The air smelled of cut grass and diesel, which is the smell of summer here.

My assignment was flowers. Every midsummer pole needs a covering of leaves and blossoms, and the association had asked for volunteers to collect greenery from the woods at the edge of the meadow. Mira and I set out with two buckets and a pair of secateurs, following a woman called Astrid who has decorated the pole for thirty-one years. She showed us which birch branches to cut, how to pick wild flowers without pulling out the roots, and why you should never take more than one bloom in ten. We found buttercups, cow parsley, and a few late lilacs, and Astrid wove them into long garlands on the grass, her fingers moving faster than I could follow.

By eleven we had a dozen garlands, and there were forty children queuing to help wind them round the pole. This is the most chaotic part of the day; every child wants to hold something, and every parent wants a picture. Astrid ran the operation like a small general, handing out wreaths and giving instructions in a voice that carried across the meadow. The pole was raised at noon by six men and a great deal of shouting, and a cheer went up when it stood upright without swaying. Someone struck up an accordion and the first dancers began circling the pole, awkward and delighted.

Lunch was a long communal meal on trestles under the tents. The menu is fixed by tradition and defended fiercely: new potatoes with dill, three kinds of herring, sour cream and chives, boiled eggs, a cold salmon, and rye crackers. Mira and I sat between a retired fisherman and a teenage boy who was pretending not to be there. There were small glasses of schnapps and a few songs in between, the sort that everyone knows and no one can explain. The fisherman taught me the song about the little frogs, with its dance, and I made a fool of myself with dignity. A pot of strawberries with cream was brought out for dessert, and the whole tent went briefly silent.

The afternoon belonged to the games. There was a sack race, a three-legged race, a tug of war between the north and south ends of the village, and a competition to throw a rubber boot as far as possible. I was press-ganged into the tug of war on the south team, which lost in three seconds, since the north team had brought two rugby players. Mira won the boot throw with a spectacular hurl that nearly hit the accordionist, and received a small ribbon and a bag of sweets. Afterwards I sat on a hay bale watching a toddler in a flower crown negotiating with a goat.

Around four, a storm rolled in from the west. The sky turned the colour of a bruise and a cold wind whipped the tent flaps. Everyone rushed to secure things, and for twenty minutes it hammered down so hard that the accordion had to fall silent. We crowded under the largest tent, packed like sardines with wet children and steaming coats, and someone started a song to keep spirits up. When the rain stopped, the meadow smelled of earth and green, and a rainbow stretched over the lake. The pole was dripping but intact, and the small flowers had somehow survived. Astrid declared it an omen.

The evening programme moved to the shore, where the association had built a bonfire on the sand. I was assigned to fire duty, which meant standing with a bucket of water and looking responsible. The bonfire was lit at eleven, after a short speech from the chair of the association about how the village has held this celebration for two hundred years, and how it will need young hands to continue. Flames leapt up against the pale night sky. It never quite gets dark at this latitude in June; the horizon just glows, as if the sun is thinking about coming back. People sang, and someone passed round cups of warm spiced juice.

By midnight the party had thinned to a few dozen. Mira and I sat on a log with the fisherman and Astrid, sharing a thermos, watching the last embers. Astrid told us that in her youth girls would pick seven kinds of flowers and put them under their pillows to dream of their future husbands. Mira asked whether it worked, and Astrid said that it worked well enough for her to marry the man who cut the birches. We cleaned up until one, stacking chairs in the dim light, and I fell asleep in the car within five minutes. The next morning I found petals in my pockets.

Notes to self. Sign up again next year, and offer to help with the garlands from the start. Bring a proper raincoat, since the umbrella was useless in that wind. Send Astrid the photo of the pole with the rainbow, which is possibly the best picture I have ever taken. Pay the association's small volunteer fee of one hundred crowns by the end of the month, which includes the meal. And learn the second verse of the frog song, since the fisherman says that I pronounce the ending wrong.

Lunch-and-learn series on data visualisation, course notes and decisions. After the third dashboard review where the same chart type was argued about for forty minutes, Avery proposed a short internal course on how to draw charts that people can read. Blake volunteered to organise it, and we found a speaker in Nora, an analyst from the research group who teaches a similar module at the university. The format was six lunchtime sessions of fifty minutes, with a short reading beforehand and a small exercise at the end. Attendance was voluntary, and forty-three people signed up in the first week, well over the hall's capacity, so we moved to the big meeting hall with the folding walls.

The first session was on principles. Nora opened with a slide of a pie chart with fourteen slices and asked the audience to guess what the largest slice was; nobody could. She then showed the same data as a sorted bar chart, and the audience made a kind of collective exhale. Her main rule was to choose the encoding that lets the eye compare the thing that matters: position along a common scale beats length, which beats angle, which beats area, which beats colour. She insisted that nobody should be allowed to use three dimensions for two-dimensional data, and there was scattered applause. The exercise was to take one of our own charts and redraw it on paper.

Session two was about colour. Nora explained why a rainbow palette is misleading, since the eye sees bright bands where the data has none, and showed a demonstration of how a colour-blind viewer sees the standard red-green pair. About one man in twelve is affected, she said, and looked around the hall to see who had nodded. We then went through sequential, diverging, and categorical palettes and picked sensible defaults for our own reports. Joel, who designs our dashboards, pointed out that the brand orange fails contrast tests on white, and there followed a productive ten minutes on how to fix it without upsetting marketing.

Session three was a workshop on labelling and annotation. Nora argued that a chart without a message is decoration, and that a title should state the finding rather than describe the axes. We rewrote fifteen titles from real internal decks; the best transformation was from Revenue by region to Two regions carry seventy percent of growth. She encouraged direct labels on lines instead of legends, and gentle grey for everything that is not the point. In the last ten minutes, we split into pairs and swapped charts, annotating each other's work with sticky notes. Ana said it was the most useful hour she had spent at work in months, which was gratifying to hear.

We paused for a week because of the release, and used the break to gather feedback. The survey showed that people liked the exercises most and the slides least, and the main complaint was that the hall was too cold. Some asked for recorded versions, and we agreed to record the remaining sessions, with the speaker's consent, and store them on the shared drive. A few people also asked for a session on grids of plain numbers, which Nora immediately agreed to add, saying that a well-set grid of figures is often better than any chart. She proposed to replace the planned section on maps, which most attendees had marked as least relevant.

Session four was the one on time series and uncertainty. Nora started with a chart of monthly sign-ups with a sharp spike in March and asked what could explain it; the audience offered a dozen hypotheses, all of them plausible. She then showed how a simple confidence band and a marker for the launch date would have made the answer obvious. We spent time on scale choices and why truncating an axis to make a change look dramatic is a poor habit, however tempting. There was an interesting side discussion about smoothing, and Tove asked whether it is ever fine to hide noise; Nora said only if you say so, in the chart.

Session five moved to dashboards. We looked at four internal specimens and rated them against a checklist: purpose, audience, hierarchy, interaction, and speed to first insight. The customer support dashboard won, unexpectedly, because it had only six numbers on it. The executive one had thirty-two. Nora suggested that a dashboard should answer at most three questions, and that everything else belongs in a report. Joel took notes furiously, since he owns the executive one. By the end, there was a shared decision to run a clean-up week in May in which every team removes at least one chart from its dashboard.

Session six was a final review. Each of six volunteers presented a before-and-after of a chart they had redesigned during the course, and the audience voted for the most improved. The winner was a retention curve by Ana, who replaced a spaghetti of twelve lines with a small-multiples grid, each panel with its own trend. The runner-up was a spreadsheet grid from finance turned into a slopegraph. Nora gave a short closing talk on how to keep the habit going, recommending a monthly chart clinic and a small style guide. She gave us a reading list of six books, three of which are now in the office library. The last session was fixed early: session six was booked for the ninth of April, after the release, so the recordings would show finished dashboards.

Follow-up decisions. We will publish a short style guide, drafted by Joel and Nora, containing the palette, fonts, and annotation rules. The recordings will stay on the shared drive for a year. Blake will run a monthly chart clinic for anyone who wants feedback. We estimated the total cost at four hundred euros for hall hire and catering, with Nora's time donated by the research group in exchange for a lunch. Overall, satisfaction scored four point six out of five, and at least two teams have already changed their dashboards.

Ping-pong league, the last month of the season. I joined the Wednesday league at the community centre in January after a colleague dragged me along to a social evening and beat me eleven-two in the first game. There are four divisions, played on six courts in a converted gym, and I began in the fourth, with people who describe their forehand as enthusiastic. Our team is called the Spinning Cardigans, a name chosen by Mira's cousin Elias after a vote that lasted less than a minute; the runner-up was the Bat Pack, which Hasse vetoed on the grounds that he is not a member of any pack, and the shirts, printed in a hurry by Elias's flatmate, are the colour of stewed rhubarb. We are five players, and the captain is Hasse, a retired plumber with hands so large that the bat looks like a teaspoon.

The format is simple: each match has three singles and one doubles, each played to eleven points, best of five games. The team that wins three of four takes the night. We started the season at the bottom, losing our first four matches by embarrassing scores, and I contributed by serving into the net at crucial moments. Hasse remained cheerful, saying that losing gracefully is a skill of its own and that we were becoming masters. After the fourth defeat, a member of the opposing team, a teenager with a headband, took pity and offered to show me a topspin grip. It turned out that I had been holding the bat like a frying pan. He also lent me a spare rubber for a fortnight, and I found that the ball obeyed me in a way it never had with the club's chewed-up loan bats, which are held together with tape and optimism.

The change came in February. Tuesdays became practice nights at Hasse's basement, where he has a full-size court, a ball machine, and a wall covered in yellowing trophies from the seventies. He is a strict coach. We did footwork drills, shuffling sideways for ten minutes, then serve practice, in which I had to hit a small coin on the far end of the court. He taught me to disguise a serve by keeping the same motion but varying the spin, and after three weeks I could occasionally fool someone who was not looking. Elias improved most, thanks to a private obsession with videos of professional players, which he watched on the bus at half speed, muttering about wrist angles. Hasse also insisted on a weekly stretching routine, on the grounds that a sore back has ended more careers than any opponent.

By March we had won six in a row, mostly because we were suddenly good at doubles. Hasse and I formed a partnership, him on the backhand and me darting around like a caffeinated mouse. Our signature move was a short serve followed by a flick that opponents never expected. There was one match against a team called the Net Cords where we were two games down and came back to win, with the last point decided by an edge ball that even the referee found funny. The crowd, which consisted of three spectators and a dog, went wild. The evening ended with sausages from the community centre's grill.

April was more serious. With the top four teams in each division playing a knockout, we needed to finish third to qualify, and it came down to the final regular match against the league leaders, a team of engineers who never seem to lose. I was assigned the third singles against a woman named Ulrika, who plays with a defensive style, sending back everything with a small, irritating chop. The first game lasted twenty-two points and I lost it, but I discovered that she had trouble with a fast serve to her backhand. I won the next two, then lost the fourth, and the fifth went to eleven-nine in my favour. The team went berserk.

The semi-final was played at a neutral venue, a school gym with a smell of rubber and old sneakers, on a Saturday afternoon. We faced the Smashing Pumpkins, who were dressed in orange shirts and took it very seriously. Hasse played first and won in four games; Elias lost in five, after leading two-one. I lost my match but Hasse and I won the doubles in a deciding game that had the entire hall gathered around our court. The final score was three-one, and we were in the final for the first time in the club's history. Someone had brought a small trophy, and Hasse held it and wept slightly.

The final was against the Nets of Fury, an established team with a reputation. The whole club turned up, along with families and neighbours, and a local reporter with a notebook. We started nervously; Hasse dropped the first singles, and I lost mine in straight games, so we were two-nil down. Elias then won his match in four, and Hasse and I took the doubles in a deciding game after saving a match point with a lucky net cord. It came down to the final singles, Elias against their captain, a tall man with a magnificent moustache. The league final ended eleven to nine in the last game, and the hall erupted.

Afterwards we sat on plastic chairs eating cake that Hasse's wife had baked in the shape of a ping-pong ball. The trophy went into the cabinet with a plaque to be engraved with our name. Hasse gave a short speech thanking everyone and saying that it had been the most fun he had had since retiring. Mira said she had never seen me so hoarse, and I explained that I had been shouting at a small plastic ball. I promoted myself to the third division for next season and signed up for a Sunday clinic. I also ordered a proper bat, since Hasse says that mine belongs in a museum.

Day trip to Uppsala with Mira's parents, itinerary and comments. Her parents, Ragnar and Ulla, came to visit for the weekend, and since they had not been to Uppsala in thirty years, we planned a day trip on Saturday. The train from Stockholm takes about forty minutes, and I bought four tickets in the app on Friday evening, which involved a mysterious discount for pensioners that Ragnar viewed with suspicion. We met at the central station at nine, and Ulla, who is a planner by nature, produced a folded sheet of paper with an hour-by-hour schedule that she had drafted on the bus, with two alternatives in case of rain.

First stop was the cathedral, the largest in Scandinavia, which looms above the river with two towers like a pair of needles. We spent about an hour inside, walking slowly from chapel to chapel and reading the plaques. Ragnar wanted to see the tomb of King Gustav Vasa and was slightly disappointed that it was crowded with schoolchildren who were more interested in the echo. Ulla found a stone bench under a stained-glass panel and sat down with her guide book, refusing to be hurried. I climbed a narrow staircase to the museum in the tower, where a display of medieval textiles showed embroidery so fine that Mira gasped. The museum ticket was ninety kronor for adults, and Ulla read every caption twice to get her money's worth.

We then crossed the river for a walk along the bank, where students were lounging on the grass with books and cans of soda in the thin sunshine. I pointed out the botanic park on the hill, with its large glass palm house, but Ragnar was hungry, so we found a place for lunch on a side street, a small Vietnamese restaurant with a queue out of the door. We waited twenty minutes and were rewarded with a corner by the wall and four bowls of noodle soup. Ragnar, who eats meatballs as a matter of principle, tasted the broth with theatrical caution and announced that it was excellent. Ulla asked for the recipe, and the waiter smiled and said it was a secret.

After lunch we visited the university's old library, which has the famous Silver Bible, a sixth-century manuscript written in silver ink on purple parchment. The exhibit was in dim light, behind glass, and the guide gave an excellent talk in English, then Swedish for our benefit. It was the kind of object that makes you feel very small. I asked how it survived and was told a long story involving theft, a war, and a fire. Ragnar, who has a moderate interest in history, took notes, and Ulla whispered to me that she had not seen him this animated since the football final in 1994. The gift shop sold replicas of the bookmarks.

The afternoon's plan was a walk to the castle on the hill, which took longer than we expected because Ulla stopped at every second house to admire the front doors. The route wound up through cobbled streets with yellow-painted houses and flower boxes exploding with geraniums. At the top, the castle terrace offers a wide view over the plain, with the cathedral looking small and the river like a strip of foil. We took turns taking photos, and a passing Italian tourist offered to take a group picture. In it, everyone is squinting, except Ragnar, who looks solemn, and Mira, who looks as though she is trying not to laugh.

At four we had cake in a cafe that Mira had read about. The cafe occupies a corner in a courtyard, with mismatched china, mismatched chairs, and a cat asleep on a radiator. Ulla ordered a slice of princess cake, green and domed like a small hill, and pronounced it too sweet before finishing every crumb. Ragnar had a cardamom bun and a glass of milk. I chose a chocolate cake so dense that it needed a second spoon. We talked about their trip to Uppsala in the seventies, when they came to see a concert and got locked out of a hostel, and about how a city can change without changing at all.

There was an unexpected turn when a street performer began a show near the cafe, juggling flaming torches while reciting poetry, an act that Ulla found more moving than she wanted to admit. She dropped a coin in his hat and lingered for the whole show. Meanwhile, Ragnar discovered a second-hand record shop across the courtyard and disappeared for forty minutes, emerging with three vinyl records and a delighted expression. Mira and I sat on a low wall beside a bicycle parked against a lamp post with a child's seat, eating the last of the biscuits and making plans for the following weekend. The light was changing to gold, and the air had the flat smell of late afternoon.

We walked slowly back to the station, arm in arm along the wide pavement in the thickening dusk, passing a river bank where a rowing team was launching a long boat, and took the 18:07 train home. On the train Ulla dozed with her head on Ragnar's shoulder and a paper bag of pastries on her lap. He whispered that he had not felt so relaxed in years, and Mira squeezed my hand. Back home, we made a simple supper of soup and boiled eggs, and the parents were in bed by nine, after promising to come again in the spring. Ulla texted a photograph of the house key she nearly left in the cafe; Mira has taken it as a sign that we should hold the next visit closer to home. I wrote my expenses in the notebook: the tickets, the cake, the records, and a bit for luck, totalling just under thirteen hundred kronor for four.

Holiday party on the harbour, planning and after-action notes. For the first time in five years the team party was going to be on the water rather than in a restaurant back parlour, and Blake and I were given the job because we had, in a weak moment, said we liked boats. The budget was set at sixty-five euros a head for around fifty guests, which is tight for December. We began by phoning three operators who run charter cruises among the islands, and in the end chose a family firm with a heated saloon, a small galley, and a captain called Mattias, who answered every question with a dry joke and a precise figure.

The route was a slow loop of about two hours through the archipelago, passing lit-up villas and the old fortress, with a mid-point stop at a jetty where the boat would hold for twenty minutes while people took photographs. Mattias warned us that December weather can be sharp, and that the outer deck would be closed if wind exceeded a certain speed. We asked for a weather backup, and he agreed that if the forecast was poor, the boat would stay inside the inner channel and sail a shorter loop. Blake wrote this into the contract himself, in a form the owner called touchingly formal, and we both signed it on the deck of the boat with a borrowed pen.

Catering was included in the price but customisable. We went for a winter buffet with hot mulled berry juice, smoked salmon, roast pork with apple, pickled beetroot, potato gratin, and a large tray of saffron buns for dessert. The boat's cook, a man named Osman with forearms like a blacksmith, offered to add vegetarian gratin and a chickpea dish for the ten guests who had asked. We agreed on a small bar with mulled wine and a few bottles of sparkling something, provided by the boat. Ana, who handles the finance side, asked for a written cap on drinks, and Mattias stared at her for a second before agreeing that a cap was fair.

Boarding was the part everyone forgot to ask about. The jetty was at the old customs quay, a ten-minute walk from the tram, and the boat departs at half past five sharp, since the tides in the inner channel do not wait and the light disappears by three thirty in December. We sent a message to everyone with the address, a map, and a photo of the boat, and repeated the departure time in bold. Joel, who is chronically late, received a personal call. We also arranged for two people to stand at the quay with hi-vis vests and a torch, greeting the guests and ticking names off on a clipboard while a light drizzle began to fall.

The evening started in the saloon, which was warm and slightly steamy, with fairy lights strung across the ceiling and a low murmur of conversation. Mattias gave a welcome speech and a safety briefing that was, to everyone's surprise, funny; he demonstrated the life jackets with a sock puppet. The boat cast off at exactly the right time, and the harbour lights began to slide by. Tove brought out a game she had prepared, a treasure hunt in which each team had to find six items on board, including a knot, a lifebuoy stamp, and a photograph of the chef. Teams raced around the deck in their coats, shrieking, and the winning group received a bottle of aquavit.

At the halfway jetty we all crowded onto the deck for group photographs, wrapped in scarves and blankets, with the fortress lit up behind us. A gust arrived and whipped a hat into the water; Mattias circled around, and one of the crew fished it out with a boathook to loud applause. The owner of the hat, Erik from the platform team, put it on again, wet, and declared it the finest moment of his year. Someone began singing a carol and soon the whole boat joined in, slightly off-key. It was too cold to stay long, and we went below to steaming plates and the good smell of roast pork.

Dinner was a triumph. People filled plates and carried them to benches and seats by the portholes, moving between groups and swapping tales. The salmon disappeared first, and the gratin followed closely. Osman received an ovation when he brought out the saffron buns, arranged in a crown shape with a candle in the middle. Ana did a quick head count and reported that no one was left out. Later, I saw Blake sitting alone at the stern, watching the wake, and joined him. He said he was thinking that the best team events are ones where nothing is required of anyone, and I agreed, though I also mentioned the treasure hunt.

We docked at eight thirty, and the crew helped everyone down the gangway, which was slippery with frost. A few of us stayed on the quay for a while, standing in the cold with paper cups of the last mulled drink and watching the boat's lights go out. Most of the team walked to the tram in twos and threes, arguing happily about the best moment. The only casualty was a scarf, left on a bench and later returned by Mattias in a padded envelope, together with a handwritten note reading better luck next year. Blake is displaying the note on the office noticeboard.

Cost review. The final cost was three thousand one hundred euros, about ten percent below budget because fewer guests took the second round of drinks and the weather backup was not needed. We paid Mattias by bank transfer within the week. Feedback so far has been warm. Two people would have liked more time on the outer deck, and one person says the treasure hunt was too competitive, which is the sort of thing said by people who lost. Everyone agreed that the heated saloon made all the difference. Blake will ask Mattias about the summer rates for a midsummer trip.

Handmade pasta, three experiments with flour ratios. My friend Ines, who grew up in Bologna and has opinions, said last month that I could not call myself a cook until I had made pasta by hand, without a machine, and she left a bag of doppio zero flour on my doorstep as if it were a dare. This Sunday I finally made time. The plan was to test three doughs side by side: one with whole eggs, one with only yolks, and one with a mix of flour and semolina and just water. I bought a dozen eggs from the farm stall near the station, which is run by a man who names his hens after opera singers and told me that the freckled one lays best on Wednesdays, a bag of coarse semolina, and a wooden rolling pin longer than my arm, which took up the whole diagonal of the rucksack.

I started with the classic. On a clean worktop I made a mound of a hundred grams of flour per egg, dug a well in the middle, cracked in two eggs, and began whisking them gently with a fork, pulling in flour from the walls of the well. The walls collapsed within a minute and egg ran across the counter towards the edge, which Ines had warned me would happen. I rescued the situation with a scraper and a good deal of noise. Once the mass came together, I kneaded it for ten minutes, pushing with the heel of my hand and folding it over, until the surface turned smooth and slightly tacky. It was a stiff dough, and my forearms ached.

Then it needed rest. The books all agree on this point and disagree on everything else, from the water in the well to the number of yolks, so I decided to trust Ines and ignore the internet. I wrapped the ball in cling film and, following Ines's instruction, left it on the counter at ambient temperature; the dough rested for forty minutes while I prepared the second batch and washed the fork. Resting lets the gluten relax, which makes the dough easier to roll thin. During the wait I read a page of a cookbook by an Italian grandmother, who insists that pasta must be rolled until you can read a newspaper through it, and I decided to aim for the sports section. Mira watched from the doorway, holding a mug, and asked whether it was normal for the flat to smell like a raw omelette.

The second dough used only yolks, six for two hundred grams of flour, and it behaved quite differently: it came together faster, was a bright saffron yellow, and felt silky. I kneaded it for eight minutes and noticed that it needed less flour on the surface. The third dough, semolina and water, was the humblest and the hardest. It had no fat from eggs, and it was crumbly until I added water, a teaspoon at a time. The resulting dough was pale, firm and slightly rough, more like modelling clay. I made small ear-shaped orecchiette from it by pressing a piece with my thumb against the board and dragging, and my first ten looked more like slippers.

Rolling was a workout. I dusted the surface, flattened the first dough with my palm, and started rolling from the centre outwards, giving the sheet a quarter turn after every stroke, as the grandmother recommended. The dough fought back, then relented. After fifteen minutes it was about a millimetre thick and the size of a small blanket. I folded it loosely into a flat roll and cut it into ribbons with a long knife, which turned out to be an unexpectedly meditative act. I unrolled the tagliatelle and hung them over the back of a chair to dry for a few minutes, where they draped like a very small orange curtain.

I cooked the three pastas separately in salted water, one after another, with a fresh pot for each to keep the tasting fair. The egg tagliatelle took only two minutes and came out tender, with a slight bite. The yolk one took the same time but was richer, almost custardy, and slid around the fork. The semolina ones needed nine minutes and had a firm chew, and the little ears carried sauce nicely. I dressed everything with butter, sage, and a scrape of hard grated ewe's-milk dairy from the back of the fridge, and served it on three plates for a blind tasting by Mira, who took it extremely seriously.

Her verdict was as follows. She ranked the yolk dough first, saying it tasted like something you would eat in a film, the whole-egg dough second for its balance, and the semolina third for its texture, which she called honest. She then admitted that she had guessed which was which by the colour, so the test was not entirely blind. I put the leftovers in a jar and sent a photo to Ines, who replied with a single thumbs-up followed a minute later by a paragraph of advice about resting time and salt in the water. I have chosen to interpret that as approval.

Notes for next time. Use slightly less flour when kneading the yolk dough. Keep the dough covered while I roll, since the edges dry out. Get a proper pastry scraper and a dusting sieve. Try adding a spoon of olive oil to the whole-egg batch. Make a filled pasta, perhaps ravioli with ricotta and lemon, when I have another free Sunday. Also, wipe the flour off the light switch, which I discovered only when the flat was dark. The whole afternoon cost about fifteen euros, mostly the rolling pin, and I think it was the best value of my month.

Library book sale, volunteer shift on the sorting crew. The public library holds its big annual sale in the last week of October, and this year I signed up for the Thursday sorting shift after seeing a poster on the noticeboard at the bus stop. The sale raises money for the children's section, and the volunteers are mostly retirees, a few students, and people like me who cannot resist a hall full of paper. I arrived at eight thirty at the back entrance with a sandwich and a pair of gloves, and was handed a lanyard and directed to the basement by a cheerful woman named Brita, who coordinates the volunteers with an air of quiet, unshakable authority.

The basement was a cave of cardboard. Boxes of donated books stood in stacks up to the ceiling pipes, along the walls, and in two long rows down the middle. Some had labels in careful handwriting, others were tied with string, and a few were simply grocery bags with a title poking out. Brita explained the system: fiction goes on the left, non-fiction on the right, children's books at the far end, and anything damaged, mouldy, or missing pages goes in a separate crate marked recycling. Valuable-looking items, such as first editions or signed copies, go to a special shelf for the librarian to evaluate. Everything else gets sorted by category and then alphabetically by author.

I was paired with Hakan, a retired ship's engineer who talks slowly and works quickly. He showed me how to check a book in fifteen seconds: sniff for damp, riffle the pages to shake out bookmarks and forgotten notes, look at the spine, and flip to the last page. Bookmarks, it turns out, are a fascinating archive. In the first box we found a bus ticket from 1987, three pressed flowers, a pharmacy receipt, and a note reading remember the milk. Hakan stacks these in a small biscuit tin for the library's display case, and told me that once he found a fifty-krona note, which he returned to the collection box.

By ten, a rhythm had developed. We would open a box, sort into piles, carry them to the correct section, and repeat. Behind us, the music of the stacker cart squeaked in a steady beat. At half past ten, there was a tea break in the staff lounge with a plate of cinnamon rolls, and the volunteers compared finds. A student named Josefin had discovered a first Swedish edition of a well-known children's novel, and Brita took it away with reverence. Another volunteer found a dictionary of nautical terms and pressed it into Hakan's hands, which pleased him greatly.

The system worked well until eleven, when a van arrived with an entire estate: the library of a professor who had died in the spring, shipped in forty boxes by his family. We formed a chain, passing boxes hand to hand up the stairs. Brita counted as they arrived, and when the last was placed in the corner, she consulted her clipboard and told us that there were 412 volumes in the cart just from the first delivery of the estate, which would need a day on its own. The books were mostly philosophy, linguistics, and mathematics, in five languages, with pencilled comments in tiny handwriting.

We spent the afternoon on the professor's books, which required more care. Many were old, with cloth covers, and had to be placed flat rather than stacked. Hakan handled them like small animals. Brita called over the librarian, a soft-spoken man named Anders, who evaluated the collection and decided that about sixty were worth listing separately for an online sale. The rest would go on the regular trestles in the main hall, at a flat price of ten crowns per paperback and twenty for hardcovers. There was some argument about whether a book with a signature in the margin counted as damaged, resolved by a majority vote of the tea-break committee.

At three we stopped for the day. My hands were black with dust and my back ached. I had sorted, by Hakan's tally, about six hundred books, or possibly seven, since we lost count after lunch. Brita thanked us each by name, which is more than most employers do. She gave everyone a free choice of one book from the special shelf, and I chose a small worn volume of poems with someone's name written in pencil on the flyleaf. The sale itself opens on Saturday morning and always has a queue around the block, and I promised to return then to help at the till.

On my way out, I stopped at the children's section to look at the crates. There were shelves of picture books with dinosaurs, moles, and enormous hungry caterpillars, sorted by a group of teenagers who had come with a school. One of them was reading aloud to another, doing all the voices. I thought about the money the sale would raise, which last year was enough to buy new beanbags and a set of large-print books. That seems like a good reason to spend a Thursday in a basement, and I will do it again.

Basic electronics evening course, weeks one to five. I signed up for this course at the technical college because after the repair cafe I realised that I understood far less about circuits than I pretended. It runs on Tuesday evenings for eight weeks in a lab with long benches, oscilloscopes, and a wall of small drawers labelled with resistor values. The teacher is an engineer called Viktoria, who works during the day on power supplies for medical equipment and has the patience of someone who spends her evenings explaining Ohm's law to adults. There are fourteen of us, ranging from a retired teacher to a nineteen-year-old with an enormous beard.

Week one began with a lecture on voltage, current, and resistance, illustrated by a bucket of water with a hose. Viktoria drew the analogy on the board: voltage is pressure, current is flow, and resistance is a narrow pipe. Then she gave us each a prototype board, a nine-volt battery, a few resistors, and an LED, and told us to light it up without frying it. Half the class did it instantly and the other half, including me, produced a small puff of smoke. Viktoria calmly explained that the LED needs a resistor in series to limit the current, and that I had just performed a very traditional experiment.

We learned to calculate the value of the resistor: the supply voltage minus the LED's forward voltage, divided by the desired current. With a nine-volt battery, a red LED at two volts and a target of ten milliamps, that gives seven hundred ohms, so we chose the nearest standard value. I wrote it in the margin of my notes and drew a star next to it. Viktoria taught us to read the coloured bands on resistors with a mnemonic that is not fit for repeating here, and I discovered that my colour vision is not perfect, which the retired teacher kindly resolved by lending me a magnifying glass and a multimeter.

Week two was on capacitors and the multimeter. We charged a capacitor through a resistor and watched the voltage climb on the meter, and then calculated the time constant and compared it with what we measured. My result was off by thirty percent, which Viktoria found fine for a first try and a cheap meter. She showed us how to test diodes and transistors with the meter, and then how to identify pins on an unmarked transistor by trial and error. The bearded nineteen-year-old announced that he was building a guitar pedal, and half the class immediately asked to join him. By the end of the evening we had a plan for a group project.

The third week was soldering, the lesson I had been waiting for. Viktoria gave a demonstration at the front, with a camera pointed at her hands and the image projected on the wall. She explained that a good joint is shiny, concave, and clean, and that a dull, lumpy one is a cold joint that will fail in a year. She warned us that lead-free solder needs a hotter tip than the leaded reel we were given. Everyone got a small board with a row of holes and a handful of components. I made eleven joints, seven of which were fine, and I was rather proud.

By the end of week three I had built a simple flashing LED circuit using a small timer chip, two resistors, a capacitor, and a battery clip. When I connected the battery, the LED began blinking at about once per second, and I actually cheered. The retired teacher next to me, who had built hers in half the time, gave me a thumbs-up and offered a tip about clipping the leads flush. I carried the little board home in a plastic box and put it on the shelf next to the toaster, and Mira looked at it with the wary respect one gives to a new pet.

Week four introduced transistors as switches and amplifiers. We built a light-sensitive switch which turned on an LED in the dark, using a photoresistor and a transistor, and this time we soldered it onto a strip board. Our instructor set the soldering iron to 350 degrees for the whole class, which she said suits leaded solder for beginners. Viktoria gave an excellent explanation of biasing that I understood while she was speaking and forgot on the bus. We talked about safety, including the rules on mains voltage: never work on live circuits, always use an isolation transformer, and treat any capacitor in a power supply as a live wire until proven otherwise. A story followed about a colleague who once forgot the last rule with a camera flash, and everyone winced in unison.

Week five was the first of the project sessions. Our group of four decided to build a small audio amplifier, and we spent the evening sketching the schematic, choosing components, and arguing about heatsinks. I was assigned to the power supply, which meant working out a fuse rating and a smoothing capacitor size. It was the first time I had designed anything with a clear purpose, and I found it very satisfying. The cost of parts is about thirty euros per group, paid to the school. I ordered a decent iron and a set of tweezers for home, and I am reading a book on analogue design that Viktoria recommended.

Customer appreciation dinner, planning and run of show. Every autumn we host a dinner for a dozen or so of our longest-standing customers, and this year Avery asked me to take it over from Sanna, who has moved to the partnerships team but left a folder of very useful notes. The dinner is not a sales event; the rule is that nobody pitches, and the only slides are on the walls in the form of photographs from projects we did together. The goal is to say thank you and to listen. I began by reading the last three years of feedback forms and found that the most repeated word was warm.

Choosing the restaurant took a week of calls. We wanted somewhere quiet enough to hear the person across from you, with good food and a private space that felt like a home rather than a function hall. Sanna's notes recommended a small place in the old town run by a married couple, where the husband cooks and the wife runs the floor. I visited on a Tuesday for lunch, ordered the set menu, and asked to see the back hall. It has a low vaulted ceiling, a fireplace that they light on request, and a long oak board that can be divided.

Next came the guest list, which I checked with Avery and the account managers. We invited representatives from twelve customers, leaving out two that have gone through a difficult patch and would need a separate conversation. For each guest I wrote a short profile with how long they had worked with us, the projects they cared about, and any dietary needs. This was Sanna's idea, and it turned out to be the most useful part: with the profiles printed on small cards, every host knew something personal about the person they would sit beside, such as that Henrik keeps bees and that Marianne had recently run her first half marathon.

Seating was planned like a chess problem. We put hosts and guests alternately, avoided placing anybody next to their biggest competitor, and kept the two most talkative guests apart. I pinned a paper layout to the wall by my desk and moved name cards with tape, and Avery came by and suggested swapping two people so that a customer who speaks little English sat next to one of our multilingual account managers. We also decided to have no formal speeches, only a short welcome by Avery before the first course, and a toast by one of the customers, who volunteered, at the end. That saves everyone from a long evening of sitting politely.

The menu was agreed with the chef in a phone call that lasted forty minutes and covered mostly onions. He proposed five small courses: a cold pumpkin soup with toasted seeds, a beetroot and goat curd starter, pan-fried char with a lemon butter sauce, slow-cooked venison with a juniper jus, and a baked apple with cinnamon ice cream to finish. A vegetarian alternative for the main was a wild-fungi and barley risotto that the chef said would be the best thing on the plate. For drinks we ordered a good white, a red from the same family estate, and a sparkling non-alcoholic option made from elderflower.

Gifts were another item on the checklist. Sanna had always given a small jar of honey from a local beekeeper, and I wanted to keep the tradition but with a twist. I visited the beekeeper and ordered fourteen jars with labels printed with the name of each customer and the year we started working together. She agreed to do it for a small fee, and the labels were drawn by hand by her daughter. Henrik will surely enjoy getting honey from a competitor, and I plan to ask him to rate it in the next feedback form. The jars are being packed in kraft-paper bags with a card.

On the day, I arrived at the restaurant at three to check the hall. The fireplace was lit, the board was laid with white cloths and small pine branches, and the name cards were in place. The private hall seats twenty-two, so with fourteen guests and eight hosts it was full without feeling crowded. The wife, Lisbet, showed me a bottle of aquavit she wanted to serve with the fish, an idea I loved. We rehearsed the flow: guests arrive at six, drinks in the front bar until half past, then move to the back hall for the first course. Avery arrived at five with the photographs, framed and fixed to the walls with picture hooks that we had brought in a pouch, and we spent half an hour adjusting them.

The evening was gentle and long. The first customers arrived a few minutes early, and by half past six everybody had a glass and a conversation. In the back hall, the fireplace crackled and the light was low. The soup was praised; the venison was declared perfect by a man who hunts. Around the third course someone asked whether they could see the photograph from the harbour project, and Avery took them round the walls telling stories, which drew a small crowd. Marianne raised a toast to the team, said something moving about trust, and told a joke about our support line that made the whole hall laugh.

Afterwards, we sat on for another hour over tea and the last of the ice cream, with hosts and guests mixed in the way we had hoped. Several customers said it was the best evening of the year, and two mentioned ideas for future collaboration, which I noted without acting on. Henrik took his honey jar out of the bag, looked at it for a long time, and said that he would compare it with his own. We finished at eleven, and I paid the bill of about two thousand six hundred euros, slightly over budget because of the extra wine, which Avery agreed was worth it.

Ice-cream experiments, a hot week in July. The heatwave arrived on Monday with thirty-three degrees, and by Tuesday evening the flat felt like a greenhouse. I had recently been given an ice-cream maker by Mira's brother Elias, who bought it in a moment of ambition and never used it, and it had been sitting unopened on top of the wardrobe. This seemed like the moment. I decided to make three flavours in one week: a classic vanilla custard base, a lemon sorbet, and something I called experimental, though at that point I did not know what.

The maker is a small machine with a bowl that you freeze overnight, a paddle, and a motor that sounds like a nervous bee. The instructions were terse. They said to chill the base thoroughly before churning, which I ignored on the first evening, and paid for. The vanilla base is a proper custard: milk, cream, egg yolks, sugar, and a vanilla pod split lengthwise with the seeds scraped out. I heated the milk and cream gently with the pod, whisked the yolks and sugar until pale, and combined the two in a slow stream, stirring all the time so the eggs did not scramble. Then I cooked it back to the point where it coated a spoon.

At this stage, the custard should be cooled fast, so I set the pan in a sink of cold water and stirred it until it stopped steaming. That took about twenty minutes and turned the flat into a sauna. I sieved it into a jug, covered it with cling film touching the surface to prevent a skin, and put it in the fridge to rest overnight. The recipe I followed was from an old cookbook by a woman in Bologna, and it used the ratio of one part cream to two parts milk, four yolks to half a litre, and a modest amount of sugar. According to her, sugar should be kept modest, since freezing dulls sweetness.

On Wednesday evening I poured the chilled custard into the frozen bowl and switched on the machine. For ten minutes, it whirred, and the mixture slowly thickened and expanded, first like a milkshake and then like soft-serve. I stood there with a spoon and did not blink. When it looked done, I scooped it into a container and put it in the freezer for two hours to firm up. I tasted a spoonful straight from the machine: it was cold, creamy, and lightly perfumed, and quite the best thing I had eaten all week. Mira, who had been reading in the next flat, appeared like a cat and asked what that smell was.

Thursday was the sorbet. I squeezed twelve lemons with more effort than expected, since my old juicer had cracked and I had to use a fork, and zested three of them into a syrup made from water and sugar. The mixture was intensely sour, and I added more syrup until it tasted like lemonade for grown-ups. A splash of vodka is supposed to keep it soft in the freezer; I added a spoonful. Churning took only fifteen minutes, and the result was pale, glistening, and slightly slushy. I froze it and, forty minutes later, scraped a scoop into a glass with a mint leaf. It was so refreshing that I had a second scoop before I remembered I was supposed to be taking notes.

The experimental flavour came from a jar of leftover tahini and half a bag of dates I found in the cupboard. I blended the dates with warm milk and a pinch of salt, whisked in the tahini, and added a spoonful of honey. The idea was a sesame date ice cream, a sort of halva in frozen form. It went into the maker on Friday evening. The texture was velvety and the flavour deep and nutty, with a faint bitterness that I liked. Elias, who came over with a bottle of cold cider, said it was the strangest and best thing he had tasted in a while, and requested a scoop for his lunchbox.

On Saturday, we held a tasting on the balcony, with friends and neighbours squeezed around a plastic crate. Dagny brought a bag of strawberries and declared them the natural companion to the vanilla. The sorbet went first, and the sesame date flavour was the most divisive; three people loved it, two politely finished it, and the child from downstairs said it tasted like a biscuit that had been in a fight. The vanilla remained the favourite. The base needed two hundred grams of sugar for a full litre, and Dagny, who has a sweet tooth, claimed it could take fifty more. I photographed the plates and noticed that everything melted in about four minutes, which for once seemed like a fair reward for effort.

Lessons from the week. Chill the base fully, at least eight hours, or the maker struggles. Freeze the bowl for a full day, not overnight, since the temperature in the freezer drifted up during the heatwave. Do not overfill; the mixture expands by about half. Keep the container in the coldest part of the freezer, and eat it within a week or it turns icy. Tahini and dates were a good combination, and I might try miso and caramel next. Total cost of the week's experiments: about twenty-five euros. Elias has generously agreed that the machine now lives at our flat.

Sauna and cold plunge weekend at the lakeside retreat. Mira gave me a voucher for my birthday: two nights at a small retreat two hours north of the city, with a wood-fired sauna, a jetty, and a group of guests who apparently sit in silence. The invitation said to bring wool socks, a book, and nothing that needs charging. I said I could manage that for exactly one afternoon. We drove up on Friday after work, through a landscape of long thin lakes and red farmhouses, and arrived at about seven, just as the light was turning blue. The host, a woman named Gerd with a grey braid and the calm of someone who has never checked a phone at dinner, showed us to a cabin with two beds and a stove.

Dinner was in a long, low hall with a woodstove in the corner, and eleven other guests sat at a communal board. We were served barley soup with dill, dark rye crisps, and a dish of pickled cucumber, followed by baked apples. Nobody spoke much, but it was not awkward; the silence was full of small sounds of spoons and crackling wood. After dinner, Gerd explained the house rules, which were few: no shoes indoors, quiet after nine, and everyone must try the sauna at least once, without a swimsuit if they feel easy about it and with one if they do not. I wrapped myself in a heavy blanket and read forty pages of a novel before falling asleep.

Saturday began with a walk through the forest to a viewpoint above the lake. Gerd led, and we followed in single file, boots squelching on wet moss, and she stopped every few minutes to show us something: a nest of wood ants, a fallen birch with a stripe of bright orange fungus, an elk track in the mud. At the viewpoint the mist lay in the valleys like milk in a saucer, and the sun climbed slowly. We stood there for ten minutes and nobody took a photograph. That may have been the point. On the way down I got chatting with a man who taught physics and had come alone to finish writing a textbook.

Gerd said the fire had been lit at dawn by a neighbour's son, a shy teenager who refused all thanks and disappeared into the woodshed with a paperback. The sauna was heated from noon, and by three, when we went down, it had reached eighty-five degrees. It was a small log building next to the water, with a stone stove, two tiers of benches, and a low ceiling that made everyone hunch. Gerd threw a ladle of water on the stones and the heat crashed down on us like a wave. For the first five minutes it was intolerable, then oddly pleasant, then boring, and finally deeply relaxing. Mira, who is more heat-resistant than I am, stayed for twenty minutes and left with a glow. I sat on the lower bench and tried to think of nothing, without much success. Steam curled off my shoulders, and a spider on the rafter watched me with what I took to be professional interest.

Then came the plunge. A ladder led from the jetty into the lake, where a section had been cleared of ice a week earlier, and Gerd had hung a small wooden sign beside it reading think twice. She told us to go in slowly, to exhale as we entered, and to stay no longer than a minute. I stood on the ladder for a full thirty seconds arguing with myself. Then I went in up to my neck, gasped, laughed, and shouted something incoherent. My skin tingled like a thousand small pins, and when I climbed out I felt as light as a cork.

On the slate by the ladder Gerd had chalked the morning's lake reading, which was four degrees. The afternoon was spent recovering on wooden loungers wrapped in blankets, drinking hot blackcurrant juice, and staring at the lake. The plunge leaves a peculiar glow, a warm hum that lasts for hours. Mira went in three times and each time came out looking more pleased. We talked about how we sometimes forget to do nothing on purpose, and decided that we should build one unplanned hour into every week. Gerd came by with a plate of cinnamon buns, and we ate them silently, looking at a bird that hopped along the jetty. It was the best day in a long time, and I hardly said a word.

Dinner on the second night was more animated. A few guests had begun to speak, and the man who writes physics textbooks told a long story about a train that ran on the wrong side of the tracks. Gerd served a stew of roots, greens and venison, and someone brought out a bottle of homemade rowan berry liqueur, which tasted of medicine and sunshine. After the meal, we went out onto the jetty to look at the stars. There were no lights for miles, and the sky was scattered with them like spilled salt. We lay on our backs on the planks, wrapped in every blanket we could find, and counted satellites.

We left on Sunday after breakfast, with slightly wobbly legs and a heavy calm. Gerd hugged each of us at the door, and gave us a jar of blackcurrant jam and a card with the address of the retreat. On the drive home, we hardly spoke for the first hour. I noticed I had been holding the wheel more gently than usual. When we reached the city, the noise struck me like a slap. I resolved to go again in the spring, when the ice is gone and the plunge will be far warmer, and to leave my phone in the glove box for a whole weekend.

Tree-planting day with the city parks department, team report. The city runs a spring programme in which businesses adopt a patch of degraded land and plant native trees, and when the invitation reached Avery's inbox she forwarded it to me with the words your kind of thing. Nine of us signed up for a Saturday morning at a strip of former farmland beside the river on the eastern edge of town. The site was to become a small woodland, part of a larger green belt, and the parks department provided saplings, tools, gloves and two rangers, in exchange for a promise of four hours of work and a photograph for their annual report.

We met at the tram terminus at seven forty and walked twenty minutes along a farm track, the grass grey with dew. The site itself was a big open field, gently sloping, with a few old fence posts and a heap of stones where a barn once stood. A ranger named Ylva was waiting with a trailer of equipment, wearing a green fleece with a badge and the alert calm of someone who has organised a hundred of these. She gave us a short talk: the field had been ploughed for eighty years and its soil was compacted, so the trees needed a proper start, with space for their roots and a ring of mulch.

The species list was chosen for the local soil: oak, hazel, rowan, wild cherry, alder near the water, and small shrubs like guelder rose and hawthorn to feed the birds. Ylva explained that a good young woodland is a mix, not a plantation, and that the saplings would be planted in loose groups rather than in rows, so it would look natural in ten years. Each of us was handed a spade, a bucket, and a pair of stout gloves, and paired with a colleague. I teamed up with Joel, who had never dug anything larger than a flower pot but showed the enthusiasm of a convert.

The technique was demonstrated on the first sapling. You cut a square of turf, set it aside grass-side down, dig a hole twice as wide as the roots, loosen the soil at the bottom, and set the sapling so that the root collar sits at ground level. Then you fill in, firm the soil with your heel, water it with a bucket from the ditch, and place a plastic guard around the stem to protect it from voles and deer. Ylva insisted that we should not compress the earth too tightly or leave any air pockets, and that we should give each sapling a gentle tug at the end to test it.

By nine we had found a rhythm. Tove and Ana handled the alders near the ditch, where the ground was soft, and reported that their boots had been sucked off twice. Blake and I worked along the slope with the oaks, and Joel dug so vigorously that he unearthed a rusty horseshoe, which he presented to Ylva with a flourish. She said it was the seventh she had found on this site, and that they were collecting them for a display at the park office. At half past nine there was a break with flasks of tea and sweet buns, which some of us ate sitting on the heap of barn stones.

The morning warmed up quickly. Jackets were shed and sleeves rolled, and the row of orange guards spread across the hillside like small tents. Every so often a cheer went up when a group finished a patch. Ana discovered that she could plant twice as fast if she stood the sapling upright with one hand and shovelled with the other, and started a race. Ylva took a photo of the whole team in a line, holding spades like a very cheerful army. Overhead, a pair of buzzards circled, and a lark rose from the grass, singing so hard that we stopped to listen for a minute.

There was a small crisis around eleven when the water ran short. The ditch had dried up along one section, and the trailer's tank was empty. Ylva sent two of us to fetch more from a stand pipe by the road, a walk of half a kilometre with a wheelbarrow of buckets. Blake volunteered and returned an hour later with a face redder than the buckets, having, in his words, discovered that water is heavy. In the meantime we mulched the saplings with wood chips from a pile by the gate, which shielded the roots and made the whole hillside smell like a sawmill.

At twelve, we assembled at the trailer for a rest and a count. There was a modest ceremony: Ylva thanked us and explained that our patch would be recorded on a map with the company's name, so that in years to come, a visitor could look it up. She checked the tally sheet against the piles of empty pots. The count came to well above the forty saplings per person that the programme expects, she said. We stood a little straighter. Then she passed round a box of small metal badges shaped like a leaf, one for each of us, and Tove pinned hers to her jacket.

A picnic lunch was laid out on the tailgate of a van, and the whole team ate it sitting on the grass, feeling smug and hungry. Ana had brought a large pot of lentil soup, and Tove a box of ginger biscuits. Ylva joined us for a while and told us how the earlier plantings on the site were doing: the first oaks had reached shoulder height in five years, and last summer a pair of nightingales had nested in the hawthorn. She invited us to return in the autumn for the second phase and to bring anyone who wanted to come. I said we would bring the whole department, and Joel said we should bring cake.

Follow-up items. In the final sweep Blake counted three hundred and sixty saplings, which is the number I will quote in the report. I will send the photograph and a short paragraph to the parks department by Tuesday, as promised. Avery will book the volunteering hours in the system so the day counts towards the annual target. We will ask facilities whether the horseshoe can be displayed in the lobby, or at least photographed. Nine sore backs, nine cheerful faces, and a small woodland; I think that is a good exchange. Blake has suggested that we set up a small fund to adopt a permanent patch of woodland each year, and I have put it on the agenda for the next planning meeting.

Open-water swimming, the first club session of the season. I have swum lengths in a pool for years, but I have never been brave enough for the sea, until a colleague of Mira's mentioned that the local club runs beginner sessions on Thursday evenings from May at a bay north of the city, with wetsuits to borrow. I signed up on a whim and paid a membership fee of two hundred and fifty crowns, which includes insurance and a bright orange swim cap. The email from the coordinator, a woman called Elsa, said to arrive at six with a towel, a tow float, and a sense of adventure. I already owned the towel.

The bay is a crescent of grey pebbles with a small wooden jetty and a hut where the club keeps its floats. It was a cool evening, eleven degrees in the air, with a light wind ruffling the surface, and about thirty people milling around in various stages of undress. Elsa gathered the newcomers, eight of us, in a semicircle on the stones and gave a safety briefing that lasted ten minutes and covered everything: cold shock, currents, cramps, how to signal for help, and the rule that nobody swims alone. She checked our floats and made us practise blowing the whistle attached to the strap. I felt slightly foolish, then appreciative, particularly when a girl of about twelve blew hers with professional flair and looked at me as if I were the one who needed the lesson.

The next step was the wetsuit. The club has a rack of them in assorted sizes, smelling faintly of the sea and old rubber. I tried three before finding one that fitted, and the process involved a lot of hopping, tugging and mutual assistance, plus a small tub of talc that Elsa swears is the secret to wrestling the sleeves over wet forearms and that turned my hands and half the jetty white. A retired dentist named Kjell, who has swum here for twenty years and wears only trunks, watched with an expression of gentle amusement. He explained that a wetsuit traps a thin layer of water against the skin, which the body warms, and that the sensation of the first minute is the price of entry. I zipped up, pulled on my cap and goggles, and shuffled to the edge of the water like a penguin.

Entering slowly is the golden rule. We waded in to the knees, then the waist, splashing our faces and wrists to let the body adjust. The water was nine degrees, which is a shock even through neoprene, and my chest felt as if a hand were squeezing it. Elsa told us to breathe out slowly and focus on the exhale, and after a minute the sensation eased. We spent five minutes just floating and getting used to it, looking at the low hills in the distance. A pair of eider ducks paddled by, entirely uninterested. Someone laughed with pure nerves and it turned into a real laugh. Elsa timed us by a big watch on her wrist and called us out after exactly five minutes, leaving us tingling and grinning like schoolchildren after a snowball fight.

Then we swam. Elsa split us into pairs and set a short loop between the jetty and a yellow buoy about a hundred and fifty metres away. My breathing was ragged at first, and I lifted my head every third stroke to check that I was heading in the right direction, which ruined my rhythm. Kjell swam alongside me for the first stretch, calling out advice in a calm voice: look at the horizon, not the water, bend your elbow, relax your shoulders. By the time I reached the buoy I had settled into a steady rhythm, and I touched it with a sense of triumph that I could not have explained to anyone who had not tried.

The swim back was easier. The sun had begun to sink and the water glowed with a faint pink, and the wake of my strokes made small gold ripples. I felt oddly weightless, as if the sea were carrying me, and briefly forgot every email I owed. I lost track of time and had to be reminded by a whistle. Back at the shore, I stumbled out with wobbly legs and the peculiar tingling in my hands that Elsa calls the afterdrop, a delayed chill that arrives ten minutes after you leave the water. She insisted on a strict routine: get dry, get dressed from the top down, and eat something sweet.

Sitting on the jetty wrapped in a huge dry robe borrowed from the club cupboard, with my feet swinging above the water, I drank hot chocolate from a flask that Elsa passed around. The group swapped stories about their first swims: one woman had come after a health scare, a man after a divorce, and a young couple for a dare. Kjell gave a talk about tides and the local hazards, including a strong current around the point and a patch of weed that can snag ankles. He told us that the club runs longer swims through the summer, culminating in a crossing of the bay. The full route is a rectangle marked with buoys, and the buoy line sat at 1.5 kilometres for the standard distance.

Elsa handed out logbooks for the season so that each swimmer can record temperature, distance, and how they felt. I wrote my first entry: nine degrees, one hundred and fifty metres, elated. There was a checklist at the back with milestones, such as first swim without a wetsuit, first kilometre, and first swim in the rain. I marked none of them and put a small star next to the first. Kjell told me I was welcome to join the Sunday dawn swim, where a group goes out before breakfast, and I said I would think about it, which we both understood to mean yes.

On the way home I bought a proper woollen hat, two pairs of neoprene gloves and a thermometer for the jetty, which I intend to donate to the club. My skin glowed for hours, and I slept like a stone. Mira asked in the morning whether I had been abducted by a friendly octopus, because I was humming. I have been telling everyone about it, including the man at the bakery. The next session is in a week, and this time I want to swim to the buoy and back without stopping, and to keep my head down long enough to see the seabed.

Pickling and preserving weekend, beets, cucumbers and plums. When my neighbour Dagny announced that her allotment had produced more cucumbers than a small army could eat, I said I would take a crate, and by Saturday morning I was staring at forty of them on my hallway floor and a stack of borrowed jars in the corner. Mira, who has watched me before, made a tactful retreat to her sister's and left a note saying good luck. I decided to make it a proper preserving weekend, with three recipes: dill pickles, spiced beetroot, and plums in syrup. I made a schedule on the back of an envelope, with times, amounts and a column for worries.

First I sterilised the jars. I washed forty of them with hot soapy water, rinsed them, and put them on baking trays in the oven at a hundred and thirty degrees for twenty minutes, along with the lids in a pan of simmering water. The flat filled with a steamy, sweet-sour smell. While they cooled, I scrubbed the cucumbers under the tap with a brush, cut off the blossom ends, since they contain an enzyme that softens the pickles, and sorted them by size. The small ones would go in whole, the medium ones in spears, and the fat ones into slices for burgers. It took an hour, longer than the schedule allowed, and gave me a new respect for anyone who does this for a living. Halfway through, Dagny's husband leaned over the balcony rail and shouted down that his grandmother always dropped an oak leaf into each jar to keep the pickles crisp, and that she had never once been wrong about anything, so I fetched a leaf from the courtyard tree and tucked a few in, purely for luck.

The brine was simple, and I wrote the proportions on a card taped to the cupboard so I would not have to trust my memory, which by then had begun to smell of vinegar. For the cucumbers I used a litre of water, half a litre of vinegar, fifty grams of salt, and a spoonful of sugar, with a handful of black peppercorns, mustard seeds, and bay leaves in each jar, plus a large sprig of dill and two cloves of garlic. I packed the cucumbers tightly, standing them upright like soldiers, and poured the hot brine over them, leaving a centimetre of headspace. Then I tapped each jar on the counter to release air bubbles and wiped the rims. I put on the lids, tightened them fingertip-tight, and lowered the jars into a large pot of simmering water for a ten-minute bath.

While the first batch was processing, I moved on to the beetroot. I had bought four kilos at the market on Friday, dark and muddy, and I boiled them in their skins until a knife slid in easily, about forty-five minutes. I let them cool, slipped off the skins under running water, and my hands turned the colour of a bruise. Then I sliced them and, wearing rubber gloves this time, packed them into jars with red onion rings, cloves, and cinnamon sticks, and poured over a sweeter brine with more sugar and a little orange peel. The galley looked like the scene of a very tidy crime, and Dagny, who dropped by, said it smelled like Christmas.

I put up the cucumber jars to cool on a towel by the balcony door and listened for the pop of each lid as the vacuum seal formed. It is a satisfying little sound, like a very small applause. By early evening, twelve jars stood in a row, glinting in the low sun, and the first lid pinged when I was making tea. I was too tired to start on the plums, so I ate supper standing up, with the last cucumber sliced thinly over rice, and went to bed with sore feet, a pleasant ache across the shoulders from all the lifting and stirring, and a strong sense of accomplishment. My hands smelled of dill for a day and a half, and the smell followed me to the bus on Monday.

Sunday was plum day. Dagny had also given me three kilos of small yellow plums from her tree, dusky and dimpled and slightly overripe, with wasps hovering. I halved them, removed the stones, and packed them into jars with a stick of cinnamon and a star anise, then poured over a hot syrup of sugar, water and a splash of vanilla. The trick is to leave the fruit slightly firm, since it will soften in the jar. I processed them for twenty minutes and left them to cool. They came out a glowing amber, with the pale halves floating like small golden moons. A wasp had drowned in the syrup of the first jar, which I fished out and then re-processed with great embarrassment. I ate the leftovers from the pan with a spoon and considered it quality control.

The final count came on Sunday evening. I lined everything up on the shelves in the cool cupboard under the stairs and counted: twelve jars of dill pickles, nine of beetroot, and eleven of plums, thirty-two in total, with a few odd ones left over for immediate use. The jars held eleven litres in all, by my reckoning, which is more than I will ever eat, and I have already promised jars to Dagny, Mira's sister, my colleague Tuva, and the neighbour with the dog. I labelled each with masking tape.

Costs and lessons. Vinegar, sugar, spices and the beetroot came to about forty euros, and the jars were mostly borrowed or reused. Next time I will use fewer garlic cloves, since two per jar overpowers the dill, and try a hot pepper in some jars. Cool the jars more slowly to avoid cracking; two of them broke in the bath, which was a sticky lesson. I also need to buy a proper jar lifter, because tongs are dangerous.

The real test comes in a month, when the pickles have matured. The recipe says to wait four weeks before opening, which will be a trial for Mira, who has been eyeing the first jar. In the meantime, I have made a list of what to eat with them: cold potato salad, sausage rolls, a ham sandwich if I am feeling nostalgic, and the beetroot with goat curd and walnuts. If all goes well I might make this an annual tradition and invite Dagny to bring her surplus before she has to ask.
